Wraps launchdarkly-js-client-sdk (created and initialized by the app).

import * as LDClient from "launchdarkly-js-client-sdk";
import { FeatureFlagsProvider, createLaunchDarklyFeatureFlagsAdapter } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const client = LDClient.initialize(import.meta.env.VITE_LD_CLIENT_ID, {
    kind: "user",
    key: userId,
});
await client.waitUntilReady();

const adapter = createLaunchDarklyFeatureFlagsAdapter({ client });

<FeatureFlagsProvider adapter={adapter}>{children}</FeatureFlagsProvider>;

Mapping:

FeatureFlagsAdapter LDClient isEnabled(key, default) client.variation(key, default) === true get(key, default) client.variation(key, default) onChange(listener) client.on("change", listener) + client.off on cleanup

The injection pattern is identical to Telemetry's

The GrowthBookLike / LDClientLike types declare only the subset used — handy for mocking in tests. For any new provider (Unleash, Split, Cloudflare), the same pattern applies: caller injects the instance, adapter exposes <X>Like, direct stateless mapping. See Telemetry — it's the same recipe.

docs.title: Custom adapter
docs.text:
The interface is tiny — ~20 lines for any SDK:

import type { FeatureFlagsAdapter } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import unleash from "unleash-proxy-client";

export const unleashAdapter: FeatureFlagsAdapter = {
  isEnabled: (key, defaultValue = false) => unleash.isEnabled(key) ?? defaultValue,
  get: (key, defaultValue) => unleash.getVariant(key)?.payload?.value ?? defaultValue,
  onChange: (listener) => {
    unleash.on("update", listener);
    return () => unleash.off("update", listener);
  },
};

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
• Always a safe default — useFlagValue<number>("k", 10). If the provider is offline or still loading, you get the fallback.
  • Don't use it for UI state — only for rollouts (new-checkout) and kill-switches (disable_payments). UI state goes to Zustand/local state.
  • It doesn't cache the type — useFlagValue<number>("k") returns the raw declared value; do the narrowing/coercion at the call site when needed.
  • Track exposures — combine with Telemetry to record who saw which variant: telemetry?.track({ name: "flag.exposure", properties: { flag, variant } }).

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Program against FeatureFlagsAdapter (isEnabled / get / onChange?) — switching provider is trivial.
  • <FeatureFlagsProvider> is mandatory — the hooks throw without it (unlike useTelemetry).
  • useFeatureFlag → boolean; useFlagValue<T> → typed value; both re-render via onChange.
  • Adapters inject the already-configured instance ({ growthbook }, { client }) — never a peer dep.
  • Always pass a safe default; flags are for rollouts and kill-switches, not UI state.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Telemetry — track flag exposures; adapters follow the exact same injection pattern

docs.title: Forms BR — masks, validators, ViaCEP
docs.text:
Everything Brazilian apps use daily: really validate CPF/CNPJ, mask input as the user types, and fill an address from the ZIP code (CEP). Pairs with zod + react-hook-form or a manual controlled form.

Why not just check the length?

"It has 11 digits" does not mean the CPF exists. Brazilian documents carry check digits computed from the others — that is how the tax-authority backend rejects mistyped numbers. Checking only the length lets 123.456.789-00 and any repeated sequence through. The functions below run the full algorithm.

Section br-forms of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: Validators
docs.text:
import { validateCPF, validateCNPJ } from "tempest-react-sdk";

validateCPF("529.982.247-25"); // true
validateCPF("111.111.111-11"); // false (rejects all-equal)
validateCPF("12345678900"); // false (invalid check digit)
validateCNPJ("11.222.333/0001-81"); // true

Full algorithm (check digits), not just "11 digits". Accepts a string with or without a mask.

Why reject repeated digits

111.111.111-11, 000.000.000-00, etc. pass the check-digit math by mathematical coincidence — the raw algorithm would accept them. Since none of those is a real document, both validators have an explicit short-circuit (/^(\d)\1+$/) that rejects any value with all-equal digits before computing.

They are pure — combine freely

validateCPF / validateCNPJ take a string and return a boolean, with no state and no React. Use them directly in an onBlur, in a zod .refine() (see the end of the page), or on the server — it is the same code on both sides.

docs.title: Masked inputs
Optional field: nullable
docs.text:
With value: number the field is never empty: clearing it goes back to R$ 0,00, the placeholder disappears and "not informed" becomes zero. For an optional field (price per litre, extra fee), pass nullable: value then accepts null, an empty field shows the placeholder, and deleting every digit (or typing only zeros) calls onChange(null).

import { useState } from "react";
import { MoneyInput } from "tempest-react-sdk";

function OptionalPriceExample() {
  const [cents, setCents] = useState<number | null>(null);
  return (
    <MoneyInput
      nullable
      value={cents}
      onChange={setCents}
      label="Price per litre"
      placeholder="R$ 0,00"
      maxCents={99_999}
    />
  );
}

maxCents is the ceiling in cents: a digit that would pass it is ignored (the amount stays where it was) instead of becoming a number nobody typed. Default: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.

Why nullable is a prop, not just value: number | null

The type of onChange is what your setState has to match. Without nullable the contract is the old one — onChange(cents: number), clearing reports 0 — and a useState(0) keeps compiling without ever receiving null. With nullable it is onChange(cents: number | null).

docs.title: Uncontrolled forms: name
docs.text:
The visible text is formatted (R$ 12,34), so FormData read from it is useless to a backend. With name, MoneyInput renders an <input type="hidden"> holding the raw amount; the visible field carries no name. nameFormat picks the format: "cents" (default, "1234") or "decimal" (major unit with a dot, "12.34"). Empty becomes ""; a disabled field stays out of FormData, like the visible one.

import { useState } from "react";
import type { FormEvent } from "react";
import { MoneyInput } from "tempest-react-sdk";

function StopForm() {
  const [cents, setCents] = useState<number | null>(null);

  function submit(event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>): void {
    event.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
    console.log(data.get("price")); // "12.34" — or "" when empty
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={submit}>
      <MoneyInput nullable value={cents} onChange={setCents} name="price" nameFormat="decimal" label="Price" />
      <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}

docs.title: Frameless: useMoneyMask
docs.text:
MoneyInput is the SDK's <Input> (label, border, error). When the app's field already has its own box with an icon, spread the mask straight on your <input>: useMoneyMask({ value, onChange, maxCents }) returns { type, inputMode, value, onChange, onFocus, onClick, onSelect }, with value: number | null and onChange(cents: number | null). It is exactly what MoneyInput uses underneath.

import { useState } from "react";
import { useMoneyMask } from "tempest-react-sdk";

function BankStyleField() {
  const [cents, setCents] = useState<number | null>(null);
  const mask = useMoneyMask({ value: cents, onChange: setCents, maxCents: 1_000_000 });
  return (
    <label className="my-field">
      <span aria-hidden="true">💰</span>
      <input {...mask} aria-label="Amount" placeholder="R$ 0,00" />
      <input type="hidden" name="amount" value={cents ?? ""} />
    </label>
  );
}

Caret always at the end

Click, arrow keys and focus put the caret back at the end of the text. Without it, measured in Chromium against 0.91.0: with R$ 12,34 and the caret after the 1, typing 5 gave R$ 152,34 (instead of R$ 123,45) and Backspace deleted the 1, giving R$ 52,34. A selection (select all and paste, or delete) still works — it replaces the whole amount.

The digit-reading rule is pure and exported, so the server or a zod schema can run the same code: centsFromDigits(text, maxCents?) → cents or null.

import { centsFromDigits } from "tempest-react-sdk";

centsFromDigits("R$ 1.234,56 (à vista)"); // 123456
centsFromDigits("R$ 0,00");               // null
centsFromDigits("99999", 10_000);         // 9999

docs.title: unmask — digits only
docs.text:
import { unmask } from "tempest-react-sdk";

unmask("529.982.247-25"); // "52998224725"

Use it before sending to the backend, which usually expects raw digits. formatCEP and formatCNPJ are also exported if you need to mask a string outside a controlled input.

docs.title: Mobile-only field — formatPhone({ mobile: true })
docs.text:
By default the grouping is decided by length, which is right for a field that takes both landlines and mobiles. In a mobile-only field it is wrong as you type: anything up to ten digits reads as a landline and the hyphen lands after the fourth subscriber digit.

import { formatPhone } from "tempest-react-sdk";

formatPhone("1191234");                      // "(11) 9123-4"     ← hyphen too early
formatPhone("1191234", { mobile: true });    // "(11) 91234"      ← separator in place
formatPhone("1112345678", { mobile: true }); // "(11) 91234-5678" ← inserts the 9

Both agree once all 11 digits are in; the difference shows while typing, where the default's hyphen jumps backwards as the eleventh digit lands. mobile also inserts the mandatory 9, so a ten-digit number is corrected rather than masked as a landline.

docs.title: ViaCEP
docs.text:
useViaCEP queries the public ViaCEP service and returns the address fields — no backend of your own.

import { useState } from "react";
import { CEPInput, Input, useViaCEP } from "tempest-react-sdk";

function AddressForm() {
  const [cep, setCep] = useState("");
  const [street, setStreet] = useState("");
  const [city, setCity] = useState("");
  const [uf, setUf] = useState("");
  const viacep = useViaCEP();

  async function handleLookup() {
    const result = await viacep.lookup(cep);
    if (result) {
      setStreet(result.logradouro);
      setCity(result.localidade);
      setUf(result.uf);
    }
  }

  return (
    <>
      <CEPInput value={cep} onChange={setCep} onBlur={handleLookup} label="ZIP" />
      {viacep.loading && <span>Searching…</span>}
      {viacep.error && <span role="alert">{viacep.error}</span>}
      <Input value={street} onChange={(e) => setStreet(e.target.value)} label="Street" />
      <Input value={city} onChange={(e) => setCity(e.target.value)} label="City" />
      <Input value={uf} onChange={(e) => setUf(e.target.value)} label="State" />
    </>
  );
}

No backend — uses https://viacep.com.br/ws/<cep>/json/.

Two kinds of failure

viacep.error is set both for an invalid format (≠ 8 digits, no network call) and for a not-found CEP (the API replied { erro: true }). In both cases lookup resolves with null — always check the return value before using it.

Fire on onBlur, not on every keystroke

lookup makes an HTTP request. Call it when the field loses focus (onBlur) or once the 8 digits are complete — not on every keystroke, to avoid hammering the public service.

docs.title: Combining with react-hook-form
docs.text:
Because the validators are pure functions, they drop straight into a zod .refine(), and the masked input is wired with a <Controller> (or with the SDK's <FormField>, which removes the boilerplate):

import { Controller, useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { CPFInput, validateCPF, zodResolver } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  cpf: z.string().refine(validateCPF, "Invalid CPF"),
});

function CPFField() {
  const form = useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema), defaultValues: { cpf: "" } });
  return (
    <Controller
      control={form.control}
      name="cpf"
      render={({ field, fieldState }) => (
        <CPFInput
          value={field.value ?? ""}
          onChange={field.onChange}
          onBlur={field.onBlur}
          error={fieldState.error?.message}
          label="CPF"
        />
      )}
    />
  );
}

Less boilerplate with FormField

The <Controller> above can collapse to one line with the SDK's <FormField> inside a <FormProvider>: <FormField name="cpf" label="CPF"><CPFInput /></FormField>. See the end-to-end example.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• validateCPF / validateCNPJ run the full check-digit algorithm and reject repeated sequences — pure functions reusable on client and server.
  • The masked inputs are controlled and call onChange(string) (not an event); MoneyInput works in integer cents.
  • unmask strips the mask before sending to the backend.
  • useViaCEP resolves null on any failure (invalid format or non-existent CEP) — always check the return; fire on onBlur.
  • Plug the validators into zod via .refine() and wire the inputs with <Controller> or <FormField>.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Forms (zod) — useZodForm, FormField, layout, and the end-to-end example
  • HTTP — parseResponse validates the API response
  • Hooks — useDebounce to defer the CEP lookup while typing

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Forms almost always stall on two problems that have nothing to do with each other: how the fields lay out on screen and how the values are validated. The SDK splits those two axes on purpose — you can adopt one without the other.

  1. Layout — Form / FormSection / FormRow / FormActions handle how fields are arranged on screen.
  2. Validation — validateForm / zodResolver / useZodForm handle validating values with zod.

Use them together or separately — the Form component is not coupled to any form library.

Why zod as the source of truth?

Instead of declaring the form's type and then writing validation rules that can drift from it, you write a single zod schema and the TypeScript type is inferred with z.infer. Schema and type never go out of sync, and the same rule runs on the client (validateForm/zodResolver) and on the server.

docs.title: Layout — Form + subcomponents
docs.text:
Replaces the <form><Stack> boilerplate pattern when you want a layout-opinionated wrapper.

import { Form, FormSection, FormRow, FormActions, Input, Select, Button } from "tempest-react-sdk";

Where the examples' form comes from

The snippets in this section are about layout, so they show the JSX only. The form you see in them (form.register, form.handleSubmit, form.formState) is react-hook-form's return value, created once at the top of the component:

const form = useZodForm(schema, { defaultValues: { name: "", email: "" } });

The first example below — Stacked — is complete, schema, imports and component included. See useZodForm for the hook and End-to-end example for a full form. If you already call useForm directly, const form = useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) }) works just as well — Form is not coupled to any form library.

docs.title: layout variants
docs.text:
layout Behavior "stack" (default) — flex column, gap = gap (default 4 → 16px). "inline" Flex row with flex-wrap: wrap + align-items: flex-end. Filter bars, short login, etc. "grid" display: grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(columns, minmax(0, 1fr)).

columns accepts a number (repeat(N, minmax(0, 1fr))) or a string ("2fr 1fr", "min-content auto").

gap accepts a number (4px scale: 2 → 8px, 4 → 16px) or a string (any CSS length: "1.5rem", "20px"). The number is a step, not pixels: gap={24} gives 96px, and in development a number above 12 warns once in the console — see gap={24} is not 24px.

docs.title: Stacked
docs.text:
The default: one column, one field per row. This example is complete — copy, paste and run.

import { Form, FormActions, Input, Button, useZodForm } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { z } from "zod";

const signupSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(2, "Enter your name"),
  email: z.string().email("Invalid email"),
  password: z.string().min(8, "At least 8 characters"),
});

type SignupValues = z.infer<typeof signupSchema>;

export function SignupForm() {
  const form = useZodForm(signupSchema, {
    defaultValues: { name: "", email: "", password: "" },
  });

  const onSubmit = async (values: SignupValues) => {
    await api.post("/signup", values);
  };

  return (
    <Form layout="stack" gap={4} onSubmit={form.handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      <Input label="Name" {...form.register("name")} error={form.formState.errors.name?.message} />
      <Input
        label="Email"
        type="email"
        {...form.register("email")}
        error={form.formState.errors.email?.message}
      />
      <Input
        label="Password"
        type="password"
        {...form.register("password")}
        error={form.formState.errors.password?.message}
      />
      <FormActions align="end">
        <Button type="submit" loading={form.formState.isSubmitting}>
          Create account
        </Button>
      </FormActions>
    </Form>
  );
}

The examples below show the Form JSX only — form and onSubmit come from the same place as here.

docs.title: Grid
docs.text:
<Form layout="grid" columns={2} gap={4} onSubmit={form.handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
  <Input label="First name" {...form.register("name")} />
  <Input label="Last name" {...form.register("last_name")} />
  <Input label="Email" type="email" {...form.register("email")} />
  <Input label="Phone" {...form.register("phone")} />
  <FormActions align="end" style={{ gridColumn: "1 / -1" }}>
    <Button type="submit">Save</Button>
  </FormActions>
</Form>

Full-row span

Use gridColumn: "1 / -1" to make a field (or FormActions) span the whole grid row, regardless of how many columns there are.

docs.title: Inline
docs.text:
A filter bar needs no form library at all — onSubmit here is the native <form> handler, which Form forwards straight through.

const statusOptions = [
  { value: "active", label: "Active" },
  { value: "archived", label: "Archived" },
];

function handleFilter(event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
  setFilters({ q: String(data.get("q") ?? ""), status: String(data.get("status") ?? "") });
}

<Form layout="inline" gap={2} onSubmit={handleFilter}>
  <Input name="q" label="Search" placeholder="name…" />
  <Select name="status" label="Status" options={statusOptions} />
  <Button type="submit">Filter</Button>
</Form>;

Typical filter bars: align-items: flex-end keeps the buttons aligned with the inputs' baseline.

docs.title: FormSection — subgroups with independent layout
docs.text:
<Form layout="stack" gap={5}>
  <Input label="Email" {...form.register("email")} />

  <FormSection title="Address" description="Used for delivery" layout="grid" columns={3} gap={3}>
    <Input label="ZIP" {...form.register("cep")} />
    <Input label="City" {...form.register("city")} />
    <Input label="State" {...form.register("state")} />
    <Input label="Street" style={{ gridColumn: "1 / -1" }} {...form.register("street")} />
  </FormSection>

  <FormActions align="end">
    <Button type="submit">Save</Button>
  </FormActions>
</Form>

FormSection renders a <section> with a <header> (when title or description is present) + body. The body has its own layout / columns / gap.

docs.title: FormRow — side-by-side inside a stack
docs.text:
<Form layout="stack" gap={4}>
  <Input label="Card number" />
  <FormRow gap={3}>
    <Input label="Expiry" placeholder="MM/YY" />
    <Input label="CVV" />
  </FormRow>
</Form>

FormRow is always horizontal with flex-wrap: wrap. Children share the width equally (flex: 1 1 0).

docs.title: FormActions — footer buttons
docs.text:
<FormActions align="between" gap={2}>
  <Button variant="ghost" type="button" onClick={onCancel}>
    Cancel
  </Button>
  <Button type="submit" loading={form.formState.isSubmitting}>
    Save
  </Button>
</FormActions>

align: "start" / "center" / "end" (default) / "between".

docs.title: Validation — zod
docs.text: Three levels of zod integration, from lightest to most opinionated. The schema is the source of truth — the type is inferred.

docs.title: 1. validateForm — agnostic
docs.text:
Does not require react-hook-form. Useful for manual controlled forms or batch validation.

import { validateForm } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const result = validateForm(schema, values);
if (!result.success) {
  setErrors(result.errors); // Record<path, message>
  return;
}
await save(result.data);

Path in dot-notation ("address.city", "items.0.name"). Root errors: _root.

First error per field wins

validateForm keeps only the first issue per path in the error map — form UIs almost always show one message per field. If you need all the messages (e.g. a password-rules checklist), read schema.safeParse(values).error.issues directly.

docs.title: 2. zodResolver — react-hook-form
docs.text:
Replaces @hookform/resolvers/zod (no extra dependency).

import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const form = useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(loginSchema) });

A field named like an Object.prototype member

validateForm and zodResolver write each error as an own property and check it with hasOwnProperty. Before, a field named constructor or toString looked as if it already had an error (inherited from the prototype) and lost its message, and an issue a superRefine filed under __proto__ replaced the map's prototype instead of becoming a key.

docs.title: 3. useZodForm — all-in-one
docs.text:
const form = useZodForm(loginSchema, { defaultValues: { email: "", password: "" } });

<Form layout="stack" onSubmit={form.handleSubmit(login)}>
  <Input label="Email" {...form.register("email")} error={form.formState.errors.email?.message} />
  <Input
    label="Password"
    type="password"
    {...form.register("password")}
    error={form.formState.errors.password?.message}
  />
  <FormActions>
    <Button type="submit" loading={form.formState.isSubmitting}>
      Sign in
    </Button>
  </FormActions>
</Form>;

docs.title: End-to-end example — schema → provider → fields → submit
docs.text:
The three snippets above are slices of the same story. Here is an end-to-end signup form: a single schema drives types, validation and <FormField> wires the RHF state into every control without a repeated <Controller>.

import {
  Form,
  FormField,
  FormProvider,
  FormActions,
  Button,
  Input,
  useZodForm,
  type SubmitHandler,
} from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { z } from "zod";

// 1. Schema = source of truth. The SignupValues type is inferred from it.
const signupSchema = z
  .object({
    name: z.string().min(2, "Enter your name"),
    email: z.string().email("Invalid email"),
    password: z.string().min(8, "At least 8 characters"),
    confirm: z.string(),
  })
  .refine((data) => data.password === data.confirm, {
    message: "Passwords do not match",
    path: ["confirm"], // error attached to the "confirm" field
  });

type SignupValues = z.infer<typeof signupSchema>;

export function SignupForm() {
  // 2. useZodForm wires the zod resolver + infers SignupValues automatically.
  const form = useZodForm(signupSchema, {
    defaultValues: { name: "", email: "", password: "", confirm: "" },
  });

  // 4. handleSubmit only fires the submit once the schema passes.
  const onSubmit: SubmitHandler<SignupValues> = async (values) => {
    await fetch("/api/signup", {
      method: "POST",
      body: JSON.stringify(values),
    });
  };

  return (
    // 3. FormProvider exposes `control` to the tree; FormField reads it from context.
    <FormProvider {...form}>
      <Form layout="stack" gap={4} onSubmit={form.handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
        <FormField name="name" label="Name" required>
          <Input />
        </FormField>
        <FormField name="email" label="Email" required>
          <Input type="email" />
        </FormField>
        <FormField name="password" label="Password" required>
          <Input type="password" />
        </FormField>
        <FormField name="confirm" label="Confirm password" required>
          <Input type="password" />
        </FormField>
        <FormActions align="end">
          <Button type="submit" loading={form.formState.isSubmitting}>
            Create account
          </Button>
        </FormActions>
      </Form>
    </FormProvider>
  );
}

How the pieces fit together:

  • useZodForm(schema) returns react-hook-form's UseFormReturn object, with the zod resolver already plugged in. You get register, handleSubmit, formState, control, etc., typed against SignupValues.
  • <FormProvider {...form}> publishes that return value into RHF's context. This is what lets <FormField> find control on its own.
  • <FormField name="..." label="..."> wraps a <Controller> under the hood and uses cloneElement to inject value / onChange / onBlur / ref / error / aria-invalid into the child control. You pass a "dumb" <Input /> and FormField wires everything up.
  • form.handleSubmit(onSubmit) runs the schema first; onSubmit only ever receives already-validated, typed values.

FormField removes the repeated <Controller>

Without it, each controlled field becomes a 5-line <Controller name=... render={({ field, fieldState }) => ...} />. <FormField> does that render-prop once and forwards error + aria-invalid to the control automatically.

FormField needs a control or a Provider

<FormField> looks up control from the <FormProvider> context. If you don't want a provider, pass control={form.control} explicitly on each <FormField>. With neither, it throws "FormField requires either a control prop or a <FormProvider> in the tree.".

The child control must accept the injected props

<FormField> expects the child to accept value / onChange / onBlur / ref / error / label. The SDK components (Input, Select, and the BR masked inputs) already do — a raw DOM <input> does not understand error/label and will warn about unknown props.

Cross-field errors

Validations that depend on two fields (password × confirmation) go in a .refine() on the schema with path: ["field"] — that way the error shows up attached to the right field in formState.errors.

docs.title: react-hook-form comes out of the same barrel
docs.text:
The SDK re-exports the react-hook-form hooks you would reach for alongside useZodForm, so a form file has one import:

import {
  FormProvider,
  useFieldArray,
  useFormContext,
  useFormState,
  useWatch,
  useZodForm,
} from "tempest-react-sdk";
Hook What it is for useFieldArray Dynamic list of fields (order lines, phone numbers) with append/remove. useFormContext Reaches the form from inside a child component, with no control prop threading. useWatch Watches a field re-rendering only the watcher, not the whole form. useFormState Reads errors/isDirty/isSubmitting with the same subscription granularity.

These are the react-hook-form hooks, unwrapped: their documentation applies literally, and importing straight from react-hook-form behaves identically. The re-export exists so your app need not declare a dependency the SDK already ships.

useWatch and useFormState exist for performance

form.watch("field") and form.formState.errors re-render the component holding the form — on a large form that is the whole screen on every keystroke. These hooks subscribe to just the watched slice, in the component that watches it.

\"FormField found no form to bind to\" with a <FormProvider> visible above it

When this happens with the provider mounted right above, the cause is not what the sentence suggests: the app and the SDK are resolving two copies of react-hook-form. <FormProvider> publishes on one copy's context and the useFormContext inside <FormField> reads the other's, which is empty.

Same mechanism as useNavigate() may be used only in the context of a <Router>, and it goes unnoticed for the same reason: nobody looks in node_modules while looking at the provider on screen. That is why the SDK's error message names both causes as of v0.52.1.

Fix: npm dedupe, or npx tempest doctor to list the duplicates.

docs.title: Schema pattern
docs.text: Keep schemas in src/schemas/<domain>.ts, export the z.infer in src/types/<domain>.ts via declare global when you want global types. Convention inherited from alofans-frontend.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The SDK splits layout (Form/FormSection/FormRow/FormActions) from validation (zod) — adopt one without the other.
  • Validation has three rungs: validateForm (agnostic), zodResolver (RHF), useZodForm (all-in-one).
  • A single zod schema drives the type (z.infer), validation, and error messages.
  • <FormProvider> + <FormField> remove the repeated <Controller> and propagate error + aria-invalid to the controls.
  • handleSubmit only calls your onSubmit with already-validated values.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Forms BR — CPFInput / CNPJInput / CEPInput / MoneyInput / useViaCEP / BR validation algorithms
  • HTTP — parseResponse uses the same zod
  • Components — Input / Select / Textarea that live inside the Form
  • Hooks — useAsync for submit state when you are not using RHF

docs.title: Gallery — visual + functional catalogue
docs.text: An interactive demo of every SDK component and feature. Runs as a Vite + React app in examples/gallery.

docs.title: What is the gallery?
docs.text: The gallery is a real Vite + React app that consumes the SDK exactly the way a production app would — via an npm install pointing at file:../... It stands in for Storybook: each section mounts components with varied props, exercises hooks live (SSE, toast, pagination) and acts as a visual test bench whenever you touch styles or layout. If a component looks right in the gallery, it looks right in consumer apps.

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
# repo root
npm install
npm run build           # generates the SDK's dist/

cd examples/gallery
npm install
npm run dev             # http://127.0.0.1:5173

tempest-react-sdk is consumed via file:../.. — any rebuild from the root shows up in the gallery after a reload.

Run the root npm run dev in parallel

The gallery serves the SDK's dist/. To see SDK changes instantly, keep an npm run dev (vite build --watch) running at the root in one tab and the gallery's npm run dev in another — each rebuild reloads the page.

Validate UI at both breakpoints

The gallery is where you check responsiveness: resize to ≤ 430px (mobile) and ≥ 1024px (desktop) before calling a visual change done. Stack/Grid/Modal/ Drawer/Table all have responsive behavior here.

docs.title: Captures in the documentation pages
docs.text:
Every gallery section has a versioned capture under docs/assets/gallery/, and that is what shows up on the component pages. Two commands keep it current:

npm run e2e:build          # build the SDK and the gallery (prerequisite)
npm run docs:shots         # capture one image per section
npm run docs:gallery       # place the images into the .md pages

docs:shots serves the gallery's production build, walks every section.gallery-section[id] and writes docs/assets/gallery/<id>.webp. The sections where the theme is the point also get an <id>.dark.webp.

Re-running does not dirty the diff

A file is only written when its bytes change. On an untouched gallery a second run leaves git status clean — a diff shows up only when the component actually changed.

Why versioned WebP instead of a build artifact

The image has to render on the MkDocs site and in the .md as GitHub renders it. An artifact produced only at publish time satisfies the first and leaves the second with a broken image. WebP halves the bytes against PNG and is encoded by Playwright's own Chromium, with no new dependency.

docs:gallery inserts a marked block (<!-- gallery:<id> -->) under the first component of each section across docs/components/, in both languages. Pass --check to fail without writing — that is what the docs guard uses.

docs.title: Geolocation
docs.text:
A 100% self-hosted geolocation module: capture latitude/longitude through the browser API, compute distance/trajectory, and plot maps — with no paid or external API. The default map is a tile-free SVG plot (no tile images, no requests). It mirrors the geo module of tempest-fastapi-sdk, so types and math match between client and server.

Why tile-free?

Any image map (OpenStreetMap, Mapbox, Google) downloads tiles from an external server. That clashes with the "nothing external" requirement. So TrajectoryMap draws the projected trajectory in SVG (Web Mercator) with no background — zero requests. If you host your own tile server, you can enable the optional Leaflet layer by passing tileUrl.

Section geo of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Capture the user's position (once or continuously) via navigator.geolocation.
  • Record and display a trajectory (run, delivery, trail).
  • Compute distance between points or estimate travel time offline.
  • Follow a trip live: planned route, trail, vehicle and pickup points.
  • Plot everything without depending on a paid/external map.

docs.title: Types — Coordinate, TrackPoint, TravelEstimate
docs.text:
Types mirror the FastAPI SDK schemas (snake_case preserved on TravelEstimate so a response deserializes directly):

import type { Coordinate, TrackPoint, TravelEstimate, TravelMode } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const sp: Coordinate = { latitude: -23.5505, longitude: -46.6333 };

// TrackPoint = Coordinate + capture time (+ optional accuracy, speed and heading)
const point: TrackPoint = { ...sp, timestamp: Date.now(), accuracy: 12, speed: 8.3, heading: 90 };

// TravelMode = "car" | "motorcycle" | "bus"
const mode: TravelMode = "car";

Utility validators: isValidLatitude, isValidLongitude, isCoordinate (type guard), clampLatitude, normalizeLongitude (antimeridian wrap).

docs.title: Distance and trajectory — haversineKm, pathLengthKm, bearingDeg
docs.text:
Pure math, no network, identical to the server:

import { haversineKm, pathLengthKm, bearingDeg } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const sp = { latitude: -23.5505, longitude: -46.6333 };
const rio = { latitude: -22.9068, longitude: -43.1729 };

haversineKm(sp, rio); // ≈ 360.9 (km, great-circle)

// Total length of a trajectory (sum of legs):
pathLengthKm([sp, { latitude: -23.2, longitude: -45 }, rio]);

// Initial bearing (degrees, 0 = north, clockwise):
bearingDeg(sp, rio); // ≈ 65 (north-east)

docs.title: Framing a set of points — boundingBox, boundsCenter, expandBounds
docs.text:
To center a map on a track, or decide the zoom that covers it:

import { boundingBox, boundsCenter, expandBounds } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const bounds = boundingBox([sp, rio]); // { north, south, east, west } | null

if (bounds) {
  boundsCenter(bounds); // the midpoint, to center on
  expandBounds(bounds, 0.1); // 10% of slack, so the route does not touch the edge
}

boundingBox returns null for an empty list — there is no frame around no points, and returning a zeroed box would put the map in the Atlantic.

expandBounds exists because framing exactly on the extremes puts the first and last point against the frame — the margin is what makes the path fit visually.

docs.title: The raw math
docs.text:
haversineKm is the ready-made formula, but its two pieces come out on their own for callers building a calculation of their own: EARTH_RADIUS_KM (6371, the mean radius the formula assumes) and toRadians(degrees). And unprojectMercator is projectMercator's counterpart — it converts screen coordinates back to lat/long, which is what a click on the map needs.

import { EARTH_RADIUS_KM, projectMercator, toRadians, unprojectMercator } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const xy = projectMercator({ latitude: -23.55, longitude: -46.63 });
unprojectMercator(xy); // back to the lat/long pair

EARTH_RADIUS_KM * toRadians(1); // ≈ 111.2 km per degree of latitude

docs.title: Offline travel estimate — estimateTravel
docs.text:
No network: great-circle distance × circuity factor, duration from a mode-adjusted average speed. Mirrors estimate_travel from the FastAPI SDK.

import { estimateTravel } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const est = estimateTravel(sp, rio, "car");
// { mode: "car", distance_km: ~469, duration_minutes: ~562, source: "heuristic" }

// A bus is ~1.6× slower than a car over the same leg:
estimateTravel(sp, rio, "bus").duration_minutes;

// Tune the factors:
estimateTravel(sp, rio, "car", { circuityFactor: 1.4, carSpeedKmh: 60 });

Default factors

circuityFactor = 1.3 (roads are ~30% longer than the straight line), carSpeedKmh = 50, duration multipliers car: 1.0 · motorcycle: 0.95 · bus: 1.6.

They are exported too — DEFAULT_CIRCUITY_FACTOR, DEFAULT_CAR_SPEED_KMH and DEFAULT_MODE_DURATION_FACTORS — so a settings screen can show the value it is about to override instead of restating it and drifting.

docs.title: Real routing (opt-in) — createOSRMBackend
docs.text:
When you host an OSRM and want real street routing, build a backend injecting your server URL. It is the only piece that makes a request — and only when you create it.

import { createOSRMBackend } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const backend = createOSRMBackend({ baseUrl: "https://osrm.internal" });
const est = await backend.route(sp, rio, { mode: "car" });
// { …, source: "osrm" }

This makes a network request

The SDK ships no endpoint. Point baseUrl at a routing engine you host. For a zero-network estimate, use estimateTravel.

Any engine (Valhalla, GraphHopper) works: implement the RoutingBackend interface (route(origin, destination, { mode }) => Promise<TravelEstimate>).

docs.title: Live tracking — usePositionTracker
docs.text:
Records a trajectory from watchPosition, filtering jitter and accumulating distance. Lifecycle tied to the component (the watch is cleared on unmount).

import { usePositionTracker, TrajectoryMap } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function LiveRun() {
  const { points, lastPoint, distanceKm, isTracking, start, stop, clear } =
    usePositionTracker({ minDistanceKm: 0.01, positionOptions: { enableHighAccuracy: true } });

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={isTracking ? stop : start}>
        {isTracking ? "Stop" : "Track"}
      </button>
      <button onClick={clear}>Clear</button>
      <span>{distanceKm.toFixed(2)} km · {points.length} points</span>
      <TrajectoryMap points={points} current={lastPoint} height={360} />
    </div>
  );
}
  • minDistanceKm (default 0.005 = 5 m) discards samples that are too close — filters GPS jitter while standing still.
  • maxPoints caps the retained array (total distance keeps counting).
  • autoStart: true starts tracking on mount.
  • Each point carries speed (m/s, the browser's unit — × 3.6 gives km/h) and heading (degrees from north), null when the device does not report them. The NaN heading some browsers send while the device is stationary becomes null too.

docs.title: Transient error, refusal and lastError
docs.text:
In a tunnel or an area without signal the browser sends POSITION_UNAVAILABLE (code 2) or TIMEOUT (code 3) and status becomes "error", but the watch stays alive: the next reading moves status back to "tracking" — even one the jitter filter discards, because it already proves the signal is back. Repeated TIMEOUTs keep "error" and call onError each time.

PERMISSION_DENIED (code 1) is terminal: the browser sends no further readings, so the watch is released and status stays "error" until a new start(). lastError (on the hook and on the tracker) tells the screen which of the two cases it is in; it goes back to null on recovery, on start(), on stop() and on clear().

import { usePositionTracker } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function TrackingStatus() {
  const { status, lastError, lastPoint, start } = usePositionTracker({ autoStart: true });

  if (status === "error" && lastError?.code === 1) {
    return (
      <p>
        Allow location access. <button onClick={start}>Try again</button>
      </p>
    );
  }
  if (status === "error") return <p>No GPS signal — waiting for the next reading…</p>;

  const kmh = lastPoint?.speed != null ? (lastPoint.speed * 3.6).toFixed(0) : "—";
  const direction = lastPoint?.heading != null ? `${lastPoint.heading.toFixed(0)}°` : "—";
  return (
    <p>
      {kmh} km/h · heading {direction}
    </p>
  );
}

docs.title: Imperative version — createPositionTracker
docs.text:
Outside React (services), the controller exposes start/stop/clear + points/distanceKm/status/lastError getters:

import { createPositionTracker } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const tracker = createPositionTracker({
  minDistanceKm: 0.01,
  onUpdate: (pts) => console.log(pts.length),
});
tracker.start();
// …later
tracker.stop();
console.log(tracker.distanceKm);

docs.title: Map plot — TrajectoryMap
docs.text:
By default, a tile-free SVG plot: it projects the points (Web Mercator), auto-fits the bounds, and draws the polyline + markers (green start, pulsing current) + grid + a km scale bar. Zero dependency, zero network.

import { TrajectoryMap } from "tempest-react-sdk";

<TrajectoryMap
  points={points}
  current={lastPoint}
  height={360}
  showGrid
  showScale
/>;

docs.title: Real tiles (opt-in) with Leaflet
docs.text:
If you host your own tiles, pass tileUrl — the component loads Leaflet on demand (dynamic import) and mounts a real tile layer. Requires leaflet installed in the app and its stylesheet imported once.

// npm install leaflet
import "leaflet/dist/leaflet.css";
import { TrajectoryMap } from "tempest-react-sdk";

<TrajectoryMap
  points={points}
  tileUrl="https://tiles.YOUR-SERVER/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"
  tileAttribution="© Your map data"
  height={420}
/>;

Leaflet is an optional peer

Without tileUrl, Leaflet never enters the bundle (the import is lazy). If tileUrl is passed and leaflet is not installed, the component shows a message instead of crashing.

Prop Type Default Description points readonly Coordinate[] — Trajectory to draw. current Coordinate \| null — Current-position marker (pulsing). height number 320 Viewport height in px. padding number 24 Inner padding in px. showGrid / showScale boolean true Grid and scale bar (SVG mode). strokeColor string primary token Path color. tileUrl string — {z}/{x}/{y} template of your tile server → enables Leaflet. tileAttribution string — Attribution over the tiles.

docs.title: Live trip map — LiveRouteMap
docs.text:
TrajectoryMap plots a recorded trajectory and refits the map on every change. On a trip that is happening, that gets in the way: every new vehicle position (over SSE, every few seconds) would zoom out. LiveRouteMap is the map of a trip in progress:

  • the planned route (route, e.g. the OSRM geometry) dashed, and the traveled trail (trail) solid on top;
  • the vehicle with a heading arrow (vehicle.heading), gliding between two positions instead of jumping;
  • the trip points (markers) by kind — origin, stop, destination —, with a numeric badge and content that opens by tap, click or keyboard;
  • follow mode (follow): a new position does not refit the map; it only pans, at the same zoom, when the vehicle nears an edge. If the user drags the map, follow pauses and a recenter button shows up.

A complete example — route, trail, vehicle with heading and 3 pickup points with content:

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { LiveRouteMap, bearingDeg, type Coordinate, type LiveRouteMarker } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const ROUTE: Coordinate[] = [
  { latitude: -23.5505, longitude: -46.6333 },
  { latitude: -23.5535, longitude: -46.6301 },
  { latitude: -23.5571, longitude: -46.6268 },
  { latitude: -23.5612, longitude: -46.6239 },
  { latitude: -23.5648, longitude: -46.6197 },
];

const STOPS: LiveRouteMarker[] = [
  {
    id: "se",
    label: "Praça da Sé",
    kind: "origin",
    badge: 2,
    ...ROUTE[0],
    content: <p>Ana and Bruno board here.</p>,
  },
  {
    id: "liberdade",
    label: "Liberdade",
    kind: "stop",
    badge: 3,
    ...ROUTE[2],
    content: (
      <ul>
        <li>Carla</li>
        <li>Diego</li>
        <li>Elisa</li>
      </ul>
    ),
  },
  {
    id: "paraiso",
    label: "Paraíso",
    kind: "destination",
    ...ROUTE[4],
    content: <p>Expected arrival at 08:40.</p>,
  },
];

export function TripMap() {
  const [traveled, setTraveled] = useState<Coordinate[]>([ROUTE[0]]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = window.setInterval(() => {
      setTraveled((prev) =>
        prev.length < ROUTE.length ? [...prev, ROUTE[prev.length]] : prev,
      );
    }, 3000);
    return () => window.clearInterval(timer);
  }, []);

  const position = traveled[traveled.length - 1];
  const previous = traveled[traveled.length - 2];
  const heading = previous ? bearingDeg(previous, position) : null;
  const minutes = (ROUTE.length - traveled.length) * 2;

  return (
    <LiveRouteMap
      route={ROUTE}
      trail={traveled}
      vehicle={{ position, heading, label: "Bus 42" }}
      markers={STOPS}
      follow
      etaLabel={`Estimated arrival in ${minutes} minutes`}
      label="Trip map"
      recenterLabel="Recenter"
      closeLabel="Close"
      kindLabels={{ origin: "origin", stop: "stop", destination: "destination" }}
      height={400}
    />
  );
}

Piece by piece:

  • route decides the initial framing, together with the markers. The vehicle and the trail are not part of it — that is what prevents the zoom-out on every position.
  • vehicle.heading is the bearing in degrees (0 = north, clockwise). Without it the vehicle is a dot. If your backend already sends the heading, pass it through; if not, bearingDeg(previous, current) computes it.
  • markers[].content is any ReactNode. The marker is a button: it opens on click/tap, Enter or Space; focus moves into the panel and Esc closes it and returns focus to the marker.
  • etaLabel is the text the screen reader announces (a polite status region). The map does not compute the ETA: it comes from the app, which already knows where to get it.
  • The default texts are PT-BR; label, recenterLabel, closeLabel and kindLabels translate them.

Reduced motion

The vehicle glides for animationMs (600 ms by default) between two positions. With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce on the system it jumps straight there, with nothing for you to do. animationMs={0} turns it off for everyone.

Offline by default, tiles if you host them

Without tileUrl it is pure SVG: zero requests, works offline and in tests. With tileUrl pointing at your tile server, the map draws the tiles under the lines, in the same projection — no Leaflet, no new dependency. There is no Google Maps path.

Prop Type Default Description route readonly Coordinate[] — Planned route, dashed. Frames the map. trail readonly Coordinate[] — Traveled path, solid. vehicle LiveVehicle \| null — { position, heading?, label? }. markers readonly LiveRouteMarker[] — { id, label, latitude, longitude, kind?, badge?, emphasis?, glyphText?, icon?, content? }. follow boolean false Keeps the vehicle in sight without changing the zoom. etaLabel string — Text announced to the screen reader. height / padding number 360 / 32 Height and framing margin, in px. markerScale number 1 Size of the marker glyphs. The touch target is 44 px at any scale. animationMs number 600 Vehicle glide duration. 0 jumps. showScale boolean true Scale bar in m/km. tileUrl / tileAttribution / tileMaxZoom string / string / number — / — / 19 Tiles from your server. label / recenterLabel / closeLabel string "Mapa da viagem" / "Recentralizar" / "Fechar" Accessible texts. kindLabels Partial<Record<LiveRouteMarkerKind, string>> origem / parada / destino Spoken name of each kind. onMarkerOpenChange (id: string \| null) => void — A marker panel opened (id) or closed (null). roads RoadGraph<E> — Graph from createRoadGraph: draws the roads and snaps the vehicle and trail. onMatch (match: MatchedFix<E> \| null) => void — Each new snapped position (your edge, point, distance), or null off every road. Only with roads.

docs.title: Symbology: emphasis, number, icon and size
docs.text:
Colors and spoken names you already change with tokens and kindLabels. Four fields change the glyph itself:

  • emphasis sets one marker apart from the others — the passenger's "Your pickup" among the line's stops. The glyph grows 1.4× and gets a halo in its own color, so it stays the same kind.
  • glyphText writes short text inside the glyph, such as the stop order ("1", "2"). badge stays free for the count.
  • icon draws SVG inside the glyph, in a 24×24 box — a lucide-react icon fits as is. The finish flag is icon: <Flag /> on the destination.
  • markerScale (on the map) grows every glyph together — shape, badge and focus ring.
import { Flag } from "lucide-react";
import { LiveRouteMap, type Coordinate, type LiveRouteMarker } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const ROUTE: Coordinate[] = [
  { latitude: -23.5505, longitude: -46.6333 },
  { latitude: -23.5571, longitude: -46.6268 },
  { latitude: -23.5612, longitude: -46.6239 },
  { latitude: -23.5648, longitude: -46.6197 },
];

const STOPS: LiveRouteMarker[] = [
  { id: "p1", label: "Stop 1 — Praça da Sé", kind: "origin", glyphText: "1", ...ROUTE[0] },
  { id: "p2", label: "Stop 2 — Liberdade", glyphText: "2", badge: 3, ...ROUTE[1] },
  {
    id: "p3",
    label: "Your pickup — Stop 3, São Joaquim",
    glyphText: "3",
    emphasis: true,
    ...ROUTE[2],
  },
  { id: "end", label: "Arrival — Paraíso", kind: "destination", icon: <Flag />, ...ROUTE[3] },
];

export function PassengerMap() {
  return (
    <LiveRouteMap
      route={ROUTE}
      markers={STOPS}
      markerScale={1.25}
      kindLabels={{ origin: "origin", stop: "stop", destination: "destination" }}
      height={360}
    />
  );
}

Piece by piece:

  • emphasis, glyphText and icon are visual only. The screen reader reads the label and the kind — which is why the example puts "Your pickup" and "Stop 3" in the label too.
  • With glyphText or icon, a stop grows from 16 to 20 px, so the text fits at 12 px. One or two characters read best; longer text shrinks to fit. When both are set, glyphText wins.
  • icon takes the glyph's ink through currentColor — lucide-react icons already paint that way.

A 44 px touch target, at any size

Measured in Chromium on the 0.91.0 gallery (elementFromPoint in 16 directions, every 2 px): a stop answered only inside its 16 px disc, and then only on a 3 px ring 16 px from the center — the transparent stroke of the focus ring. Each marker now has an invisible 44 px circle (WCAG 2.2, SC 2.5.5) that takes the touch, and markerScale never shrinks it. That is why markerScale still defaults to 1: it is for reading the glyph from afar, not for being able to tap it.

docs.title: Legend — LiveRouteMapLegend
docs.text:
Each app drew its own legend, imitating the SDK glyphs with SVG of its own — and a theme or glyph change left the legend behind. LiveRouteMapLegend draws the same glyphs, with the same classes and tokens as the map:

import { Flag } from "lucide-react";
import { LiveRouteMapLegend } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function PassengerLegend() {
  return (
    <LiveRouteMapLegend
      label="Map legend"
      markerScale={1.25}
      items={[
        { symbol: "stop", label: "Your pickup", emphasis: true },
        { symbol: "stop", label: "Stop (trip order)", glyphText: "1" },
        { symbol: "destination", label: "Arrival", icon: <Flag /> },
        { symbol: "vehicle", label: "Bus" },
        { symbol: "route", label: "Planned route" },
        { symbol: "trail", label: "Already traveled" },
      ]}
    />
  );
}
  • symbol is a marker kind ("origin", "stop", "destination"), "vehicle" or one of the lines ("route", "trail"). emphasis, glyphText and icon apply to the marker kinds, the same as on LiveRouteMarker.
  • Without items, the legend lists the six symbols with PT-BR labels.
  • Pass the map's markerScale so the glyphs match; the vehicle and the lines do not scale, as on the map.
  • It is a list (<ul>) with the accessible name "Legenda do mapa" (change it with label); the drawings are aria-hidden, and the screen reader reads the text.
Prop Type Default Description items readonly LiveRouteLegendItem[] the six symbols, PT-BR { symbol, label, emphasis?, glyphText?, icon? }, in order. markerScale number 1 The same factor as the map. label string "Legenda do mapa" Accessible name of the list.

docs.title: CSS variables the map reads
docs.text:
The map and the legend are themed by tokens only. To recolor, override them on :root or on a common ancestor — the legend follows.

Variable Where it shows Default --tempest-surface-2 / --tempest-border Map background and border theme --tempest-text / --tempest-text-muted Text, scale bar / planned route theme --tempest-surface Outline of glyphs and lines, panel, origin dot theme --tempest-success-fg Origin glyph theme --tempest-info-solid Stop glyph theme --tempest-danger-solid Destination glyph theme --tempest-primary / --tempest-primary-foreground Trail and vehicle / vehicle arrow theme --tempest-focus-ring-color Marker focus ring theme --tempest-live-route-badge / --tempest-live-route-badge-text badge background / number --tempest-gray-700 / --tempest-neutral-on-solid --tempest-live-route-origin-ink glyphText and icon on the origin --tempest-surface --tempest-live-route-stop-ink glyphText and icon on a stop --tempest-info-on-solid --tempest-live-route-destination-ink glyphText and icon on the destination --tempest-danger-on-solid --tempest-live-route-road / --tempest-live-route-road-casing roads streets --tempest-bg / --tempest-text-subtle

Why the badge no longer uses --tempest-text over --tempest-bg

Up to 0.91.0 the badge was --tempest-text behind a number in --tempest-bg — the inverted pair. In the SDK's own theme that gave 17.75:1 (light) and 17.51:1 (dark). But the contrast hung on two tokens an app overrides separately: a theme that lightened --tempest-text and left --tempest-bg white put a white number on an almost-white badge — 1.11:1, measured in Chromium. The badge now uses the fixed neutral pair (--tempest-gray-700 + --tempest-neutral-on-solid), the same as the solid neutral Badge: 10.46:1 in both themes, and with the partial theme too. Glyph inks use the measured *-solid/*-on-solid pairs — 5.17 and 4.83:1 in light, 5.25 and 5.13:1 in dark; the origin, --tempest-surface over --tempest-success-fg (8.65 and 10.28:1). If your theme changes --tempest-surface without --tempest-success-fg, set --tempest-live-route-origin-ink along with it.

docs.title: Roads on the map and the vehicle on the road — roads
docs.text:
GPS is off by 3 to 30 m in a city. Drawn raw, the bus "drives" on the sidewalk, cuts across the block at a corner and, on an avenue with a parallel street next to it, jumps from one to the other. Pass the region's road graph in roads and the map handles it with no code in the app:

  • it draws the graph's roads as a vector layer under the route and the trail — no tiles, works offline;
  • it runs each vehicle.position through an internal createRoadMatcher and draws the vehicle at the point snapped to the road;
  • when the position has no heading, the arrow follows the direction of the road the vehicle is on;
  • it draws the trail along the matched roads, turning the corner instead of cutting the block.
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import {
  LiveRouteMap,
  createRoadGraph,
  type Coordinate,
  type MatchedFix,
  type RoadEdge,
  type RoadGraph,
} from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface Street extends RoadEdge {
  id: string;
  name: string;
}

interface RoadTile {
  nodes: Coordinate[];
  edges: Street[];
}

export function BusOnTheStreet({ fixes }: { fixes: Coordinate[] }) {
  const [roads, setRoads] = useState<RoadGraph<Street> | undefined>(undefined);
  const [street, setStreet] = useState<string>("");

  useEffect(() => {
    let alive = true;
    fetch("/api/roads?bbox=-46.66,-23.57,-46.64,-23.55")
      .then((response) => response.json() as Promise<RoadTile>)
      .then((tile) => {
        if (alive) setRoads(createRoadGraph({ ...tile, twoWay: true }));
      });
    return () => {
      alive = false;
    };
  }, []);

  const onMatch = (match: MatchedFix<Street> | null): void => {
    setStreet(match ? match.edge.name : "off the road network");
  };

  return (
    <>
      <p aria-live="polite">{street}</p>
      <LiveRouteMap
        trail={fixes}
        vehicle={{ position: fixes[fixes.length - 1], label: "Bus 7" }}
        roads={roads}
        onMatch={onMatch}
        follow
        height={400}
      />
    </>
  );
}

Piece by piece:

  • roads is the same RoadGraph from createRoadGraph. Build it once per region and pass the same instance on every render: snapping keeps its history while the object stays the same, and a new graph starts a new chain.
  • vehicle.position is still the raw position. You snap nothing: the map does. If your backend sends heading, it wins; without it, the arrow follows the road.
  • A position with a timestamp stays chained even when sparse. If the vehicle reports every 5–30 s, send each position's timestamp (a TrackPoint has one): the snapping then accepts the trip round the block between two reports instead of cutting the chain. Without timestamp, everything works as before — see Sparse sources.
  • onMatch is called on each new position with the match — the edge (your object, with name, id, speed limit), the point on the road (point) and the distance (distanceM) — or with null when the position is far from every road.
  • The graph does not enter the framing. A whole city of streets does not zoom the map out: route and markers still decide the framing.

Off every road, the vehicle shows where it is

With no road within 200 m (the matcher's radiusM) there is nothing to snap to: the vehicle is drawn at the raw position, with its halo replaced by a dashed ring, and onMatch gets null. The vehicle never disappears — in a bus yard or on a street the graph does not have yet, it stays visible.

Apps that never pass roads never download the matcher

Snapping (createRoadMatcher + matchToRoads) comes in through a dynamic import, the first time a map with roads mounts. Without roads nothing changes: the map draws exactly what it drew, and the bundler leaves the matcher in a separate chunk nobody requests.

The roads use two tokens of their own, which you override in the theme: --tempest-live-route-road (the road surface, default --tempest-bg) and --tempest-live-route-road-casing (the edge, default --tempest-text-subtle).

Technical details: what the map does underneath
  • The vehicle runs through a createRoadMatcher(roads) with the measured defaults (lag 5). The drawn point is current — the best guess for the position that just arrived, which already weighs every earlier one. That is what holds the vehicle on the avenue when the noise puts it closer to the parallel street.
  • The whole trail runs through matchToRoads on every change (~3 ms per thousand positions, measured on desktop), and each unbroken run becomes a line through the nodes of the roads driven. Positions with no road in reach are left out of that line.
  • Only the roads that cross the screen go into the SVG.
  • Weight, measured on the 0.90.0 dist with esbuild (bundle + minify, CSS out, the dynamic import kept external — the chunk the app's bundler splits off), in brotli: { LiveRouteMap } comes to 5.33 kB brotli, against 4.67 kB before roads; with the matcher in the same file it would be 8.42 kB.

docs.title: Snapping to the road (map-matching) — createRoadGraph, matchToRoads, createRoadMatcher
docs.text:
City GPS is off by 3 to 30 m, sometimes much more. Snapping each position to the nearest road looks like the fix, but it is wrong on 1 position in 7: the parallel street 15 m away, the other side of the intersection, the opposite carriageway. matchToRoads looks at the sequence: a road the vehicle could not have reached in one second loses to the road it is driving on.

It is the hidden Markov model of Newson & Krumm (2009), decoded with Viterbi:

  • Candidates: the roads within radiusM of the position, at most maxCandidates.
  • Emission: a Gaussian on the distance from the position to the road (sigmaM) — a near road is more likely.
  • Transition: an exponential on |straight line − network distance| (betaM) — between two consecutive positions, the path along the network should be as long as the move. The network distance comes from a bounded Dijkstra (maxDetourM, which grows with the interval when the position carries a timestamp).

docs.title: Where the graph comes from
docs.text:
The API is source-agnostic: nodes are coordinates and edges are pairs of node indices (from → to), each carrying whatever your app wants (id, name, speed limit). The recommended path is OpenStreetMap served by your backend, per tile or region:

  • every way with highway=* becomes one edge per pair of consecutive nodes;
  • oneway=yes becomes twoWay: false; no oneway, twoWay: true; oneway=-1, swap from/to;
  • the backend cuts the region (bounding box or tile) and sends the JSON below, which the app caches.
{
  "nodes": [{ "latitude": -5.0892, "longitude": -42.8016 }, { "latitude": -5.0901, "longitude": -42.8003 }],
  "edges": [{ "from": 0, "to": 1, "twoWay": true, "id": "way/24680", "name": "Av. Frei Serafim" }]
}

Build the graph once per region and reuse it for every trace: building is the expensive part (the spatial index and the adjacency); querying is cheap.

docs.title: Matching a recorded trace
docs.text:
import {
  createRoadGraph,
  matchToRoads,
  type Coordinate,
  type RoadEdge,
  type RoadGraph,
} from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface Street extends RoadEdge {
  id: string;
  name: string;
}

interface RoadTile {
  nodes: Coordinate[];
  edges: Street[];
}

export async function loadRoads(bbox: string): Promise<RoadGraph<Street>> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/roads?bbox=${bbox}`);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`roads: HTTP ${response.status}`);
  const tile = (await response.json()) as RoadTile;
  return createRoadGraph(tile);
}

export async function streetsDriven(trace: Coordinate[]): Promise<string[]> {
  const graph = await loadRoads("-42.83,-5.11,-42.78,-5.06");
  const result = matchToRoads(trace, graph);

  for (const [i, match] of result.matches.entries()) {
    if (match === null) console.warn(`position ${i}: no road within 200 m`);
  }
  console.log(`${result.breaks} breaks, ${result.dropped} stopped positions`);

  return result.routes.flatMap((route) => route.edges.map((step) => step.edge.name));
}

Piece by piece:

  • matches has one entry per position, in order: the edge (edge, your object), the point projected on the road (point), the distance (distanceM), the position along the edge (offsetM), and reversed when a two-way road is driven from to to from. null when no road is within radiusM.
  • routes is the inferred route: the edges driven, in order, including the ones between two positions, recovered by the shortest path on the network.
  • Break (breaks): when no transition is possible (a signal gap, a road missing from the graph), the chain restarts at that position instead of failing. Each unbroken run becomes one entry in routes.
  • Stopped position (dropped): a position closer than minSpacingM (default 2 × sigmaM) to the previous one skips the model — the vehicle moved less than the GPS noise. It is projected onto the previous position's edge and comes back with inferred: true, never null.

TrackPoint is a Coordinate with a timestamp, so the points of usePositionTracker go straight in — and their timestamp already keeps the chain on a sparse source.

docs.title: On the live map — createRoadMatcher
docs.text:
matchToRoads needs the whole trace. To draw the vehicle now, createRoadMatcher runs the same model one position at a time, with fixed-lag Viterbi:

On LiveRouteMap, just pass roads

If your map is LiveRouteMap, you do not call the matcher: roads does it inside. Use createRoadMatcher directly when the drawing is yours.

import { createRoadMatcher, type Coordinate, type RoadGraph } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function snapLive(graph: RoadGraph): (fix: Coordinate) => Coordinate {
  const matcher = createRoadMatcher(graph, { lag: 5 });
  return (fix) => {
    const { current, committed } = matcher.push(fix);
    for (const final of committed) {
      console.log(`position ${final.index} confirmed on`, final.match?.edge);
    }
    return current?.point ?? fix;
  };
}
  • current is the best guess for the position that just arrived: draw the vehicle with it. It can still change.
  • committed holds the positions that became final: each waits for lag newer positions before it is decided. A confirmed position never changes.
  • Memory is bounded by lag; flush() confirms what is left (end of the trip). The route between positions is not rebuilt here: run matchToRoads on the finished trace for it.

docs.title: Sparse sources — timestamp
docs.text:
The fixed maximum detour (maxDetourM, 100 m) was calibrated at 1 Hz. With one position every 5, 10 or 30 s, the vehicle turns corners and goes round the block between two points, the path along the network exceeds the straight line by more than 100 m, and the chain breaks. Raising maxDetourM for everyone does not work: at 1 Hz it lets the model invent loops that never happened.

The way out is to say when each position was taken. With a timestamp on both positions, the detour allowed between them becomes:

maxDetourM + detourPerSecondM × min(Δt, maxIntervalS)

Tight where positions are dense, loose where they are sparse. Without timestamp (or with a clock that repeats or goes back), the bound is exactly the one before.

import { matchToRoads, type RoadFix, type RoadGraph } from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface Ping {
  lat: number;
  lon: number;
  sentAt: string;
}

export function tripRuns(pings: Ping[], graph: RoadGraph): number {
  const fixes: RoadFix[] = pings.map((ping) => ({
    latitude: ping.lat,
    longitude: ping.lon,
    timestamp: Date.parse(ping.sentAt),
  }));
  const result = matchToRoads(fixes, graph);
  console.log(`${result.breaks} breaks in ${fixes.length} positions`);
  return result.routes.length;
}
  • timestamp is in milliseconds since the epoch, the same as GeolocationPosition.timestamp. The points of usePositionTracker already carry it.
  • createRoadMatcher and LiveRouteMap with roads use the timestamp the same way: matcher.push({ latitude, longitude, timestamp }).
  • detourPerSecondM (default 2) is how much detour each second of interval earns. maxIntervalS (default 60) is where that stops: after a 10-minute hole the bound is the 60 s one, and Dijkstra does not sweep the city.

What breaks remain are wrong-way driving

Measured on Brazilian traces (below), almost every break left with a sparse source vanishes once every road is made two-way: it is a bicycle, or a wrong oneway in OSM, going against the direction. For those, more slack does not help — it trades the break for a loop round the block that never happened, which is why the default is small.

Technical details: how the defaults were chosen

Two datasets, the same sweep (detourPerSecondM 1/2/3/5/10, maxIntervalS 30/60/no cap, against the fixed detour of 100/300/1000 m), each trace thinned by its own clock:

  • Kubicka (npm run build && node --expose-gc scripts/bench-map-matching.mjs), with the true route;
  • public OSM traces in five Brazilian city centres (npm run build && node scripts/bench-br-osm.mjs [cache-dir]), compared with the dense match of the same run.

2 is the largest rate that does not hurt 1 Hz (92.33% → 92.34% right road on Kubicka, with timestamp); 3 already loses 0.05 pp. Without a cap, the long holes inside the 1 Hz traces cost 0.2 pp (92.13%); with 60 s, they do not.

Brazil, all runs (default without → with timestamp) 5 s 10 s 30 s Breaks per 1000 positions 5.7 → 5.4 10.1 → 8.9 24.2 → 13.8 Extra route 1.3% → 1.6% 1.4% → 1.9% 3.6% → 4.4% Same way as the 1 Hz match 95.0% → 95.0% 93.7% → 93.7% 89.6% → 90.1% Breaks, runs at ≥ 6 m/s only 0.8 → 0 1.5 → 0 9.3 → 0 Breaks with every road two-way, with timestamp 0.3 0.6 0

For comparison: the fixed 1000 m detour brings breaks down to 1.9 at 5 s, but the extra route up to 6.1%.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
npm run build && node --expose-gc scripts/bench-map-matching.mjs, on the Kubicka et al. dataset (Zenodo 57731, CC BY-SA 4.0): 100 real drives worldwide, 247 251 positions at ~1 Hz, each with its ground-truth route and OpenStreetMap excerpt. "Right road" is the same metric as the naive snap: the matched edge belongs to the true route (direction ignored); null counts as wrong.

Measure (defaults) Result Right road, snap to the nearest road 85.7% Right road, matchToRoads, all 100 drives 92.33% Right road, without the 3 drives tagged hives (97 drives) 98.53% Right road, median per drive 99.9% (88 of 100 drives ≥ 97%) Length of the true route recovered 99.27% (0.78% extra length) Breaks 48 over 100 drives createRoadMatcher, lag 0 / 1 / 5 / 20 89.04% / 91.10% / 92.23% / 92.32% Time (Node 24, i9-13900F) 8.1 µs per position; 1 h at 1 Hz (3600 positions) in 11 ms

The measured limit

Two drives (5 844 and 19 313 positions, 10% of the dataset) wander through yards and areas with no road in the OSM excerpt — the dataset itself tags them hives — and score 18% and 43%. No parameter saves them: there is no right road to snap to. It is the same "road the base does not have" signal the backend inference will handle. Without them, matching is above 97%.

Performance on the device

Measured on a desktop, not on a phone. A 16-thousand-edge graph (a mid-sized city) builds in 8 ms and takes ~1 MB; the dataset's largest, 307 thousand edges, builds in 68 ms and takes 47 MB — cut the region into tiles. Matching 1 h at 1 Hz allocates ~30 MB of short-lived memory and retains almost nothing; the live mode costs ~3 µs per position. Even on a phone 10× slower, that is under 1 ms per position.

Option Default What it does sigmaM 7 GPS noise, in metres (Gaussian emission). betaM 3 Transition scale, in metres. Smaller punishes detours harder. radiusM 200 Roads farther than this are not candidates. maxCandidates 16 At most this many roads per position (a two-way road counts once). minSpacingM 2 × sigmaM Positions closer than this to the previous one skip the model. maxDetourM 100 Maximum network detour over the straight line. Beyond it the transition is impossible. detourPerSecondM 2 Extra detour per second between two positions with a timestamp. 0 turns it off. maxIntervalS 60 Interval past which the detour stops growing. lag (createRoadMatcher only) 5 Newer positions before one is confirmed.

The defaults live in ROAD_MATCH_DEFAULTS and ROAD_MATCHER_DEFAULT_LAG. The full sweep table (radius × k, σ × β, detour, pre-filter) comes out of the same command.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Capture: usePositionTracker / createPositionTracker record a trajectory via navigator.geolocation, filtering jitter — all in the browser.
  • Math: haversineKm, pathLengthKm, bearingDeg, estimateTravel — offline, mirroring tempest-fastapi-sdk.
  • Map: TrajectoryMap plots tile-free SVG by default; tileUrl enables Leaflet only with a server you host.
  • Live trip: LiveRouteMap shows planned route + trail + vehicle with heading, and follows the vehicle without refitting on every position. With roads, it draws the streets and snaps the vehicle and trail to them, with no code in the app. emphasis, glyphText, icon and markerScale change the glyph, and LiveRouteMapLegend draws the legend with the same glyphs.
  • Road snapping: createRoadGraph + matchToRoads (whole trace) and createRoadMatcher (live) put each position on the right road — 98.5% measured outside the road-less areas. With timestamp, one position every 5–30 s does not break the chain at the corner.
  • Real routing: createOSRMBackend is opt-in and points at your OSRM — the only piece that touches the network.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Utility hooks — useGeolocation (single fix / low-level watch)
  • HTTP — send the trajectory to the backend
  • Offline — persist the trajectory locally

docs.title: Utility hooks
docs.text:
Every React app rewrites the same wrappers: "debounce this input", "close the menu on Escape", "store the theme in localStorage", "re-render when the window resizes". They are small, but each one has a trap — listener cleanup, running without window, the dependency array. The SDK packages these patterns into granular, tested, browser-guarded and independent hooks — import only what you need.

Each hook is a standalone piece

No hook depends on another or on a provider. import { useDebounce } from "tempest-react-sdk" and you're done — the bundler tree-shakes the rest. They are grouped by purpose in these docs, not by coupling.

Browser-guarded is not SSR support

Several hooks below guard on typeof window === "undefined" and return a default instead of throwing. That exists for Node tests, the service-worker context and build plugins — it is not a promise of server rendering. The SDK is client-only by decision (see Architecture).

Section hooks-state of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

Section hooks-dom of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: DOM / viewport
docs.text: Hook What it does useMediaQuery(query) Subscribes to matchMedia and re-renders on change. useBreakpoint() { current, width, above, below, isMobile, isTablet, isDesktop } — reactive breakpoint (xs/sm/md/lg/xl/2xl). useWindowSize() { width, height } of the window, reactive. useEventListener(name, handler, target?, opts?) Generic browser-guarded wrapper. target default = window. Accepts a ref or an EventTarget directly. useOnline(opts?) Reactive navigator.onLine; { pingUrl, intervalMs, timeoutMs } adds a real-reachability probe (catches captive portals / dead links). useDocumentVisibility() Reactive document.visibilityState. useIntersectionObserver(ref, opts?) IntersectionObserverEntry or null. useResizeObserver(ref) { width, height } of the reference. useScrollOverflow(ref, axis?) true while the content overflows its box — use it to give a scroll container a tab stop only when there is something to scroll. useScrollLock(active) Locks body.overflow. useFocusTrap(ref, active) Confines Tab within the container. useHover(ref) / useLongPress(handler, opts?) Pointer gestures (reactive hover / long-press). useBeforeInstallPrompt() Deferred PWA install prompt (installable, installed, isStandalone, prompt()). useServiceWorkerUpdate({ url }) Registers the SW and exposes { updateAvailable, applyUpdate, registration } — consent-based update flow (pairs with <UpdatePrompt>). See PWA. useStorageEstimate({ pollMs? }) { usage, quota, ratio, persisted, requestPersist, refresh } — Storage API quota + persist(). Pure pairs: estimateStorage, requestPersistentStorage. useIdle(timeout?) True when the user is idle for timeout ms. useFullscreen(ref?) { isFullscreen, supported, enter, exit, toggle } — immersive mode whose state is driven by fullscreenchange, so Esc and the browser's own button update the UI. Pure pair: isFullscreenSupported. usePushToTalk({ code, onDown, onUp }) Hold to transmit. blur releases (alt-tab never delivers the keyup), auto-repeat is ignored, and a text field wins. Pairs: pushToTalkKeyLabel, PUSH_TO_TALK_KEYS. useGeolocation(opts?) Position + error + loading. useClickOutside(handler) Returns a ref; calls handler on a mousedown/touchstart outside the element. browser-guarded. useDocumentTitle(title) Sets document.title while mounted, restoring the previous one on unmount. browser-guarded. useFavicon(href) Swaps the favicon via <link rel="icon"> (creating the element if missing). browser-guarded. useAnnounce() Returns announce(message, politeness?) — speaks to screen readers through one shared live region. Pure pairs: announce, clearAnnouncer.

docs.title: Input / interaction
docs.text: Hook What it does useDebounce(value, delay?) Returns the value stabilized after delay ms without changes. useThrottle(value, interval?) Limits updates to at most one per interval ms. useClipboard(opts?) { copied, copy, reset } with a configurable TTL. useKeyboardShortcut(shortcut, handler, opts?) Global shortcut; accepts mod (Ctrl/Cmd).

docs.title: State
docs.text: Hook What it does usePagination(initialPage?, initialSize?) { page, size, setPage, setSize, reset }. useClientFilter(items, search, keysOrPredicate) Client-side filter by keys or predicate (memoized). Items are objects (T extends Record<string, unknown>). useDraftFilters(initial, { onApply?, isEqual? }) Draft vs applied state for a server-side filter: { draft, applied, isDirty, set, apply, clear, discard }. Applying happens in the event, never in an effect — one click, one request. useLocalStorage<T>(key, default) State persisted to localStorage + synced cross-tab via the storage event. browser-guarded. useToggle(initial?) [value, { toggle, setTrue, setFalse, set }] — sugar for boolean state. useAsync<T>(fn, deps?, { immediate? }) Tracks idle/pending/success/error. { status, data, error, run, reset }. Distinct from React Query (no cache). usePrevious(value) The value from the previous render. useDisclosure(initial?) [opened, { open, close, toggle }] — stable handlers for modals/drawers/popovers. useCounter(initial?, { min, max }) [count, { increment, decrement, set, reset }] — numeric counter with an optional clamp. useListState<T>(initial?) [list, handlers] with append/prepend/insert/remove/reorder/setItem/setState/apply/clear. useMap<K, V>(initial?) { map, set, delete, clear, get, has, size } — reactive Map (a fresh reference on each mutation). useSet<T>(initial?) { set, add, delete, clear, has, toggle, size } — reactive Set (a fresh reference on each mutation). useQueue<T>({ initialValues, limit }) { queue, add, update, cleanQueue, size } — FIFO queue with a limit and an overflow buffer. useIsFirstRender() true on the component's first render, false after. useObjectUrl(blob) Creates URL.createObjectURL(blob) and revokes it on unmount / when the blob changes; null for nullish input.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text: Hook What it does useInterval(callback, delay) Declarative setInterval; delay = null pauses. useTimeout(callback, delay) Declarative setTimeout; delay = null cancels. useCountdown(durationMs, startedAt, { tickMs }) Time left on a window, recomputed from the clock each tick. Clamps at 0 and stops the interval. useTypewriter(text, speedMs) { displayedText, isComplete, skip } — reveals text character by character. speedMs <= 0 renders it all at once.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Hook What it does useStableCallback(fn) Stable ref that calls the current callback. useLatestRef(value) Stable ref whose current is always the newest value. useDeepMemo(value) Memoization with structural equality.

browser-guarded by default

The hooks that touch browser APIs (useMediaQuery, useBreakpoint, useWindowSize, useOnline, useDocumentVisibility, useLocalStorage, useEventListener) check typeof window === "undefined" and return a safe default on the server, hydrating the real value after mount. That is why the first client render may briefly show the default (e.g. width: 0).

docs.title: Global shortcut — useKeyboardShortcut
docs.text:
import { useState } from "react";
import { useKeyboardShortcut } from "tempest-react-sdk";

function CommandPalette() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  useKeyboardShortcut({ key: "k", mod: true }, () => setOpen(true));
  return open ? <div role="dialog">Command palette…</div> : null;
}

mod: true accepts Ctrl or Cmd, simplifying cross-OS.

Doesn't fire inside inputs
