Before the first write, gen api checks the --out, every route-group folder and every file: a symlink (dangling included) in place of any of them, a path outside the project and an ancestor that is a symlink leading out are refused, and nothing is written. A src/api that is a link in a cloned repository does not carry the generated files somewhere else on disk.

Validates input, types the output

The method validates the body with Schema.parse(...) (fails early on invalid data) and types the response. The response is not validated at runtime by default — trust the backend contract, or validate manually with the matching schema if you need a guarantee.

Current support

v1 covers the common FastAPI spec: components.schemas (object, enum, array, $ref, nullable, anyOf/oneOf/allOf), path/query/header params (from the operation and the path item), JSON body and response, grouped by the first tag. YAML and multiple content-types are not supported yet — point at the /openapi.json (JSON).

Third-party spec text never becomes code

Every string from the spec reaches the generated TypeScript escaped for the position it lands in: a tag, summary or path inside a comment cannot close the /** */, path segments become template-literal text, and pattern becomes new RegExp("..."). A name that must be an identifier and is not — {user-id}, user.Response, User-Out — becomes a valid one: camelCase for a parameter (userId), PascalCase for a schema or type (UserResponse), a _ prefix for a reserved word or a leading digit (_string, _2fa). Wherever the name matters at runtime the original wins: the URL fills {user-id} with the value of userId, and an object key is an escaped string ("display-name"). A name that already is an identifier is kept. Two schemas emitted in the same group that map to the same identifier (User-Out and user.Out) are refused with an error naming both, and so is a path {placeholder} that is not a declared parameter — there is no safe variable for it.

The same goes for names the generator itself uses. A path parameter that would land on body, params, headers, S, encodeIdSegment or headerRecord becomes bodyParam/paramsParam/headersParam/SParam/ encodeIdSegmentParam/headerRecordParam; an operationId of constructor or api becomes constructor2/api2; a schema named ApiClient, OffsetPage, CursorPage, Promise, Record, z, S, encodeIdSegment or headerRecord gets a _ prefix; and two tags whose barrel names coincide (user 1 and user1) are refused, naming both. A pattern that does not compile as a JavaScript regex fails generation, naming the schema and the property path — instead of breaking the app on import.

Text that would turn into something else at its destination is refused too, before the first write:

  • A path that does not start with / (https://other.example/x) — the client passes an absolute URL through as is, so the method would call another origin — and a path with a . or .. segment (/../x, /%2e%2e/x, /a\..\x), which leaves the baseURL's path prefix once the URL is normalized. A dot inside a segment (/v1.2/..cache) or in the query is still fine.
  • A property named __proto__, or a __proto__ key inside a default: in the generated object literal it swaps the prototype instead of declaring the field, and Zod 4 drops it even as a computed key — there is no code that validates it.

These checks (and the pattern one) reach every sub-schema, including the schema of a property whose name is a JSON Schema keyword — pattern, default, $ref, items, enum. Before, a property named pattern or default was skipped as if it were the keyword, and whatever sat inside it was generated unchecked.

A pattern that compiles but has a nested quantifier (^(a+)+$, (\w+\s?)*) is generated as usual and printed as a warning (!) in the terminal: on a near-miss value it backtracks exponentially — 28 characters took 873 ms on Node 24 and each extra one doubles it — and freezes the tab that validates it. It is a heuristic for that shape, not a safety proof: ^([a-z0-9]+-)*[a-z0-9]+$ (every repetition ends on a mandatory -) is not flagged, and overlapping alternation ((a|aa)+) is not analysed.

What the CLI prints from the spec — tag names, warnings and error messages — comes out without C0/C1 control characters: a tag carrying ESC ] 0 ; neither retitles the terminal nor prints a hidden OSC 8 link.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• tempest gen api <url|file> --out src/api generates, per route group, three files: schemas.ts (Zod), types.ts (z.infer) and service.ts (class).
  • The service class takes an injected ApiClient and validates the body with Zod before calling the API.
  • Every path parameter goes through encodeIdSegment: it stays in one segment, and ""/"."/".." throw before the request.
  • Path-item parameters join the operation's (the operation wins on the same name + in); headers become the headers argument, and cookies stay with the browser.
  • A schema no route reaches, such as FastAPI's orphan enum, is not generated.
  • Treat src/api/ as a generated artifact — regenerate when the contract changes.
  • See also: HTTP / createApiClient · Query · tempest CLI.

docs.title: Passkeys (WebAuthn)
docs.text:
Passwordless sign-in, using the biometrics the user already unlocks their device with.

The SDK covers the client half: both ceremonies (navigator.credentials.create and .get), the base64url ↔ ArrayBuffer plumbing everybody re-implements badly, the capability probes, and error classification. The other half is your backend — and this page says exactly what it must send and receive, because a WebAuthn client that documents only its own half is useless.

Why a passkey instead of a password

The private key never leaves the device, so there is no password database to leak and no phishing that works: the browser only signs for the domain that registered the credential. For the user it is one touch on a sensor.

Section recipe-passkeys of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: The surface
docs.text: Symbol What it is for createPasskeyClient Framework-free client: register + authenticate + probes usePasskeyRegistration Hook for the "create a passkey" flow usePasskeySignIn Hook for the "sign in with a passkey" flow, autofill optional usePasskeyCapabilities Just the three probes, when you decide the UI up front isPasskeySupported The browser has WebAuthn isPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable This device has Face ID / Hello / a fingerprint reader isConditionalMediationAvailable Passkey autofill is available classifyPasskeyError / PasskeyError An error with a kind your UI can switch on base64UrlToBytes / bytesToBase64Url The plumbing, exposed because you will need it

docs.title: Start with the hook
docs.text:
Two buttons, two hooks. This is enrolment, on the account screen:

import { usePasskeyRegistration } from "tempest-react-sdk";

import { api } from "../lib/api";

export function CreatePasskey() {
  const passkey = usePasskeyRegistration({
    getOptions: () => api.post("/api/webauthn/register/begin"),
    verify: (credential) =>
      api.post("/api/webauthn/register/finish", { body: credential }),
  });

  if (passkey.platformAvailable === null) return null;

  if (passkey.error?.kind === "already-registered") {
    return <p>This device already has a passkey for your account. 👍</p>;
  }

  return (
    <>
      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => void passkey.register()}
        disabled={passkey.status === "prompting" || passkey.status === "verifying"}
      >
        {passkey.status === "prompting" ? "Confirm on your device…" : "Create a passkey"}
      </button>
      {passkey.error && <p role="alert">{passkey.error.message}</p>}
      {passkey.status === "success" && <p>Passkey created. ✅</p>}
    </>
  );
}

Piece by piece:

  • getOptions is your begin route. The server mints the challenge and returns the options.
  • verify is your finish route. It receives the JSON the SDK serialized.
  • platformAvailable === null means "I do not know yet" — the probe is async. Render nothing passkey-related in that state.
  • register() resolves; it never rejects. Every failure is already state (status, error.kind) the UI has to draw; forcing a try/catch inside a button handler would only duplicate what the hook holds.

platformAvailable === false is not "no passkeys"

It means "no built-in authenticator here". The user can still use their phone over QR/hybrid. Offer it as "use my phone", not as one tap.

docs.title: Sign-in, and the autofill that makes the difference
docs.text:
import { usePasskeySignIn } from "tempest-react-sdk";

import { api } from "../lib/api";
import { useAuthStore } from "../store/auth";

export function LoginForm() {
  const passkey = usePasskeySignIn<{ access_token: string }>({
    conditional: true,
    getOptions: () => api.post("/api/webauthn/signin/begin"),
    verify: (assertion) =>
      api.post<{ access_token: string }>("/api/webauthn/signin/finish", {
        body: assertion,
      }),
    onSuccess: ({ access_token }) => useAuthStore.getState().setToken(access_token),
  });

  return (
    <form>
      <label htmlFor="email">E-mail</label>
      <input id="email" name="email" autoComplete="username webauthn" />

      <button type="button" onClick={() => void passkey.signIn()}>
        Sign in with a passkey
      </button>
      {passkey.error && <p role="alert">{passkey.error.message}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

conditional: true arms the autofill flow: no modal appears; the browser lists the user's passkeys inside the e-mail field. They tap one and they are in, without typing anything.

autocomplete="username webauthn" is not optional

Without that attribute on the input the list never appears — and there is no error, the request just hangs. The hook cannot do this part for you: only your screen knows which field identifies the user.

Two more rules of conditional mediation:

  • One per page. A second concurrent conditional request kills the first.
  • Aborting is not a failure. If the user types a password instead of picking the passkey, or the screen unmounts, the request is aborted and the hook does not set an error — nothing failed, they chose another door.

docs.title: The errors, and what to do with each
docs.text:
error.kind is what the UI branches on. error.message is English text that is safe to show, but normally you write your own copy per kind:

kind Cause What the UI does cancelled NotAllowedError Nothing red. Return to the initial state already-registered InvalidStateError Success in disguise: "already set up on this device" rp-mismatch SecurityError Your bug: rp.id does not match the origin not-supported NotSupportedError No authenticator accepts the requested algorithms invalid-options TypeError begin sent broken base64url insecure Page served over HTTP Serve it over HTTPS unsupported Browser without WebAuthn Hide the option aborted Your own signal fired Stay quiet unknown Everything else Log it plus a generic message

cancelled means "dismissed or timed out" — and there is no way to tell

NotAllowedError covers both by design: telling the site "this account has no credential here" would leak account existence. Treat it as one event and never claim "you cancelled".

rp-mismatch is integration bug #1

rp.id must be the page's domain or a registrable parent of it. app.acme.com may use acme.com; acme.com may not use app.acme.com. On localhost, leave rp.id out.

docs.title: Without React: createPasskeyClient
docs.text:
The hooks are a shell. The client does the work, and it fits a plain form, a worker, or a test:

import { createPasskeyClient } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const passkeys = createPasskeyClient({ rpId: "acme.com", timeoutMs: 60_000 });

const options = await fetch("/api/webauthn/signin/begin", { method: "POST" }).then((r) =>
  r.json(),
);
const assertion = await passkeys.authenticate(options);
await fetch("/api/webauthn/signin/finish", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(assertion),
});

rpId and timeoutMs are only defaults: whatever the server sends always wins.

Injecting a fake credentials (tests)

createPasskeyClient({ credentials }) accepts any object with create and get — the CredentialsContainerLike interface. That is how the SDK tests the ceremonies itself, since jsdom has no navigator.credentials.

docs.title: What your backend must implement
docs.text: Four routes. The SDK never talks to any of them on its own: you pass getOptions and verify.

docs.title: 1. POST /webauthn/register/begin → options
docs.text:
Return a PasskeyCreationOptionsJSON. Every binary field is base64url:

{
  "challenge": "9WVvY2..._Q",
  "rp": { "name": "Acme", "id": "acme.com" },
  "user": { "id": "dXNlci0x", "name": "ada@acme.com", "displayName": "Ada Lovelace" },
  "pubKeyCredParams": [{ "type": "public-key", "alg": -7 }],
  "excludeCredentials": [{ "id": "AQID", "type": "public-key" }],
  "authenticatorSelection": { "residentKey": "required", "userVerification": "preferred" }
}
  • challenge: ≥16 random bytes, stored against the session, single use.
  • user.id: an opaque, stable identifier. Never the e-mail — it changes, and it is burned into the authenticator.
  • excludeCredentials: the credentials the user already has. This is what makes the authenticator answer InvalidStateError (→ already-registered) instead of creating a duplicate.
  • pubKeyCredParams may be omitted: the SDK offers -8 (Ed25519), -7 (ES256) and -257 (RS256) — the exact list is exported as DEFAULT_PUB_KEY_CRED_PARAMS, so the backend can declare the same set without restating the numbers.
  • residentKey: "required" is what makes the passkey discoverable — a prerequisite for signing in without typing anything.

docs.title: 2. POST /webauthn/register/finish ← credential
docs.text:
Receives a PasskeyRegistrationJSON. On the server:

  1. Decode response.clientDataJSON and check type === "webauthn.create", the stored challenge, and the origin.
  2. Parse response.attestationObject, extract the public key and the signature counter.
  3. Store id, the public key, the counter, and response.transports (it helps the later sign-in).

docs.title: 3. POST /webauthn/signin/begin → options
docs.text: A PasskeyRequestOptionsJSON with a fresh challenge. Omit allowCredentials for usernameless sign-in and for autofill — that is what lets the browser offer any passkey for the domain.

docs.title: 4. POST /webauthn/signin/finish ← assertion
docs.text:
Receives a PasskeyAuthenticationJSON:

  1. Look the credential up by id (or by response.userHandle, which is populated for a discoverable credential).
  2. Check clientDataJSON as in step 2, now with type === "webauthn.get".
  3. Verify response.signature over authenticatorData || sha256(clientDataJSON) with the stored public key.
  4. Reject a counter that did not grow — it indicates a cloned credential.
  5. Only then issue the session token.

On the FastAPI side

A server library (py_webauthn, for instance) does steps 1–4. What it does not do is what this page is about: keeping the challenge in the session, choosing user.id, and building excludeCredentials.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• createPasskeyClient — two ceremonies, base64url plumbing, one error type. No framework.
  • usePasskeyRegistration / usePasskeySignIn — state (status, error, data) plus the action. They resolve null on failure.
  • isPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable() decides whether the button appears; platformAvailable === null means "not known yet".
  • conditional: true + autocomplete="username webauthn" is the one-tap sign-in. The attribute is mandatory.
  • kind: "already-registered" is a success, "cancelled" is ambiguous by design, "rp-mismatch" is your bug.
  • The server implements 4 routes; the client invents none of them.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Auth — where to keep the token finish returned
  • HTTP — the api used in the examples
  • Access Control (RBAC) — what the session may do afterwards

docs.title: Payments (Pix and card via Mercado Pago)
docs.text:
The payments module is the frontend half of the tempest-fastapi-sdk checkout: the Pix screen the payer sees, card tokenization in the browser and the text that explains a decline. The other half — creating the charge, deciding it was paid, capturing, refunding — belongs to the backend, and stays there.

Why split it this way?

Two things the backend cannot do: see the card number (that puts the server in PCI DSS scope) and draw the screen. Two things the frontend must not do: decide that a Pix was paid and call the Mercado Pago API with the access token. The module exists so each side keeps its part — and so that is guaranteed by code, not by a warning in the docs.

Section payments-checkout of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: The contract that comes from the backend
docs.text:
The types in this module are the JSON a service built with tempest-fastapi-sdk answers with. They were not written from memory: every field comes from the backend's Pydantic schema (tempest_fastapi_sdk/integrations/payment/base.py, checked on origin/main ec51a886):

Type here Backend schema Line PaymentStatus PaymentStatusEnum base.py:31 PixCharge PixCharge base.py:200 CardChargeRequest CardChargeRequest base.py:514 CardCharge CardCharge base.py:561 PaymentPayer PixPayer base.py:138

Names stay in snake_case because that is what crosses the wire: the backend's BaseSchema has no alias generator. Dates arrive as ISO 8601 strings, and money always in integer cents (amount_cents), never as a float.

status decides; the rest refines

status is the canonical state (pending, authorized, paid, expired, cancelled, refunded, charged_back, in_analysis, failed, unknown). provider_status and status_detail are the provider's raw text — for support and for choosing the right sentence, never for deciding whether it was paid.

docs.title: Step 1 — The Pix screen
docs.text:
A complete program: the app creates the charge on the backend, receives a PixCharge and shows the screen until the backend says it is over.

import { Button, PixCheckout, usePixCharge, type PixCharge } from "tempest-react-sdk";

async function readCharge(id: string, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<PixCharge> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/pix/${id}`, { signal });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return (await response.json()) as PixCharge;
}

export function PixScreen({ created, onNewPix }: { created: PixCharge; onNewPix: () => void }) {
  const { charge, error } = usePixCharge(created, {
    refresh: (signal) => readCharge(created.provider_charge_id, signal),
    intervalMs: 5000,
  });

  return (
    <>
      <PixCheckout
        charge={charge}
        footer={charge.status === "expired" ? <Button onClick={onNewPix}>New Pix</Button> : undefined}
      />
      {error !== null && <p>No connection to the server — retrying.</p>}
    </>
  );
}

Piece by piece:

  1. usePixCharge(created, { refresh }) calls your endpoint every intervalMs — which re-reads the order at Mercado Pago — and stops on its own once the status is final (paid, expired, cancelled, refunded, charged_back, failed).
  2. Reads are sequential: the next one starts intervalMs after the previous one settled. A slow backend never gets overlapping requests.
  3. A failed read keeps the last charge on screen and shows up in error. Polling goes on: a lost request is not a payment state.
  4. <PixCheckout> only shows charge. It changes nothing, so it has no way to decide anything was paid.

What the screen shows, per state:

status Screen pending Amount, QR, copia-e-cola with a copy button, countdown to expires_at pending past the deadline Hides the QR and says it is confirming — not "expired" paid "Pagamento confirmado" expired / cancelled / failed The reason, no QR, and the footer (e.g. "New Pix") unknown — or any status this version does not know "Verificando o pagamento" — never paid, never declined

Why \"confirming\" and not \"expired\" when the clock hits zero?

A Pix sent in the last second can still land. Only the backend, re-reading the order, knows. The screen stops offering the QR and waits for the backend to say expired (Mercado Pago answers canceled / expired, which the backend translates).

docs.title: Where the QR comes from
docs.text:
• qr_code_base64 (Mercado Pago sends it) becomes data:image/png;base64,... — only when it is valid Base64. A strange value never ends up in an image src.
  • Without Base64 (OpenPix sends a URL), the QR is drawn locally from br_code, with the SDK's own <QRCode>. Fetching the URL would hand the payload to an image host for nothing.

docs.title: Push instead of polling
docs.text:
If your backend publishes the charge over SSE or WebSocket, pass subscribe. It combines with refresh:

import { PixCheckout, createEventStream, usePixCharge, type PixCharge } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function LivePixScreen({ created }: { created: PixCharge }) {
  const { charge } = usePixCharge(created, {
    subscribe: (emit) => {
      const stream = createEventStream<PixCharge>(`/api/pix/${created.provider_charge_id}/events`, {
        onMessage: (message) => emit(message.data),
      });
      return () => stream.close();
    },
  });
  return <PixCheckout charge={charge} />;
}

The hook ignores an update for another charge — another provider_charge_id or another provider, because an id is only unique within one provider — and never moves a final state back to a non-final one. And a paid charge only moves on to refunded or charged_back: a late expired does not replace the payment. When polling and push arrive out of order, a payer who already paid never sees "waiting for payment" flash nor is told to "generate a new Pix". The other direction stays open: expired can still become paid, because a Pix sent in the last second can settle after the deadline.

docs.title: Step 2 — Tokenize the card
docs.text:
The backend receives card_token, payment_method_id and installments (the CardChargeRequest). useMercadoPagoCard is what produces them:

import { useState, type FormEvent } from "react";
import { Button, Input, Select, useMercadoPagoCard, type CardChargeRequest } from "tempest-react-sdk";

declare const PUBLIC_KEY: string;

export function CardPayment({ amountCents, reference }: { amountCents: number; reference: string }) {
  const card = useMercadoPagoCard({
    publicKey: PUBLIC_KEY,
    amountCents,
    containers: { cardNumber: "mp-number", expirationDate: "mp-expiry", securityCode: "mp-cvv" },
  });
  const [holder, setHolder] = useState("");
  const [cpf, setCpf] = useState("");
  const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
  const [installments, setInstallments] = useState(1);

  async function pay(event: FormEvent) {
    event.preventDefault();
    const result = await card.tokenize({
      cardholderName: holder,
      installments,
      identificationType: "CPF",
      identificationNumber: cpf,
    });
    const body: CardChargeRequest = {
      amount_cents: amountCents,
      reference,
      card_token: result.token,
      payment_method_id: result.payment_method_id,
      installments: result.installments,
      payer: { email },
    };
    await fetch("/api/card-charges", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={pay}>
      <div id="mp-number" />
      <div id="mp-expiry" />
      <div id="mp-cvv" />
      <Input label="Name on card" value={holder} onChange={(e) => setHolder(e.target.value)} />
      <Input label="CPF" value={cpf} onChange={(e) => setCpf(e.target.value)} />
      <Input label="E-mail" type="email" value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} />
      <Select
        label="Installments"
        value={installments}
        onChange={(e) => setInstallments(Number(e.target.value))}
        options={card.installmentOptions.map((option) => ({
          value: option.installments,
          label: option.recommendedMessage,
        }))}
      />
      <Button type="submit" disabled={card.status !== "ready" || card.paymentMethodId === null}>
        Pay
      </Button>
    </form>
  );
}

Piece by piece:

  1. The three empty <div>s receive Mercado Pago's Secure Fields: iframes served by Mercado Pago itself. Number, expiry and CVV are typed inside them. They never exist in your page's DOM, in React state, in a callback or in a log.
  2. publicKey is the application's Public Key, not the access token. It can only tokenize; the token alone charges nothing.
  3. When the payer types the first digits, Mercado Pago reports the BIN and the hook fetches the installments. recommendedMessage is the provider's own text ("2 parcelas de R$ 57,20 (R$ 114,40)") — show it as it came: there is interest from 2x on, and the total has to be the provider's number.
  4. tokenize returns exactly { token, payment_method_id, installments }. It refuses before calling Mercado Pago when the fields have not loaded, the brand is not identified yet or the installment count is not among the options — each of those would become an opaque 400 on the backend.
  5. Once created, the token is bound to the quote: Mercado Pago returns the tokenized card's first_six_digits, and when they are not the BIN the brand and installments were quoted for, tokenize rejects. binChange is debounced inside the iframe, so a payer who swaps the number and submits at once would send the new card with the old card's brand. Show the error and let the payer submit again once the new installments arrive.
  6. Changing the publicKey remounts empty fields and forgets the previous card's BIN, brand and installments.

PCI scope: why Secure Fields and not <input>

A page that renders its own <input> for the number and calls createCardToken with it has handled cardholder data, however quickly it discards it — and lands in SAQ A-EP. With Secure Fields the number never goes through your JavaScript, which is the condition for SAQ A. That is why the hook does not take the number as a parameter: there is no way to use it wrong.

docs.title: Mercado Pago's script
docs.text:
MercadoPago.js is loaded from https://sdk.mercadopago.com/js/v2 (MERCADO_PAGO_SCRIPT_URL) the first time the hook mounts — one tag only, even with several checkouts on the page. It is not an npm dependency: Mercado Pago publishes the script unversioned, and PCI requires the fields to come straight from the processor.

If your page has a Content-Security-Policy, allow:

script-src  https://sdk.mercadopago.com
frame-src   https://secure-fields.mercadopago.com https://api-static.mercadopago.com
connect-src https://api.mercadopago.com https://api.mercadolibre.com

The hosts were read from the script itself (js_version 2.83.6) on 2026-11-14.

docs.title: What loadMercadoPago trusts
docs.text:
loadMercadoPago trusts two things without checking them, and neither can be checked from inside the page:

  • An existing window.MercadoPago. It is used as is. Whoever can define that global already runs script on your page — and has already read everything the page reads.
  • The src you pass. The default is Mercado Pago's host. An overridden src (a proxy of yours) must serve the identical MercadoPago.js: SAQ A depends on the fields coming from the processor, and a script altered on the way takes the page out of it.

There is no cheap check the library could make instead: the script is unversioned, so there is no stable Subresource Integrity hash to pin; pinning the origin would defeat the reason src exists; and an already-defined global cannot prove where it came from. The real control is the CSP: script-src restricted to https://sdk.mercadopago.com (or your proxy) is what keeps a script from anywhere else out of the checkout page.

docs.title: Step 3 — Explain the card result
docs.text:
The backend returns a CardCharge. A decline is not an error: Mercado Pago answers HTTP 402, and the backend reads that as a charge with status: "failed" and the reason in status_detail. Show it as an answer:

import { Alert, describeCardCharge, type CardCharge } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function CardResult({ charge }: { charge: CardCharge }) {
  const outcome = describeCardCharge(charge);
  return <Alert variant={outcome.tone} title={outcome.title} description={outcome.message} />;
}
status / status_detail Title Text paid / accredited Pagamento aprovado Recebemos o seu pagamento. authorized / waiting_capture Pagamento autorizado O valor foi reservado no seu cartão e só será cobrado quando o pedido for confirmado. failed / rejected_by_issuer Pagamento recusado O banco emissor recusou o pagamento. Use outro cartão ou fale com o banco. failed / bad_filled_card_data Pagamento recusado Confira os dados do cartão: número, validade e código de segurança. failed / unknown reason Pagamento recusado O pagamento não foi aprovado. Tente outro cartão ou outro meio de pagamento.

waiting_capture is a state of its own: money reserved, not charged. The text never says "paid".

The whole table is in CARD_STATUS_DETAIL_MESSAGES — ported from the "Status da transação" table of Mercado Pago's Orders API documentation, read on 2026-11-14, and rewritten for the payer. high_risk does not mention fraud on purpose: telling the payer the anti-fraud system flagged them helps exactly the person it should not. For another language, pass the second argument:

import { describeCardCharge, type CardCharge } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function outcomeInEnglish(charge: CardCharge) {
  return describeCardCharge(charge, { rejected_by_issuer: "Your bank declined the payment." });
}

A status_detail that contradicts the status is ignored (a decline only refines failed), so "declined" and "reserved" never show up on the same screen.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
From the sandbox measured on the backend (2026-10-09), with the test seller account:

  • The test Public Key comes from the same application as the test seller.
  • A card that works: Visa 4235 6477 2802 5682, expiry 11/2030, CVV 123.
  • Holder APRO approves; holder OTHE declines with rejected_by_issuer.
  • The Mastercard test card 5031 4332 1540 6351 answered 422 in the sandbox (cause not isolated) — use the Visa.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Export What it is PixCheckout Pix screen: amount, QR, copia-e-cola, countdown and state. Controlled by charge. usePixCharge Follows the charge through refresh (polling) and/or subscribe (push) until it is final. formatPixRemaining Countdown format: mm:ss, or h:mm:ss above an hour. isFinalPaymentStatus true for paid, expired, cancelled, refunded, charged_back, failed. useMercadoPagoCard Secure Fields + installments by BIN + tokenize. loadMercadoPago Loads MercadoPago.js once per document; a failure is not cached. MERCADO_PAGO_SCRIPT_URL https://sdk.mercadopago.com/js/v2. describeCardCharge CardCharge → { status, tone, title, message, canRetry }. CARD_STATUS_DETAIL_MESSAGES PT-BR text per Orders API status_detail.

Types: PixCharge, CardCharge, CardChargeRequest, PaymentPayer, PaymentStatus, PaymentOutcome, CardTokenResult, CardInstallmentOption, UseMercadoPagoCardOptions, UsePixChargeOptions, PixCheckoutProps, PixCheckoutLabels, MercadoPagoLike, MercadoPagoCardToken.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The backend decides it was paid; the screen only shows what it says. 🔒
  • The card is typed into Mercado Pago's iframes; your code receives only { token, payment_method_id, installments }. ✅
  • Installments show the provider's text, with interest. 💡
  • A decline is an answer (status: "failed" + status_detail), not a network error; waiting_capture is "reserved", not "paid". ⚠️

docs.title: On-device inference cost
docs.text:
When inference runs on the user's device, you lose the server graph. What reaches you is a report: "the app is slow on so-and-so's phone." And without numbers, "slow" can be three different things that call for opposite fixes. 🤔

The perf module measures what a browser can actually observe about a run: how long each stage took, what the device says about itself, and how big the weights you precached are.

There is no energy counter in the browser

No web API reports joules or FLOPs. "Computational cost" here is assembled from what a page can observe from the inside. Anything the platform does not expose comes back null — never a fabricated number.

docs.title: Timing a pipeline
docs.text:
import { createInferenceProfiler } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { Detector } from "tempest-react-sdk/vision";

const profiler = createInferenceProfiler();

const detector = await profiler.stage("load-model", () =>
    Detector.create("/models/detect.onnx"),
);
const results = await profiler.stage("detect", () => detector.predict(blob));

const report = await profiler.report();
console.log(report.timings); // { "load-model": 1840.5, detect: 118.9 }
console.log(report.totalMs); // 1959.4

Three ways to record time:

Method For stage(name, fn) Async work — the resolved value passes straight through stageSync(name, fn) Sync work — same, without the await mark(name, ms) A duration you already measured elsewhere

Repeated names accumulate, so two passes of the same kind add up into a single row.

A stage that throws is still measured

stage() records the duration in a finally and rethrows. A pipeline that failed also has a timing story to tell — usually the interesting one.

docs.title: ⚠️ Concurrent stages do not partition the total
docs.text:
Stages are measured independently, not as a tiling of the run. Two stages started together are each charged their full wall-clock span:

const profiler = createInferenceProfiler();

const [model, image] = await Promise.all([
    profiler.stage("models", () => Detector.create("/models/detect.onnx")),
    profiler.stage("decode", () => createImageBitmap(blob)),
]);

const report = await profiler.report();
// timings.models + timings.decode > report.totalMs — and that is correct:
// the two ran at the same time.

That is the honest reading for a pipeline that decodes the image while the sessions are still loading. Just do not draw the bars as if they split the total — tell the user they are indicative fractions.

docs.title: Folding in /vision's speed
docs.text:
Every predict() from the /vision subpath already returns its own breakdown in results[0].speed (load, preprocess, inference, postprocess). Fold whatever matters into the report with mark:

const results = await profiler.stage("detect", () => detector.predict(blob));
profiler.mark("forward-pass", results[0].speed.inference);

Now the report holds the cost of the whole call and of the kernel — and the gap between them is exactly how much pre/post-processing you are paying for.

docs.title: The device profile
docs.text:
import { readDeviceProfile } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const device = readDeviceProfile();
// { hardwareConcurrency: 8, deviceMemoryGb: 8, jsHeapUsedMb: 137.4 }
Field Source Available in hardwareConcurrency navigator.hardwareConcurrency Every modern browser deviceMemoryGb navigator.deviceMemory Chromium only jsHeapUsedMb performance.memory Chromium only (non-standard)

On Firefox and Safari the last two are null. report() already includes this profile, so you rarely call it directly — the function exists for when you want the data outside a run.

SSR-safe

Without a navigator, every field is null instead of throwing.

docs.title: How much the models weigh
docs.text:
Models you download and precache in Cache Storage are the biggest fixed cost of an on-device inference app. report() measures the ones you list:

const report = await profiler.report({
    models: [
        { name: "detector", cacheName: "app-models", url: "/models/detect.onnx" },
        { name: "classifier", cacheName: "app-models", url: "/models/classify.onnx" },
    ],
});

console.log(report.models);
// [ { name: "detector", bytes: 12582912 }, { name: "classifier", bytes: null } ]

bytes: null means one of three things: the model is not cached, Cache Storage is unavailable, or the stored response carries no Content-Length (a chunked transfer).

Why the header and not the body

Reading (await response.blob()).size would pull tens of megabytes of weights into memory just to learn the length — on every measurement. cachedResponseBytes reads only the Content-Length.

docs.title: Rendering it
docs.text:
formatDurationMs covers the range that matters here: milliseconds for a forward pass, seconds for a cold start.

import { formatBytes, formatDurationMs } from "tempest-react-sdk";

formatDurationMs(0.04); // "<1 ms"   — measured, just very fast
formatDurationMs(142.6); // "143 ms"
formatDurationMs(4321); // "4.32 s"
formatDurationMs(NaN); // "—"

formatBytes(12582912); // "12 MB"

"<1 ms" is deliberate: "0 ms" would read as "not measured".

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• createInferenceProfiler() → stage / stageSync / mark → report(). ✅
  • Concurrent stages sum to more than totalMs — say so in the UI.
  • /vision's results[0].speed folds into the report via mark.
  • Fields the platform withholds come back null, so the UI can show "—".
  • formatDurationMs + formatBytes for display.

docs.title: Web Push + Service Worker
docs.text:
Browser push notifications have two halves that talk to each other: the main thread (your UI asks for permission and creates the subscription) and the worker thread (the service worker receives the push and draws the notification, even with the tab closed). The push module of tempest-react-sdk covers both halves — the browser side (permission, pushManager.subscribe, notificationclick) belongs to the SDK; the persistence endpoints and the push delivery belong to your app, through callbacks.

Editable diagram: push-flow.drawio (open it in draw.io).

Section notification-center of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

Section integrations of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: How Web Push works (the 30-second view)
docs.text:
1. The app asks the user for permission (Notification.requestPermission()).
  2. Once granted, the browser creates a PushSubscription signed with your VAPID public key.
  3. The app sends the subscription JSON to your backend, which stores it.
  4. Later, the backend uses the VAPID private key to send a push to the subscription's endpoint.
  5. The service worker wakes up on the push event, reads the payload, and calls showNotification.

The SDK gives you steps 1–3 (and the step-5 handlers); steps 3 (storage) and 4 (delivery) are the backend's responsibility.

What VAPID is, in one sentence

VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) is a key pair (public + private) that identifies your server to the browser's push service. The public one goes in the front end (VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY); the private one stays on the backend and is never exposed. Generate the pair once with npx web-push generate-vapid-keys.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. A backend that stores PushSubscriptionJSON and sends notifications via web-push (VAPID).
  2. A registered service worker (vite-plugin-pwa, registerServiceWorker, or navigator.serviceWorker.register).
  3. A VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY variable in the front end (the URL-safe base64 VAPID public key).
  4. HTTPS, or localhost. Service workers and the Push API do not exist on an insecure origin — including the LAN IP (http://192.168.0.10:5173) you test the phone against. Use an HTTPS tunnel (cloudflared, ngrok) for that.

The hook does NOT register the service worker

usePushSubscription assumes the SW is already registered and uses navigator.serviceWorker.ready by default. Register the SW yourself (step below) — or pass getRegistration to reuse your own registration. Without a registered SW, subscribe() never resolves.

docs.title: Adopting it in an app that already exists
docs.text:
This section is for the common case: the app is already live and you are switching push on now. Nothing here asks you to adopt the scaffold, createViteConfig, or become a PWA.

The checklist, in order:

  1. Generate the VAPID pair and put the public half in the front end.
  2. Have a service worker served from the root (three scenarios below).
  3. Install the push handlers inside that SW.
  4. Agree the contract for two endpoints with your backend.
  5. Wire usePushSubscription to a button.
  6. Tie subscribe/unsubscribe to login and logout — the step almost everybody forgets.

docs.title: 1. VAPID keys
docs.text:
npx web-push generate-vapid-keys

# .env — only the public half reaches the front end
VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=BOxx…

The private half stays on the backend. Changing this pair later invalidates every existing subscription — see key rotation.

docs.title: 2. The service worker: three scenarios
docs.text:
The SW file has to be served from the root of its scope

A service worker only controls pages under its own path: an /assets/sw-abc123.js controls /assets/… and nothing else — so navigator.serviceWorker.ready never resolves on your home page and subscribe() hangs forever, with nothing in the console.

It is the most common way switching push on fails in a bundled app: the SW cannot go through the hashed asset pipeline. It has to land at /sw.js (or be served with a Service-Worker-Allowed: / header). Check it in DevTools → Application → Service workers: Scope must read /.

a. I have no service worker at allb. I already use vite-plugin-pwac. I already have my own SW

Create src/sw.ts and bundle it separately from the app, because the app's entry goes through the asset pipeline and the SW must not:

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import {
  installNotificationClickHandler,
  installPushHandler,
  installSkipWaitingListener,
} from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

declare const self: ServiceWorkerGlobalScope;

installSkipWaitingListener();
installPushHandler({ defaultTitle: "My App", defaultIcon: "/icons/logo.png" });
installNotificationClickHandler();

// vite.sw.config.ts — builds the worker alone, to dist/sw.js
import { resolve } from "node:path";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    emptyOutDir: false, // keeps the app's dist/ intact
    lib: {
      entry: resolve(__dirname, "src/sw.ts"),
      formats: ["iife"], // classic worker, no import/export
      name: "sw",
      fileName: () => "sw.js",
    },
    rollupOptions: { output: { entryFileNames: "sw.js", inlineDynamicImports: true } },
  },
});

{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build && npm run build:sw",
    "build:sw": "vite build --config vite.sw.config.ts"
  }
}

Register it from the app entry:

// src/main.tsx
import { registerServiceWorker } from "tempest-react-sdk";

registerServiceWorker({ url: "/sw.js" });

No build step, if you prefer

A hand-written public/sw.js works too — files in public/ are copied verbatim to the root of dist/. The cost is that you cannot import the SDK helpers in there: you write the push and notificationclick listeners yourself. Fine for the simple case; past that, bundle it.

Only injectManifest mode lets you write the SW. If yours is on generateSW (the default), switch:

// vite.config.ts
VitePWA({
  strategies: "injectManifest",
  srcDir: "src",
  filename: "sw.ts",
  injectRegister: "auto",
});

Then in src/sw.ts, put the SDK handlers next to your Workbox ones — they do not compete, they are different events (push/notificationclick on one side, fetch on the other):

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import { precacheAndRoute } from "workbox-precaching";
import { installNotificationClickHandler, installPushHandler } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

declare const self: ServiceWorkerGlobalScope & { __WB_MANIFEST: unknown[] };

precacheAndRoute(self.__WB_MANIFEST); // what the plugin already did
installPushHandler({ defaultTitle: "My App" });
installNotificationClickHandler();

Keep the plugin's registration (virtual:pwa-register) — do not call registerServiceWorker as well: two registrations of the same file fight over the update cycle.

Two lines inside what you already have, and none of your code changes:

import { installNotificationClickHandler, installPushHandler } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installPushHandler({ defaultTitle: "My App" });
installNotificationClickHandler();

Already have your own addEventListener("push", …)? Pick one of the two: both handlers running show two notifications for the same push, because each one calls showNotification.

If you register the SW yourself and want to reuse that registration instead of navigator.serviceWorker.ready, pass getRegistration:

const registration = await navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js");

usePushSubscription({
  vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
  getRegistration: async () => registration,
  onSubscribe: (sub) => api.post("/webpush/subscribe", { body: sub }),
});

docs.title: 3. The contract with your backend
docs.text:
The SDK picks no route, verb or format — it hands you the PushSubscriptionJSON and you decide. This is exactly what reaches onSubscribe:

{
  "endpoint": "https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/dQw4w9Wg...",
  "expirationTime": null,
  "keys": {
    "p256dh": "BNcRdreALRFXTkOOUHK1EtK2wtaz5Ry4YfYCA_0QTpQtUbVlUls0VJXg7A8u-Ts1XbjhazAkj7I99e8QcYP7DkM=",
    "auth": "tBHItJI5svbpez7KI4CCXg=="
  }
}

Two routes close the cycle — and the natural key is the endpoint, not the user:

Route When Body POST /webpush/subscribe subscribed (or re-synced) the JSON above + the logged-in user, from the token DELETE /webpush/subscribe unsubscribed { "endpoint": "…" }

One user has N subscriptions, one per browser

Phone, work laptop, Chrome and Firefox on the same machine: each is a subscription with its own endpoint. If the backend stores one subscription per user (UPDATE … WHERE user_id = ?), every new device silently switches the previous one off — the user installs on their phone and stops receiving on the desktop, with nothing explaining why.

Store one row per endpoint, with UNIQUE(endpoint) and an indexed user_id. The POST is an upsert by endpoint: the same browser re-sending the same subscription (which happens on every subscribe() — see re-syncing) must not create a duplicate row.

docs.title: Register the SW
docs.text:
import { registerServiceWorker, skipWaiting } from "tempest-react-sdk";

registerServiceWorker({
  url: "/sw.js",
  onUpdate: (waiting) => {
    if (confirm("New version available. Reload?")) {
      skipWaiting(waiting);
      window.location.reload();
    }
  },
});

Auto-update (no vite-plugin-pwa)

If you'd rather have every deploy reach the user on its own — no "reload?" prompt — turn on autoUpdate. The helper then calls registration.update() on an interval (updateIntervalMs, default 1h) and reloads the page as soon as a new worker takes control (controllerchange), guarded against reload loops. It's the vite-plugin-pwa auto-update behaviour, implemented directly on navigator.serviceWorker with no dependency on it:

import { registerServiceWorker } from "tempest-react-sdk";

registerServiceWorker({
  url: "/sw.js",
  autoUpdate: true, // poll + reload on controllerchange
  updateIntervalMs: 60 * 60 * 1000, // 1h (default)
  reloadOnActivate: true, // default; set `false` to only poll
});

Set reloadOnActivate: false when you want to keep polling but control the reload yourself (e.g. show a toast first).

docs.title: Subscribe the user (with the hook)
docs.text:
import { usePushSubscription, Button } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const push = usePushSubscription({
  vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
  onSubscribe: (sub) => api.post("/webpush/subscribe", { body: sub }),
  onUnsubscribe: (sub) => api.delete("/webpush/subscribe", { body: { endpoint: sub.endpoint } }),
});

<Button loading={push.loading} onClick={() => push.subscribe()}>
  {push.subscribed ? "Unsubscribe" : "Receive notifications"}
</Button>;

The hook exposes supported, permission, subscribed, loading, error, subscribe(), unsubscribe(), and refresh(). Imperative version: WebPushClient. Typed errors: WebPushUnsupportedError, WebPushPermissionDeniedError.

docs.title: What subscribe() does, step by step
docs.text:
1. Notification.requestPermission() — the browser prompt. A refusal throws WebPushPermissionDeniedError.
  2. Gets the registration (navigator.serviceWorker.ready, or your getRegistration).
  3. If a subscription already exists in this browser, it reuses it and calls onSubscribe again.
  4. If none exists, it creates one with pushManager.subscribe({ userVisibleOnly: true, applicationServerKey }) and calls onSubscribe.

docs.title: What happens when a subscription already exists
docs.text:
Step 3 is deliberate, and it is what makes the button double as a re-sync: calling subscribe() in a browser that is already subscribed creates nothing new — it re-sends the same subscription to your backend. That recovers the case where the database lost the row (a restore, a migration, an environment swap) while the browser stayed subscribed: without the re-send, that device would be subscribed in the browser and unknown on the server — mute forever.

The price is on the backend: the POST must be an upsert by endpoint. A blind insert turns one device into two rows, and the user gets every notification twice.

subscribed always starts out false

Knowing whether a subscription exists takes await pushManager.getSubscription(), so the first render cannot know the answer: the hook returns false and corrects itself right after. A button that reads only subscribed flashes "Receive notifications" before turning into "Unsubscribe".

Let the state settle before deciding the label — loading is false during that window, so use your own "already checked" flag:

const push = usePushSubscription({ /* … */ });
const [checked, setChecked] = useState(false);

useEffect(() => {
    void push.refresh().finally(() => setChecked(true));
}, [push.refresh]);

if (!checked) return <Skeleton height={40} />;

refresh() is for state that changes outside your app

The user grants or blocks notifications in browser settings, or drops the subscription from chrome://settings/content/notifications, and your React never hears about it — there is no event for that. Call refresh() when the tab becomes visible again:

useEffect(() => {
    const onVisible = () => {
        if (document.visibilityState === "visible") void push.refresh();
    };
    document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", onVisible);
    return () => document.removeEventListener("visibilitychange", onVisible);
}, [push.refresh]);

docs.title: Permission and subscription flow (complete example)
docs.text:
This component shows the full lifecycle state — unsupported, permission denied, subscribed, toggle — and handles the permission-denied error:

import { usePushSubscription, WebPushPermissionDeniedError, Button } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { api } from "./api";

export function PushToggle() {
  const push = usePushSubscription({
    vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
    onSubscribe: (sub) => api.post("/webpush/subscribe", { body: sub }),
    onUnsubscribe: (sub) =>
      api.delete("/webpush/subscribe", { body: { endpoint: sub.endpoint } }),
  });

  // 1. Browser without support (iOS Safari outside a PWA, old browsers)
  if (!push.supported) {
    return <p>Notifications are not supported in this browser.</p>;
  }

  // 2. User blocked it in the browser settings
  if (push.permission === "denied") {
    return <p>Notification permission blocked. Allow it in the browser settings.</p>;
  }

  async function handleSubscribe() {
    try {
      await push.subscribe();
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof WebPushPermissionDeniedError) {
        alert("You need to allow notifications to receive them.");
      }
    }
  }

  // 3. Toggle the subscription
  return (
    <Button
      loading={push.loading}
      onClick={() => (push.subscribed ? push.unsubscribe() : handleSubscribe())}
    >
      {push.subscribed ? "Unsubscribe" : "Receive notifications"}
    </Button>
  );
}

docs.title: Unsubscribing — what almost everybody gets wrong
docs.text:
unsubscribe() does two things, in this order:

  1. it calls onUnsubscribe(subscription) — your delete route, while the endpoint is still live;
  2. it calls subscription.unsubscribe() in the browser — always, even when step 1 failed.

If the backend failed, unsubscribe() throws WebPushUnsubscribeError after releasing the browser. The error carries subscription (with the endpoint, so you can retry the DELETE later), browserUnsubscribed, and the original cause — an AggregateError holding both errors (backend first) when the browser failed too, so the endpoint is never traded for a bare DOMException. usePushSubscription already reflects it: subscribed becomes false and error holds the WebPushUnsubscribeError.

Why release the browser anyway: the two failures do not cost the same.

What is left behind when the backend fails Cost An orphaned row in the database (browser released) one send to a dead endpoint, which the push service answers with 404/410 — and the backend deletes the row (see below) A live subscription in the browser (the behaviour before 0.77.0) the browser keeps delivering this account's notifications to whoever uses it next

And the DELETE fails precisely when unsubscribing matters most: at the end of a session, when the token that authenticates it is already gone. The endpoint is not lost either — it is read before both calls and travels in the error.

docs.title: Delete by endpoint, not by session
docs.text:
const push = usePushSubscription({
  vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
  onSubscribe: (sub) => api.post("/webpush/subscribe", { body: sub }),
  // ✅ the argument is the subscription being removed — use its endpoint
  onUnsubscribe: (sub) => api.delete("/webpush/subscribe", { body: { endpoint: sub.endpoint } }),
});

// ❌ ignores the argument: the backend only knows "some device of this user left"
onUnsubscribe: () => api.delete("/webpush/my"),

The second pattern only works while the user has one device. With two, the backend either deletes them all (the phone stops receiving because you switched off on the desktop) or deletes an arbitrary one (and the desktop starts receiving again on its own later). The endpoint is what identifies the device — that is precisely why it is in the argument.

docs.title: Unsubscribing does not revoke permission
docs.text:
Notification.permission stays "granted" after unsubscribe(), and there is no API to revoke it — only the user can, in browser settings.

The practical consequence: permission === "granted" does not mean subscribed. subscribed is what decides the button label; permission only tells you whether you may still ask ("default") or are blocked from outside ("denied"). A second subscribe() after unsubscribing shows no prompt at all — the permission is already there — and comes back instantly.

docs.title: Logout and user switching
docs.text:
This is the hole that shows up in production, not in testing. The subscription belongs to the browser, not the user: if Ana logs out and Bruno logs in on the same Chrome, the endpoint is unchanged — and still tied to Ana in your database. Bruno starts receiving Ana's notifications, on his device, with the app showing his own account.

Unsubscribe when the session ends — not only on the sign-out button. The session also ends on its own (refresh token revoked, refresh failed), and that path does not go through your logout(). With createTempestAuth, the place is onSessionEnd, which runs on both:

import { WebPushClient, WebPushUnsubscribeError, createTempestAuth } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const ORPHANED_PUSH_KEY = "push-orphaned-subscriptions";

export const auth = createTempestAuth({
    baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
    onSessionEnd: async (session) => {
        const push = new WebPushClient({
            vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
            onSubscribe: () => {},
            onUnsubscribe: (sub) =>
                session.api.delete("/webpush/subscribe", { body: { endpoint: sub.endpoint } }),
        });
        try {
            await push.unsubscribe();
        } catch (error) {
            if (!(error instanceof WebPushUnsubscribeError)) return;
            const pending: PushSubscriptionJSON[] = JSON.parse(
                localStorage.getItem(ORPHANED_PUSH_KEY) ?? "[]",
            );
            localStorage.setItem(ORPHANED_PUSH_KEY, JSON.stringify([...pending, error.subscription]));
        }
    },
});

Two pieces make this work with no warning for you to remember:

  • session.api still sends the ended session's token — the store has already been cleared, so auth.api no longer does. On an explicit sign-out the DELETE goes out authenticated and deletes the row.
  • The catch keeps the WebPushUnsubscribeError's subscription: on the next login, resend the DELETE for each stored endpoint and clear the list. Dropping the error with .catch(() => false) would throw away exactly the orphaned row's endpoint.
  • On automatic expiry the server already refuses that token, the DELETE comes back 401 — and the browser is released all the same, because unsubscribe() always releases it. The orphaned row goes away on the next send, with the 404/410.

The full order, and what else to clear in the same hook, is in Auth → Ending the session. Without createTempestAuth, call the same push.unsubscribe() in your logout before discarding the token, and also on the path where your HTTP client gives up on the session.

If you do not want to lose the permission you earned

unsubscribe() on logout keeps the permission (see above), so the next login only needs a subscribe() — no prompt, instant. Call it on login success, not from an onboarding screen:

async function onLoginSuccess() {
    if (Notification.permission === "granted") await push.subscribe();
}

That also covers the device that was away for months: one subscribe() per login re-syncs the endpoint with the backend without bothering anybody.

Never call unsubscribe() in beforeunload

Closing the tab is not leaving the app — the subscription exists to receive push while the app is closed. Unsubscribing there switches push off for everyone who closes a tab, and beforeunload does not await a promise: the DELETE probably never leaves.

docs.title: Keeping the subscription alive
docs.text: A subscription is not forever, and all three ways it dies are silent.

docs.title: pushsubscriptionchange: the browser swaps it on its own
docs.text:
The browser may invalidate and recreate the subscription by itself — an internal push-service key change, a reinstall on Android, time. The endpoint changes, your database keeps the old one, and push simply stops arriving weeks after everything worked.

The SDK ships no helper for this (the event only exists inside the worker and its support is still uneven). It is 15 lines in your sw.ts:

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import { urlBase64ToUint8Array } from "tempest-react-sdk";

declare const self: ServiceWorkerGlobalScope;

const VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY = "BOxx…"; // the same one the front end uses

self.addEventListener("pushsubscriptionchange", (event: Event) => {
    const change = event as Event & { oldSubscription?: PushSubscription };
    event.waitUntil(
        (async () => {
            const fresh = await self.registration.pushManager.subscribe({
                userVisibleOnly: true,
                applicationServerKey: urlBase64ToUint8Array(VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY),
            });
            await fetch("/webpush/subscribe", {
                method: "POST",
                headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
                body: JSON.stringify({
                    subscription: fresh.toJSON(),
                    replaces: change.oldSubscription?.endpoint ?? null,
                }),
            });
        })(),
    );
});

With no session cookie, the worker needs another way to authenticate

The worker's fetch does not have your in-memory token. If your auth is an HttpOnly cookie, it rides along and this just works. If it is Authorization: Bearer, accept this route via replaces (the old endpoint already identifies the owner) or keep the token in IndexedDB to read here.

docs.title: 404/410 from the push service: delete on the backend
docs.text:
When the user revokes permission, clears site data or uninstalls the PWA, nobody tells you — the next send answers 404 Not Found or 410 Gone. Treat both as "delete this row", or your table fills with dead endpoints and every send gets slower:

# backend (pywebpush example)
from pywebpush import WebPushException, webpush

try:
    webpush(subscription_info=sub, data=payload, vapid_private_key=KEY, vapid_claims=CLAIMS)
except WebPushException as exc:
    if exc.response is not None and exc.response.status_code in (404, 410):
        subscriptions.delete(endpoint=sub["endpoint"])
    else:
        raise

docs.title: Rotating the VAPID key
docs.text:
A subscription is signed with the public key that created it. Changing the VAPID pair invalidates every one of them: sends start failing with 403.

And there is a trap here: because subscribe() reuses the existing subscription, calling it after changing the key fixes nothing — it re-sends the old subscription, signed with the old key. The way through is unsubscribe, then subscribe:

await push.unsubscribe(); // clears browser + backend
await push.subscribe(); // creates one with the new key (no prompt: permission is already granted)

If you need this across your whole base, version the key on the client and compare it against the one that created the subscription:

import { urlBase64ToUint8Array } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const sub = await client.getSubscription();
const current = sub?.options.applicationServerKey; // ArrayBuffer | null
const stale =
    !!current &&
    new Uint8Array(current).toString() !==
        new Uint8Array(urlBase64ToUint8Array(VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY)).toString();

if (stale) {
    await client.unsubscribe();
    await client.subscribe();
}

Better still: do not rotate. Keep the VAPID pair as a long-lived secret — it identifies no user, only your server.

docs.title: Imperative version — WebPushClient
docs.text:
When you need the flow outside React (a vanilla button, a setup script), use the class directly:

import { WebPushClient } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const client = new WebPushClient({
  vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY,
  onSubscribe: async (sub) => {
    await fetch("/webpush/subscribe", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(sub) });
  },
});

if (WebPushClient.isSupported()) {
  await client.subscribe(); // asks for permission + creates subscription + calls onSubscribe
}

docs.title: Worker-thread (sw.ts)
docs.text:
Inside your service worker, import the handlers from the tempest-react-sdk/sw subpath:

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import {
  installPushHandler,
  installNotificationClickHandler,
  installSkipWaitingListener,
} from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installSkipWaitingListener();

installPushHandler({
  defaultTitle: "Tempest",
  defaultIcon: "/icons/Logo.png",
  transform: (payload) => (payload.tag === "silent-ping" ? null : payload),
});

installNotificationClickHandler();

Import from tempest-react-sdk/sw, not the root barrel

The worker helpers have a dedicated subpath: tempest-react-sdk/sw. It is pure and React-free — importing from it keeps your sw.ts bundle tiny (~1 KB) and stops the SDK's component graph from leaking into the worker scope. Importing from the root barrel (tempest-react-sdk) also works thanks to tree-shaking, but the subpath is the bulletproof way. It's exactly what create-tempest-app --pwa generates.

installPushHandler tries event.data.json() and falls back to event.data.text(). Use transform to suppress (null) or enrich notifications.

installNotificationClickHandler focuses the tab that is exactly on the target URL, or opens a new window. The comparison is on the whole URL, resolved against the tab's origin: /events/1 does not focus a tab on /events/10, and / does not focus any open tab.

docs.title: Action buttons and notification options
docs.text:
Every NotificationOptions field the payload carries reaches the browser: actions, requireInteraction, vibrate, silent, renotify, timestamp, dir and lang, alongside body, icon, badge, image and tag. A missing field stays missing, and the browser applies its own default.

Each button can carry its own url. This is what the backend sends:

{
  "title": "Your event is tomorrow",
  "url": "/events/details/42",
  "actions": [
    { "action": "hello", "title": "Say hello", "url": "/events/details/42#hello" },
    { "action": "later", "title": "Later" }
  ],
  "vibrate": [100, 50, 100]
}

The click resolves like this:

Where the user clicked URL opened On the notification body top-level url (/events/details/42) On the hello button the action's url (/events/details/42#hello) On the later button, which has no url top-level url

Why the action url goes into data.actionUrls

The browser's NotificationAction only knows action, title and icon — a url there would be dropped. installPushHandler takes each button's url out and stores the map { hello: "/events/details/42#hello" } in notification.data.actionUrls; installNotificationClickHandler reads that map through event.action.

With your own resolveUrl, you get the clicked action as the second argument ("" or undefined for a body click):

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import { installNotificationClickHandler } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installNotificationClickHandler({
  resolveUrl: (data, action) => {
    const { url } = data as { url: string };
    return action === "hello" ? `${url}?compose=1` : url;
  },
});

docs.title: Where a click may go
docs.text:
Two rules apply since 0.82.0:

  • data does not override the destination. installPushHandler spreads the payload's data before writing url and actionUrls. Until 0.81.0 it was after, and { "url": "/orders/9", "data": { "url": "https://other.site" } } opened https://other.site — and data is often filled from the record that triggered the push.
  • The default resolver only opens pages of the worker's own origin. A URL on another origin, or with a scheme other than http:/https: (javascript:, data:), becomes "/". A resolveUrl of your own is how an app picks another origin — what it returns may go to any http(s), and any other scheme still becomes "/".

Upgrading from 0.81 or earlier: the destination leaves data.url

A server that sent the destination only in data.url started opening "/" in 0.82.0 — with no error: the notification looks the same, only the click loses its deep link. The SDK does not go back to reading data.url (that is the rule above), so the fix is on the server, moving the destination to the top-level url:

{ "title": "New notice", "data": { "url": "/notices/42", "noticeId": 42 } }

becomes

{ "title": "New notice", "url": "/notices/42", "data": { "noticeId": 42 } }

Since 0.87.0 installPushHandler logs one console.warn per worker when a payload arrives in the old shape (a string data.url and no top-level url). The warning does not depend on a development build — real pushes usually reach production first — and does not echo the URL. To see it: DevTools → Application → Service workers → the worker's link opens its console.

Backend on tempest-fastapi-sdk: since 0.363.0 its WebPushPayloadSchema has the top-level url and, so that code following the old example keeps working, lifts a string data["url"] into url when no top-level url was given — with tempest-fastapi-sdk>=0.363.0 the payload already ships in the right shape and the warning above never fires. The contract between both sides is pinned by tests/webpush/test_payload_contract.py in that repository.

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import { installNotificationClickHandler } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

const PARTNERS = new Set(["https://partner.example.com"]);

installNotificationClickHandler({
  resolveUrl: (data) => {
    const { url } = data as { url: string };
    return PARTNERS.has(new URL(url, self.location.origin).origin) ? url : "/";
  },
});

How many buttons show up

The browser shows up to Notification.maxActions buttons (2 on desktop Chrome) and ignores the rest. Safari and Firefox draw no buttons at all — the body click keeps working everywhere.

Offline caching lives in the same module

tempest-react-sdk/sw also exports installPrecache (offline app shell) and installRuntimeCache (per-route caching: cache-first / network-first / stale-while-revalidate). Together with the tempestPwaManifest() plugin from tempest-react-sdk/vite, they reach parity with vite-plugin-pwa for the common case — with no new dependency. It's what create-tempest-app --pwa wires for you.

urlBase64ToUint8Array and isPushSupported are exported

You rarely call them by hand — WebPushClient already uses both internally (applicationServerKey requires a Uint8Array, not the base64 string). They're in the barrel for anyone who needs a support check outside the hook (isPushSupported()) or a fully custom subscription flow.

docs.title: An in-app inbox (NotificationCenter)
docs.text:
A push shows an OS notification and then disappears — as far as your UI is concerned it never existed. A user who dismissed the toast has nowhere to find it again. That is the missing half of web push: an inbox inside the app.

The service worker runs outside the page and cannot touch React state. The bridge is a message:

// src/sw.ts — inside your push handler
self.addEventListener("push", (event) => {
    const payload = event.data?.json() ?? {};
    event.waitUntil(
        (async () => {
            await self.registration.showNotification(payload.title, payload);
            const clients = await self.clients.matchAll({ includeUncontrolled: true });
            for (const client of clients) {
                client.postMessage({ type: "tempest:notification", notification: payload });
            }
        })(),
    );
});

In the app, useNotificationInbox listens for that message by default:

import { NotificationCenter, useNotificationInbox, Popover, Button } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function NotificationsButton() {
    const inbox = useNotificationInbox();

    return (
        <Popover
            trigger={
                <Button variant="ghost" aria-label={`Notifications (${inbox.unreadCount} unread)`}>
                    🔔 {inbox.unreadCount > 0 && inbox.unreadCount}
                </Button>
            }
        >
            <NotificationCenter
                items={inbox.items}
                onMarkRead={inbox.markRead}
                onMarkAllRead={inbox.markAllRead}
                onDismiss={inbox.remove}
                onSelect={(item) => item.url && navigate(item.url)}
            />
        </Popover>
    );
}

docs.title: useNotificationInbox
NotificationCenter
Compatibility
docs.text:
• iOS Safari only works when the app is installed as a PWA (Add to Home Screen) — and the app needs a manifest.json with display: "standalone" to be installable at all. Outside that, isPushSupported() answers false on iOS even on current Safari: that is not your bug.
  • usePushSubscription exposes supported — hide the toggle when false.
  • An insecure origin (http:// that is not localhost) has neither service workers nor the Push API.

docs.title: When no notification arrives: where to look
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Where to confirm subscribe() never resolves the SW does not control the page (wrong scope, or never registered) DevTools → Application → Service workers: Scope must be / and status activated supported === false on iOS the app is not installed as a PWA Add to Home Screen, then open from the icon Subscribed, backend got nothing onSubscribe failed silently the hook's error; subscribe() re-throws, so handle the catch Push dies weeks later the browser rotated the subscription pushsubscriptionchange Send answers 403 VAPID pair changed, or the front-end public key is not the pair of the backend's private one key rotation Send answers 404/410 user revoked/cleared data; dead endpoint delete the row (above) Duplicated notification two push handlers in the SW, or a POST that is not an upsert by endpoint your sw.ts; the subscriptions table A user gets another account's notification no unsubscribe on logout logout and user switching ReferenceError: window is not defined in the SW SDK older than 0.28.1 using urlBase64ToUint8Array in the worker upgrade the SDK A click opens / instead of the deep link the server sends the destination only in data.url, which the SDK has not read since 0.82.0 the worker console (installPushHandler warning); migration

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• VAPID: public in the front end, private on the backend only. Generate it once with web-push and do not rotate — changing it invalidates every existing subscription.
  • You register the SW; the hook only subscribes/unsubscribes over a ready registration. The file has to be served at /sw.js — a hashed SW inside /assets/ does not control your home page, and then subscribe() hangs with no error.
  • In an app that already exists: three SW scenarios (none, vite-plugin-pwa on injectManifest, your own SW) — none of them asks you to adopt the rest of the SDK.
  • A subscription belongs to the browser, not the user: store one row per endpoint (UNIQUE), upsert on POST, and delete by endpoint on DELETE. A user has as many devices as they like.
  • Unsubscribe on logout, before discarding the token — otherwise the next user of that browser receives the previous one's notifications. The permission survives, so the next login re-subscribes with no prompt.
  • unsubscribe() does not revoke permission: permission === "granted" does not mean subscribed. subscribed owns the button label.
  • subscribed starts false (the check is async) and refresh() exists for state that changes outside the app (browser settings).
  • A subscription dies silently: handle pushsubscriptionchange in the worker and delete on 404/410 on the backend.
  • usePushSubscription gives you all the state (supported/permission/subscribed/loading/error) + actions; WebPushClient is the imperative version.
  • Worker handlers (installPushHandler/installNotificationClickHandler/installSkipWaitingListener) go inside your sw.ts.
  • iOS only receives push in an installed PWA — hide the toggle when !supported.
  • useNotificationInbox + NotificationCenter close the loop: the worker postMessages, the hook holds the list (filtered by type, capped by limit) and the panel shows read/unread with a per-item action. Persistence stays with the app, via onChange/initialItems.
