docs.title: PWA & Offline-First
docs.text:
tempest-react-sdk ships everything a Tempest app needs to become an offline-first PWA — with no dependency on Workbox or vite-plugin-pwa. This page is the map: service-worker registration and updates, caching, background sync, storage durability and the status UI. The sync engine (createOfflineSync) has its own recipe in Offline Sync (FastAPI) — here we cover the PWA layer around it.

The pieces

Layer What it does Where it runs tempest-react-sdk/vite generates manifest, icons, dev SW build (Vite) tempest-react-sdk/sw precache, runtime cache, background sync inside sw.ts hooks + components update, status, quota, indicators main thread (React)

docs.title: 1. Register the service worker and update with consent
docs.text:
registerServiceWorker handles register() + update detection. For the user-driven flow ("New version — update"), use the useServiceWorkerUpdate hook with the <UpdatePrompt> component:

import { useServiceWorkerUpdate, UpdatePrompt } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function ServiceWorkerGate() {
  const { updateAvailable, applyUpdate } = useServiceWorkerUpdate({ url: "/sw.js" });
  return <UpdatePrompt open={updateAvailable} onUpdate={applyUpdate} />;
}

When a new worker finishes installing, updateAvailable flips to true; applyUpdate() activates the waiting worker (skipWaiting) and reloads the page once it takes control.

It also catches the worker that was already waiting

The common case fires no event at all: the user opened the app after a deploy (the new worker installed and went to waiting), closed the tab, and came back later. On that second visit updatefound never fires — install already happened. registerServiceWorker reads registration.waiting as soon as the registration resolves, so updateAvailable flips just the same. Each worker is announced once, even when both routes apply in one session, and neither fires on a first install (no controller) — that is onReady, not an update.

Keep autoUpdate off here

useServiceWorkerUpdate exists to hand the reload decision to the user. If you want a silent reload instead, call registerServiceWorker({ url, autoUpdate: true }) directly, without the hook.

docs.title: 2. Precache + runtime cache + navigation preload
docs.text:
Inside your sw.ts, register specific routes before the precache (so they win over the catch-all):

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import { installRuntimeCache, installPrecache } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installRuntimeCache([
  { match: /\/api\//, strategy: "network-first", cacheName: "tempest-api", maxAgeSeconds: 300 },
  { match: /\.(png|jpg|webp)$/, strategy: "cache-first", cacheName: "tempest-img", maxEntries: 60 },
]);

installPrecache(); // app shell + offline navigation

installPrecache enables the Navigation Preload API on activate by default (navigationPreload: true): the browser fetches the navigation request in parallel with the worker boot and the handler serves event.preloadResponse, cutting first-navigation latency after the worker starts.

The worker can be stopped at any time, and the precache keeps working

The browser terminates an idle service worker within seconds or minutes and starts it again on the next event, without repeating install. That is why installPrecache keeps nothing in memory only: install and activate record, in an entry inside the versioned cache itself (/__tempest-precache-state__), when that version was installed and activated, and the restarted worker reads back from Cache Storage which version is active and which paths it holds. Offline navigation and precached assets keep coming from the cache after the restart, and activate deletes old versions only once it knows which one it is activating — never the current one.

Up to 0.82.0 the cache name and the paths lived in module variables filled only by install: after the first restart, offline navigation failed with "offline and no cached app shell", and an activate without install in the same run deleted every precache (#572).

In the first request after a restart, while the worker is still reading which paths are precached, a same-origin GET that no runtime route answered goes to the network through fetch(request) inside the worker instead of bypassing it — the decision to call respondWith cannot wait for Cache Storage. From then on, what is not precached bypasses the worker again.

Vary does not hide a precached asset

install stores each manifest URL for a header-less request, but the page asks for the same file with the headers its element sends: Origin on the <script type="module" crossorigin> Vite emits, Accept: text/css,… on the stylesheet. A server answering with Vary: Origin or Vary: Accept — vite preview, a CORS middleware serving static files, a CDN — produced an entry cache.match never returned: up to 0.83.0 every precached asset went to the network and, offline, the app opened blank (#582). The precache matches by URL, with ignoreVary: it holds one entry per path, written by the worker itself and never for a credential, so Vary distinguishes nothing there. installRuntimeCache keeps honouring Vary — that is what separates accounts under cacheAuthenticated.

Where the manifest comes from

installPrecache reads precache-manifest.json, emitted by the tempestPwaManifest() plugin from the tempest-react-sdk/vite subpath. See Vite config.

Deploying to a subpath (GitHub Pages and friends)

tempestPwaManifest() prefixes the URLs with Vite's base, but installPrecache runs inside the worker and cannot see that config. When your base is not /, point both path options inside it:

installPrecache({
  manifestUrl: "/my-app/precache-manifest.json",
  navigateFallback: "/my-app/index.html",
});

With the defaults (/precache-manifest.json and /index.html) the worker installs, fetches a manifest that 404s, and offline navigation never resolves.

docs.title: Authenticated responses stay out of the cache (unless you ask)
docs.text:
Cache Storage is keyed by URL and outlives logout. Left alone, account A's GET /api/me stays there and is served to account B on the same browser as soon as the network drops — or takes longer than networkTimeoutSeconds. Measured in Chromium 153 (11/10/2026), before 0.77.0: B, offline, received A's body.

So installRuntimeCache enforces six rules on its own:

  • A request carrying a credential header goes straight to the network — Authorization, X-Api-Key, X-Auth-Token and the rest of DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_HEADERS (override per route with credentialHeaders): the route neither reads nor writes the cache, as if the service worker did not exist for it.
  • A CORS fetch with credentials: "include" also goes straight through — it is what ApiClient sends under withCredentials, even on its own origin. <img>, <audio> and <video> send include too, but in no-cors mode, so they keep caching (since 0.82.0).
  • Cache-Control: no-store is never stored, and private only with the opt-in.
  • Vary: * is never stored: the Cache API rejects that response on put, and up to 0.81.0 the rejection became an error — network-first fell back to the offline path and cache-first failed, with the network response in hand. Now it is served and just not cached.
  • maxAgeSeconds also applies to the fallback: an expired entry is a miss, never an offline "last resort". This holds for network-first and stale-while-revalidate.
  • Age counts from the write, not from the Date header — which a CORS response does not expose, so for an API on another origin maxAgeSeconds never expired anything.

Do you really want authenticated data offline? Turn on cacheAuthenticated for the route:

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import { installRuntimeCache } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installRuntimeCache([
  {
    match: /\/api\//,
    strategy: "network-first",
    cacheName: "tempest-api",
    networkTimeoutSeconds: 5,
    maxAgeSeconds: 300,
    cacheAuthenticated: true,
  },
]);

With the opt-in, every entry is stored with Vary on each credential header the request carried (Vary: authorization, for example): the Cache API only returns it for the same credential. Another account (or none) misses instead of reading the data. A token rotated while online simply rewrites the entry.

The revalidation that keeps going after the response — the stale-while-revalidate refresh and the network request that lost to networkTimeoutSeconds — is handed to event.waitUntil, so the browser does not stop the worker mid-write.

Limit: cookie sessions over a plain fetch

The service worker cannot see the request's Cookie. What it can see is a fetch that asks for cookies explicitly (credentials: "include" in CORS mode), and that one already goes straight through. A plain same-origin fetch (credentials: "same-origin", the default) carries the cookie without saying so — and gating on that mode would switch off caching for every request of the origin. For such an API, cache privacy depends on two things outside the SDK:

  • the server sending Cache-Control: private (or no-store) on personal responses — the SDK honours it;
  • the app calling clearSessionData() on logout.

docs.title: 3. Background sync + periodic sync
docs.text:
installBackgroundSync queues mutating requests (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) that fail offline and replays them when the network returns — via the Background Sync API, with an opportunistic fallback for browsers without it (Safari).

import { installBackgroundSync } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installBackgroundSync({
  match: (url) => url.origin === self.location.origin && url.pathname.startsWith("/api/"),
});

To replay even without a fresh navigation, register a periodic sync on the main thread. The SW already listens for the periodicsync event:

import { registerPeriodicSync } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

const registration = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
await registerPeriodicSync({ registration, minIntervalMinutes: 360 });

registerPeriodicSync checks the periodic-background-sync permission first and returns false when unavailable (Chrome-only) — calling it unconditionally is safe.

docs.title: Credentials never reach IndexedDB
docs.text:
The queue lives in the tempest-bg-sync IndexedDB database and outlives logout. So installBackgroundSync removes the credential headers before writing — Authorization and the rest of DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_HEADERS (x-api-key, x-auth-token, x-csrf-token, …). Before 0.77.0 the bearer stayed readable there after logout and the mutation was replayed with the old identity (measured in Chromium 153, 11/10/2026).

Entries written by earlier versions are scrubbed too: on the first open after the update, the database migrates and deletes their credential headers from disk. On replay the list is applied again, so no entry goes out with the credential it stored.

On replay, the worker asks the open pages for the current credentials, over postMessage (a message of type BACKGROUND_SYNC_CREDENTIALS_MESSAGE, with a MessagePort for the answer). Install the provider once, next to your auth — the --pwa template already does it in src/pwa.tsx:

import { createTempestAuth } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { provideBackgroundSyncCredentials } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

export const auth = createTempestAuth<{ id: string }>({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com" });

provideBackgroundSyncCredentials(
  () => {
    const { token } = auth.useAuthStore.getState();
    return token ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : null;
  },
  { getPrincipal: () => auth.useAuthStore.getState().user?.id },
);

Without a provider, no mutation is replayed

The queue does not keep the token, so only the page can hand it back — and only the page can say who is signed in. Without provideBackgroundSyncCredentials, the tab does not answer, the entry's owner is unknown, and it stays pending until maxRetentionMinutes and is gone, whether or not it carried a credential header. In development builds the worker warns in the console (once per replay), and provideBackgroundSyncCredentials called without getPrincipal warns too: without it every entry is unbound and goes out with whichever session answers — B's, if A signed out without clearSessionData(). A cookie-session API with no token installs the provider all the same: provideBackgroundSyncCredentials(() => null, { getPrincipal }). An app with no sign-in at all uses ownerPolicy: "lenient".

docs.title: Every entry has an owner
docs.text:
getPrincipal binds the mutation to whoever made it. Right after queueing, the worker asks the tab that issued the request who is signed in and stores a SHA-256 fingerprint of that id on the entry — never the id or the token. The question does not delay the fetch rejection; until it comes back (up to 6 s), replay keeps the entry pending.

The owner is in one of three states:

State When Replay owned the tab answered with getPrincipal only goes out with the answer of a tab where the same owner is signed in; none matches → dropped unowned the tab answered without getPrincipal any answer will do (preferring one without a principal) unknown nobody answered, getPrincipal threw, the tab was gone (or there was none), the stamp was lost past the 6 s, or the entry predates 0.77 fails closed, with or without a credential header: only goes out when every tab that answered lacks a principal; a single tab with one → dropped; no answer → stays pending

On replay the worker asks every tab in parallel, under one 3 s deadline, and uses the answer that fits — another account's tab answering first no longer drops A's mutation. Then:

Chosen answer Replay headers including every stripped one sent with them — only the header names the original request carried, and only to the worker's origin or trustedOrigins (below) headers missing a stripped one stays pending (it does not go out anonymous to take a 401 and vanish) null (no session) dropped, unsent no valid answer stays pending until maxRetentionMinutes

Only an unowned entry with no credential header is replayed as it was, without asking. An entry whose owner is unknown asks even without a header: on a cookie-session API (credentials: "include"), the browser attaches on replay the cookie of whoever is signed in at that moment, so replaying unchecked would send A's mutation with B's session (as it did up to 0.77.0; ownerPolicy: "lenient" restores that, see below). And a tab without getPrincipal — say, still running the bundle from before the deploy — does not authorize the replay when another tab answers with a principal: it says nothing about the cookie that rides along. A provider error (getHeaders or getPrincipal throwing) comes back as an explicit { error: true }, never as silence.

Measured in Chromium 153 (11/10/2026), with a real service worker, IndexedDB and two tabs: A queues offline, B signs in without clearing anything, the sync fires — the server receives no POST; with B's tab open next to it, A's mutation goes out with A's refreshed token.

docs.title: Credentials only go back to a trusted origin
docs.text:
The header name is not enough. A request to a third party (https://payments.example/webhooks) carries that party's Authorization; the worker strips it before storing, like any credential. If the replay asked the page for the credential and applied it by name, the third party would receive the app's bearer — and up to 0.80.0 it did (#523): measured with the --pwa template's match and provider, the replay of a POST https://third.party/api/hooks with Authorization: Bearer THIRD went out with Authorization: Bearer APP.

The replay now uses the same rule as the ApiClient (isTrustedCredentialTarget): a credential only goes to the worker's own origin and to the origins in trustedOrigins.

  • An entry that carried a credential header to another origin is dropped, without asking the page and before beforeReplay. Replaying it without the credential would be a request the app never made; with the app's, a leak.
  • A Request that beforeReplay (custom or default) returns with a credentialHeaders header for another origin is dropped too, instead of sent.
  • An entry without a credential header is unchanged: the browser attaches that origin's cookies, as on the original attempt.

In development builds, each drop warns once per origin per replay. If your API lives on another origin, declare it:

import { installBackgroundSync } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installBackgroundSync({
  match: (url) => url.origin === "https://api.example.com",
  trustedOrigins: ["https://api.example.com"],
});

There is one replay per queue: sync, periodicsync and the Safari fallback firing together share the same pass, so a mutation is never sent twice. And clearBackgroundSyncQueue() reaches work in flight: each entry is checked against the database right before it goes out, and a request still failing when the queue was cleared is not written afterwards.

Outside that path, installBackgroundSync has four knobs:

  • credentialHeaders — the list of headers removed. For a custom one: [...DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_HEADERS, "x-tenant-key"]. The provider must return all of them.
  • beforeReplay(request, { queuedAt, strippedHeaders, ownerState, owner }) — replaces the request to the pages: return the Request to send, null to drop, or throw to keep it pending. Useful when the worker can get the credential by itself; ownerState/owner let it apply the same owner rule.
  • ownerPolicy — "strict" (default) or "lenient"; see ownerPolicy: an app without sign-in.
  • trustedOrigins — origins besides the worker's that may receive a credential on replay; see above.

Limit: credentials in the URL or the body

Only headers leave the queue. A token in the query string (?access_token=…) or inside the mutation body is stored as sent. Send credentials in a header.

credentialHeaders: [] brings the old behavior back

With an empty list, every header — bearer included — goes to IndexedDB in plain text and is replayed as stored. It is an explicit choice, for apps with no open page at replay time that accept the risk.

docs.title: ownerPolicy: an app without sign-in
docs.text:
The default is ownerPolicy: "strict". An app without sign-in, where no page reports a principal and there is no provider, can go back to the unchecked replay of 0.77.0 with ownerPolicy: "lenient":

import { installBackgroundSync } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installBackgroundSync({
  match: (url) => url.origin === self.location.origin && url.pathname.startsWith("/api/"),
  ownerPolicy: "lenient",
});
Entry "strict" (default) "lenient" unknown owner, no credential header asks the pages: replayed only if every answer lacks a principal, dropped if any has one, pending with no answer replayed as it was, without asking unknown owner, credential header stripped asks the pages (same rule) asks the pages (same rule) owned / unowned same in both modes same in both modes

lenient is not for a cookie session

On replay the browser attaches the cookie of whoever is signed in at that moment. Under "lenient", A's mutation whose owner was never stamped (tab closed, empty clientId, stamp lost, old entry) goes out with B's session. With cookies, stay on "strict" and install the provider with getPrincipal. A custom beforeReplay ignores the option.

docs.title: 4. Durability: request persistent storage
docs.text:
Without navigator.storage.persist(), the browser may evict IndexedDB and Cache Storage under disk pressure — fatal for offline data. useStorageEstimate shows usage/quota and exposes the action to make storage persistent:

import { useStorageEstimate } from "tempest-react-sdk";

function StorageMeter() {
  const { usage, quota, ratio, persisted, requestPersist } = useStorageEstimate();
  return (
    <div>
      <progress value={ratio ?? 0} />
      <span>
        {((usage ?? 0) / 1e6).toFixed(1)} of {((quota ?? 0) / 1e6).toFixed(0)} MB
      </span>
      {!persisted && <button onClick={requestPersist}>Make persistent</button>}
    </div>
  );
}

Outside React, use the pure functions estimateStorage() and requestPersistentStorage().

docs.title: 5. Cache observability
docs.text:
For a "X MB cached" readout or a "clear cache" button, use the main-thread helpers:

import { inspectCaches, clearCaches } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

const reports = await inspectCaches({ filter: "tempest-" });
const totalMb = reports.reduce((n, r) => n + (r.bytes ?? 0), 0) / 1e6;

await clearCaches("tempest-img"); // one specific bucket

inspectCaches measures bytes by default (reading each response); pass measureBytes: false for a fast, count-only report.

docs.title: 6. Logout: clear the session data
docs.text:
The runtime cache and the background-sync queue belong to the browser, not to the user: the next account that signs in inherits both. On logout, call clearSessionData():

import { createTempestAuth } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { clearSessionData } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

export const auth = createTempestAuth({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com" });

export async function signOut() {
  await clearSessionData();
  auth.logout();
}

It deletes every Cache Storage bucket except the app-shell precache (tempest-precache-*), plus the whole tempest-bg-sync queue. It returns { caches, queueCleared } with what it removed.

Why not a prefix: before 0.77.0 the docs said clearCaches("tempest-") on logout, and the recipe named the cache api — the prefix did not match and nothing was deleted. Worse, it would match tempest-precache-* and break the app offline. The default filter inverts the logic, so it works whatever cacheName you chose. To narrow it, pass caches (a CacheFilter); for a queue with another name, queueName. Just the queue: clearBackgroundSyncQueue().

It runs in the page

Cache Storage and IndexedDB are origin storage, reachable from window — no message to the service worker needed. If your auth exposes an end-of-session callback, call clearSessionData() there too, to cover a session that expires on its own. With getPrincipal on the provider and the token in a header, the queue no longer depends on it to keep its owner — the runtime cache still does. With a cookie session, the owner check trusts that each tab's getPrincipal reflects the cookie the browser will send; a tab with stale state (A still in memory while B signed in on another tab) authorizes the replay with B's cookie. So, with cookies, call clearSessionData() on logout even when using getPrincipal.

docs.title: 7. Offline status UI
docs.text:
Two ready-made components, driven by useOnline and the sync engine:

import { OfflineIndicator, SyncStatusBadge, useSyncStatus } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { notesSync } from "@/sync/engine";

function StatusBar() {
  const { tone, pending } = useSyncStatus(notesSync);
  return (
    <>
      <OfflineIndicator position="top" />
      <SyncStatusBadge tone={tone} pending={pending} />
    </>
  );
}
  • <OfflineIndicator> — a fixed bar that appears offline and flashes a confirmation on reconnect. Renders nothing while online, so it is safe to mount at the app root.
  • <SyncStatusBadge> — a pill with icon + label + pending count, driven by useSyncStatus(sync).tone.

docs.title: 8. Reactive sync-engine hooks
docs.text:
useOfflineSync subscribes a component to an OfflineSync engine and optionally flushes on mount, on the online event and on an interval:

import { useOfflineSync } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { notesSync } from "@/sync/engine";

function useNotesSync() {
  return useOfflineSync(notesSync, { flushOnMount: true, intervalMs: 30_000 });
  // → { phase, pending, syncing, lastSummary, lastError, lastSyncedAt, enqueue, flush }
}

For optimistic mutations that write to the outbox and patch the TanStack Query cache (with rollback on failure), use useOfflineMutation — see Query.

docs.title: 9. Conflict resolution
docs.text:
The pull overwrites the local record with the server version. When you need an explicit policy inside applyRemote, the helpers cover the two common cases (ties → remote wins):

import { lastWriteWins, higherVersionWins } from "tempest-react-sdk";

applyRemote: async (dto) => {
  const local = await store.get(dto.id);
  await store.save(lastWriteWins(local, dto, (r) => r.updatedAt));
};

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• useServiceWorkerUpdate + <UpdatePrompt> give the consent-based update flow. ✅
  • installPrecache enables navigation preload; installRuntimeCache covers the Workbox-like strategies and keeps authenticated responses out of the cache unless cacheAuthenticated.
  • installBackgroundSync + registerPeriodicSync replay offline mutations, with or without a fresh navigation — without storing credentials; provideBackgroundSyncCredentials supplies the current ones at replay.
  • clearSessionData on logout clears the runtime cache and the queue. 🔒
  • useStorageEstimate + requestPersistentStorage prevent IndexedDB eviction.
  • inspectCaches/clearCaches give cache visibility and cleanup.
  • <OfflineIndicator> / <SyncStatusBadge> / useOfflineSync / useSyncStatus assemble the reactive status UI. 🚀

docs.title: Query (TanStack Query)
docs.text:
Thin wrappers to standardize cache times, query keys, and the QueryClient. You keep using @tanstack/react-query as usual — the SDK only ships well-calibrated defaults and a typed key factory.

Why do these wrappers exist?

Without standardization, every screen guesses a staleTime and every domain hand-writes queryKey: ["user", id]. That leads to invalidations that miss (a key built differently in two places) and overly aggressive refetching. The SDK centralizes both: named presets plus a factory that guarantees the same key everywhere.

Section recipe-query of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: Provider
docs.text:
Wrap the app tree once, usually in main.tsx (or inside <AppProviders>):

import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { QueryProvider } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import "tempest-react-sdk/styles.css";
import { App } from "./App";

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <QueryProvider>
      <App />
    </QueryProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
);

Defaults applied when you do not pass a client:

  • staleTime: 5 min (STALE_TIME.DEFAULT)
  • gcTime: 30 min (CACHE_TIME.DEFAULT)
  • retry: shouldRetryQuery (queries) / 0 (mutations)
  • refetchOnWindowFocus: false

4xx is not retried — and this changed

The default used to be a flat retry: 1, which replayed a 403 on an admin-only listing and a 404 for a deleted record. The server refused on purpose in both cases: the second attempt returns the same answer, doubles the network log and holds the spinner for another round trip.

shouldRetryQuery retries once only what can change on its own: a network failure (status === 0), 5xx, 408, 425 and 429 (a refusal whose literal meaning is "later"), and an error of unknown shape — which may be a transport failure. Every other 4xx fails on the first try.

The classification comes from isRetriableStatus, the same one createApiClient({ retry: true }) and the retry() helper use. Through v0.44.0 this was a local copy missing 425 — so the same 425 Too Early was replayed by the client and not by the query.

If your app relied on retrying 4xx, the override is the usual one: defaultOptions={{ queries: { retry: 1 } }}.

To override, pass defaultOptions (merged on top of the defaults) or a ready-made client (ignores the SDK defaults):

import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { QueryProvider, STALE_TIME } from "tempest-react-sdk";

// Option A — tweak only some defaults
<QueryProvider defaultOptions={{ queries: { staleTime: STALE_TIME.LONG } }}>
  <App />
</QueryProvider>;

// Option B — bring your own client (share across roots, plug devtools, etc.)
const client = new QueryClient();
<QueryProvider client={client}>
  <App />
</QueryProvider>;

One QueryClient per app

Do not nest two QueryProviders without passing the same client. Each provider creates an isolated cache, and queries from different subtrees stop sharing data. For multiple roots, create the QueryClient once and pass it via the client prop.

\"No QueryClient set\" with the provider mounted = two copies of react-query

The client you pass is the one place the app's copy and the SDK's copy touch. If npm nested a second copy of @tanstack/react-query under the SDK, QueryClientProvider publishes your client on that copy's context — and every useQuery in the app reads the other copy's, finds nothing, and throws:

No QueryClient set, use QueryClientProvider to set one

With the provider plainly mounted three lines up. Nothing in that message points at the duplicate, which is why it costs an afternoon.

From v0.52.1 the SDK detects it and warns in development: a client from the other copy duck-types perfectly while failing instanceof, which is exactly the right discriminator. The fix is npm dedupe, and npx tempest doctor lists every duplicated dependency.

docs.title: Time presets
docs.text:
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { STALE_TIME, CACHE_TIME, REFETCH_TIME } from "tempest-react-sdk";

useQuery({
  queryKey: ["dashboard"],
  queryFn: fetchDashboard,
  staleTime: STALE_TIME.LONG, // 30 min — data rarely changes
  gcTime: CACHE_TIME.LONG, // 1 h
  refetchInterval: REFETCH_TIME.FAST, // 30 s — status polling
});
  • STALE_TIME: SHORT 30s, DEFAULT 5min, LONG 30min, INFINITE ∞
  • CACHE_TIME: SHORT 5min, DEFAULT 30min, LONG 1h
  • REFETCH_TIME: REALTIME 5s, FAST 30s, DEFAULT 60s, SLOW 5min

When to use INFINITE

STALE_TIME.INFINITE marks data as never stale — TanStack only refetches on manual invalidation. Ideal for static lists (categories, cities) that change per deploy, not per use.

docs.title: Typed query keys
docs.text:
createQueryKeys takes a scope (the domain prefix) and a map of builders. Every output already carries the scope up front, so the same key is built identically across the whole codebase:

import { createQueryKeys } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export const userKeys = createQueryKeys("user", {
  me: () => ["me"] as const,
  byId: (id: string) => [id] as const,
  list: (filters: { page: number; size: number }) => ["list", filters] as const,
});

userKeys.all; // ["user"]
userKeys.me(); // ["user", "me"]
userKeys.byId("42"); // ["user", "42"]
userKeys.list({ page: 1, size: 20 }); // ["user", "list", { page: 1, size: 20 }]

Note the all: it is generated automatically and is the broadest key of the domain — invalidating it tears down every user/* query at once.

docs.title: Full example — query + mutation + invalidation
docs.text:
This component reads the profile with useQuery, updates it with useMutation, and invalidates only the affected keys on success:

import { useQuery, useMutation, useQueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { createApiClient, createQueryKeys } from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
}

const api = createApiClient({ baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL });

export const userKeys = createQueryKeys("user", {
  me: () => ["me"] as const,
  byId: (id: string) => [id] as const,
});

export function ProfileCard() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();

  const { data: user, isLoading } = useQuery({
    queryKey: userKeys.me(),
    queryFn: () => api.get<User>("/users/me"),
  });

  const rename = useMutation({
    mutationFn: (name: string) => api.patch<User>("/users/me", { body: { name } }),
    onSuccess: (updated) => {
      // Update the local cache without a new fetch...
      queryClient.setQueryData(userKeys.me(), updated);
      // ...and invalidate the by-id record, in case another screen uses it.
      queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: userKeys.byId(updated.id) });
    },
  });

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading…</p>;

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{user?.name}</h2>
      <button disabled={rename.isPending} onClick={() => rename.mutate("New name")}>
        Rename
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

Why setQueryData + invalidateQueries?

setQueryData applies the mutation response to the cache immediately (no UI flicker), while invalidateQueries marks related queries as stale to revalidate in the background. Using a key factory guarantees the invalidated key is exactly the one the query consulted.

Organization pattern: each domain in src/constants/query-keys/<domain>.ts, grouped in a barrel.

docs.title: useOfflineMutation
docs.text:
When the app is offline-first, a mutation should not hit the network directly — it writes to the createOfflineSync outbox and syncs later. useOfflineMutation bridges the sync engine and TanStack Query: on mutate it enqueues the entry, optimistically patches the query cache, kicks a flush, and rolls back the cache if the enqueue fails.

import { useOfflineMutation } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { notesSync } from "@/sync/engine";
import type { Note } from "@/sync/types";

function useAddNote() {
  return useOfflineMutation<Note, Note[], Note>({
    sync: notesSync,
    queryKey: ["notes"],
    toEntry: (note) => ({ op: "create", recordId: note.id, payload: note }),
    applyOptimistic: (current = [], note) => [...current, note],
  });
}

// const addNote = useAddNote();
// addNote.mutate({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), text: "offline!" });
  • toEntry maps the variables to the outbox { op, recordId, payload }.
  • applyOptimistic produces the next cache value; the previous one is restored if the enqueue throws.
  • flush (default true → "after-mutation") triggers sync; false leaves it to useOfflineSync.
  • invalidate (default false) revalidates the queryKey in onSettled.

List-cache helpers

For the common case (the cache is a list), use upsertById() / removeById() instead of hand-writing the spread:

import { upsertById, removeById } from "tempest-react-sdk";

applyOptimistic: upsertById(); // insert or merge by `id`
applyOptimistic: removeById(); // remove by `id` (op "delete")
// custom field: upsertById("uuid")

Server delivery happens on flush

mutate resolves with the outbox entry id, not the server response — actual delivery runs inside the engine's flush loop, so the UI updates instantly and survives reloads and offline periods.

docs.title: persistQueryClientOffline
docs.text:
Persists the QueryClient cache to IndexedDB and restores it on boot — a reload or a cold offline start shows the last-known data instead of empty screens. Self-contained: uses dehydrate/hydrate from @tanstack/react-query directly, with no @tanstack/react-query-persist-client dependency.

import { persistQueryClientOffline } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { queryClient } from "@/lib/query";

const persistence = persistQueryClientOffline({ queryClient });
await persistence.restore(); // before the first render

export async function logout(): Promise<void> {
    await persistence.clear({ resetClient: true });
}

// on teardown:
persistence.unsubscribe();

Writes are throttled (throttleMs, default 1s) and subscribe to the cache. flush() writes immediately; unsubscribe() stops persisting; clear() ends the persisted session.

docs.title: Logout: clear() is terminal
docs.text:
clear() cancels the pending write, stops listening to the cache, waits for any write already in flight and only then deletes the snapshot. After it, restore() and flush() on that handle do nothing. That is what keeps the previous user's cache from coming back: before 0.77.0, clear() only deleted the row, and both a write pending in the last throttle window and the first cache event after logout (the next user's first query) re-wrote the signed-out user's authenticated responses — which the next boot's restore() hydrated for whoever was using the browser.

  • Call persistence.clear() in your logout flow (or in your auth's session-end hook). It is idempotent and can be called more than once, concurrently included.
  • clear({ resetClient: true }) is the one-call logout: after stopping persistence and deleting the snapshot, it also runs queryClient.clear(), so nothing from the previous user is left on disk or in memory.
  • Without the option (default false), the in-memory QueryClient is left alone — the app owns it and may want to keep public queries (a catalog, feature flags) and drop only the user-scoped keys with removeQueries. Since persistence has already stopped, the order of persistence.clear() and your manual cleanup does not matter. With auth, the client left behind still holds the ended session's responses, so it is marked as ended: no handle on it writes — not the new one created at login, nor one on another key — until the client is reset (see below).
  • To persist the next session, create a new handle on login: the old handle never writes again. In a dev build, the first restore(), flush() or new query on an ended handle logs one console.warn saying so.
  • Handles from different sessions don't trample each other. While a clear() is running, a new handle's restore() and writes on the same databaseName + key wait for it to finish — even when the logout was not awaited.
  • If the IndexedDB delete fails, resetClient still clears the QueryClient, and the error reaches the caller.
  • A session that ends without clear() (expired token, crash, tab closed while signed in) never goes through logout. For it, pass getPrincipal: () => userId: every write stamps the snapshot with a fingerprint of whoever is signed in, and restore() only hydrates a snapshot of the same owner. Another person's is skipped, not deleted — a cookie app that learns the user only after /me does not lose its own cache — and the next write replaces it. A snapshot written before the option carries no stamp and is not restored: one cold start, once.
  • The handle is bound to the first signed-in owner it sees — on a cache change, a write or a restore. The cache change is what pins the owner of the data: writes are throttled, and without it a session that expired (or another account that signed in) inside the first window got the previous user's responses, stamped as anonymous or as its own (#580). From then on, a write under another owner — nobody, because the token expired without clear(), or another account signing in on the same tab — deletes the snapshot instead of stamping the previous user's responses with the new owner (#563); if the same user comes back, the handle writes again. Writes before anyone signs in stay anonymous and are restored while nobody is signed in, so an app that persists visitor data keeps working. An anonymous snapshot written by 0.82.0 is not restored (it may hold an expired session's cache): one cold start, once. For the next session to persist, end the handle with clear({ resetClient: true }) and create a new one on login: the in-memory QueryClient still holds the previous user's responses, and a new handle on it would stamp them with the new owner. With auth, the library does not reset the client for you, but it guarantees that a new handle on a client that still holds an ended session deletes instead of writing until the client is reset (see below); with getPrincipal alone, resetting the client is up to the app.
  • Principal not known yet: isPrincipalKnown. For getPrincipal, null and undefined mean nobody is signed in — the same contract as the rest of the SDK, so () => user?.id keeps working. "I don't know yet" is a different state: a cookie-session app only learns the user after /me, and a write that ran before that stamped A's responses as anonymous; if the tab closed before the next write, the next logged-out boot hydrated them (#590). Pass isPrincipalKnown: () => false until the /me answer arrives, whatever it is. While it is false, nothing is written (the write is re-armed for the next window), a cache change does not bind the owner and restore() hydrates nothing — call it again once the principal is known. An isPrincipalKnown that throws counts as unknown. Without getPrincipal, the option is ignored.
  • A handle that hydrated an anonymous snapshot does not re-stamp it when someone signs in on it: the anonymous row may belong to an account whose principal was not known yet when it was written, and re-stamping it handed A's responses to B (#590). The write deletes the row, as on an account switch (#563), and a dev build logs one console.warn. A visitor app that later signs in loses persistence for that session; to keep persisting, call clear({ resetClient: true }) on it and create a new handle — without resetting the client, the new handle would stamp the hydrated anonymous row with the account that signed in.
import { persistQueryClientOffline } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const queryClient = new QueryClient();
let me: { id: string } | null = null;
let meResolved = false;

const persistence = persistQueryClientOffline({
    queryClient,
    getPrincipal: () => me?.id,
    isPrincipalKnown: () => meResolved,
});

export async function boot(): Promise<void> {
    const response = await fetch("/api/me", { credentials: "include" });
    me = response.ok ? ((await response.json()) as { id: string }) : null;
    meResolved = true;
    await persistence.restore();
}

docs.title: With createTempestAuth: pass auth
docs.text:
An app on createTempestAuth does not need to wire getPrincipal or isPrincipalKnown by hand: pass the preset itself as auth (#596).

import { createTempestAuth, persistQueryClientOffline } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";

interface User {
    id: string;
}

const auth = createTempestAuth<User>({
    baseURL: "https://api.example.com",
    withCredentials: true,
    logoutPath: "/api/auth/logout",
    mePath: "/api/auth/me",
});
const queryClient = new QueryClient();
const persistence = persistQueryClientOffline({ queryClient, auth });

export async function boot(): Promise<void> {
    await auth.refresh().catch(() => undefined);
    await persistence.restore();
}
  • The cache belongs to the session: the principal is auth.sessionKey(), which survives reloads and token rotations and changes on every sign-in. A new sign-in of the same account starts with a cold cache — it is a cache, and no account inherits another's.
  • "Not known yet" comes from the preset: auth.isSessionKnown() is false while a login(), a restore() or an account switch is in flight, and while the boot refresh() is still restoring the session from the cookie. In that window nothing is written, nothing binds the owner and restore() hydrates nothing. A sessionKey() that throws also reads as not known.
  • Every session installed while the cache lives counts, not only the one a cache change saw. The preset notifies each install, and the handle records the session on the QueryClient. Once a second session, or nobody after one, was installed — a logout() in another tab, a logout() in this one without clear(), another login() on top —, every write deletes the row and restore() hydrates nothing, because the cache may hold responses of the session that ended. That includes the request that left with no token and that the api client replayed with the token of a login() or boot refresh() in flight: if that session ended before the response landed, nobody was signed in either when it left or when it landed, and before this fix A's response was stamped p:anonymous for the next signed-out boot (security audit run-12, C1). Nobody followed by a session is not an end (visitor data belongs to no account), and a token rotation keeps the key.
  • The record belongs to the QueryClient, not to the handle. A new handle on the same client keeps deleting until the client is reset, and only two things reset it: clear({ resetClient: true }) of the previous handle (the record goes after queryClient.clear(), when nothing of the ended session stays in memory — as long as nobody is signed in at that moment) or a handle created on an empty client (queryClient.clear() or removeQueries() of everything first). clear() without resetClient does not reset it: the client still holds the session's responses, so the record is marked ended, and that also holds for a handle on another key on the same client. Before 0.85.0, that clear() deleted the record, and the new handle created at login stamped A's responses with B's fingerprint — which B's next boot restore() hydrated (security audit run-13, C1). Without it, following the "create a new handle after login" advice stamped A's responses, still in memory, as B's. The cost is deliberate: after a session that ends without clear() — including a saved session that expired at boot —, the next one does not persist in that page load until the client is reset or the page reloads. To avoid paying it, call clear({ resetClient: true }) at the end of every session and create the handle again.
  • The reset goes in onSessionEnd or after logout(), not before. A clear({ resetClient: true }) while A's session is still installed does not drop the record: the ended handle no longer observes the session, and an A query landing in between (a refetch, an interval, a focus, a prefetch) reached B's handle as anonymous data and was written with B's fingerprint — B's next boot hydrated A's responses (security audit run-14, C1, #609). Now the record stays marked ended until a handle is created on an empty client; when nothing of A came in meanwhile, the handle of B's login persists as usual.
  • A response of a session that ended does not reach the cache. auth.api refuses, with SessionSupersededError, the response to a request sent with the token of a session that ended before it landed — including a mutation started before logout(), whose onSuccess called setQueryData with A's data already inside B's session (on screen and in the snapshot). See Auth → Refresh in flight and account switching. A fetch of your own, outside auth.api, stays the app's responsibility.
  • A setQueryData made signed out after a session does not reach the snapshot (#653). An app promise started in A's session — an onSuccess that awaits something of its own, then calls setQueryData — can write A's data after logout() and clear({ resetClient: true }), when no handle observes the client: A's has ended, B's does not exist yet. Before, the handle created at B's login started a new record on that client and wrote A's data with B's fingerprint (measured on 0.90.0: the row came out with B's owner and a-late: ["private-of-A"]; with the new handle created right after logout, the anonymous snapshot of the gap already carried it). Now the whole client is observed from the first handle with auth or getPrincipal, and a query written by setQueryData while nobody is signed in, after someone was, is kept out of every snapshot until a fetch replaces its data. Only that query: the rest of the cache and B's persistence carry on. A query fetched in the gap — the public catalog of the login screen — is written as usual, and so is a visitor's setQueryData before any sign-in on the tab. The cost: a legitimate visitor setQueryData after a logout (an anonymous cart, a public draft) does not persist until the query is fetched again; on screen and in memory nothing changes. Reproduced in src/query/offline-persistence.signed-out-write.test.ts (npx vitest run src/query/offline-persistence.signed-out-write.test.ts).
  • What is left out: with a session object of your own in auth (not the preset), there is no install notice — the session is only read on cache changes, writes and restores, and a session installed and ended between two of them goes unseen. A handle only records sessions while it observes them: after unsubscribe(), flush() writes nothing, and a handle created on a client that already holds responses cannot know which session fetched them — create the handle at boot, before the first query. And a backend that authenticates by cookie with no bearer (withCredentials) installs no session in the SDK: what it answers is written as anonymous, as in any app without sign-in.
  • Want the user id as owner? Pass getPrincipal along with auth. Then the principal must be loaded too: with a session installed and getPrincipal answering nobody (the profile has not arrived yet), it counts as unknown — not as anonymous.
  • Call restore() after the boot refresh(). Before it, the session does not exist yet, and restore() only hydrates what belongs to nobody.

Before, the only guard was the sentence in the isPrincipalKnown item above: without it, a tab closed before /me left A's responses stamped anonymous, and the next signed-out boot hydrated them. Reproduced in src/query/offline-persistence.auth.test.ts (npx vitest run src/query/offline-persistence.auth.test.ts); the sessions installed mid-request and the new handle on the same client, in src/query/offline-persistence.lifetime.test.ts.

Changed in 0.77.0: the handle ends at clear()

Before, the same handle kept writing after clear(). If your app keeps persistence at module scope and reuses it after login, it stops persisting from 0.77.0 on. Create the handle inside the session:

import { persistQueryClientOffline, type OfflineQueryPersistence } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const queryClient = new QueryClient();
let persistence: OfflineQueryPersistence | null = null;

export async function startSession(): Promise<void> {
    persistence = persistQueryClientOffline({ queryClient });
    await persistence.restore();
}

export async function endSession(): Promise<void> {
    await persistence?.clear({ resetClient: true });
    persistence = null;
}

Call startSession() on boot with a signed-in user and after every login; endSession() on logout.

Dexie is a peer dependency of the offline store — install it (npm i dexie).

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• <QueryProvider> at the root — one per app — ships calibrated defaults; override via defaultOptions or client.
  • STALE_TIME / CACHE_TIME / REFETCH_TIME replace magic numbers with named presets.
  • createQueryKeys(scope, builders) generates typed, consistent keys, with an automatic all for broad invalidation.
  • Combine setQueryData (immediate response) with invalidateQueries (revalidation) using the same key factory.
  • useOfflineMutation bridges the offline engine to the cache: enqueue + optimistic update + flush + rollback.

docs.text:

  • Offline — combine with initialData for an offline fallback
  • PWA & Offline-First — service worker, background sync, status UI

docs.title: Release pipeline
docs.text:
How tempest-react-sdk is published to npm and how the docs site goes live — all on the maintainer's machine, with no GitHub Actions.

Why there is no workflow any more

Since 2026-11-13 the owner's rule is: GitHub Actions only in repositories of the 7rc org. This repository is outside it, so its GitHub cost is zero — no workflow, no gh run rerun, no gh workflow run. release-npm.yml and docs.yml were deleted, not just disabled: a disabled workflow is one click from running again, and the tests pinning their hardening would keep vouching for code that never runs. The last version of both is in commit 2df6e4b. What they did became two Makefile targets: make release-tag and make docs-deploy.

The rule has one exception, from 2026-11-22: a public package or open source tool repository may keep Actions on for GitHub Pages only. Pages publishes the gh-pages branch by running the built-in pages-build-deployment workflow, which belongs to GitHub but runs on Actions — with Actions off, the push lands and the site does not change. Here Actions stays on with the allowed actions limited to GitHub's own, and .github/workflows/ stays empty.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
make release TAG=X.Y.Z
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ scripts/release.sh           │
  │  1. branch release/vTAG      │
  │  2. npm version TAG          │
  │  3. closes the CHANGELOG     │
  │  4. RELEASES.md + commit     │
  │  5. make check               │
  │  6. branch push + PR         │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
       │ review + merge of the PR into main
       ▼
  make release-tag TAG=X.Y.Z
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ scripts/release-tag.sh                               │
  │  1. clean tree, npm whoami, gh auth status           │
  │  2. finds the merge commit on main                   │
  │  3. RELEASES.md row? does the tag exist already?     │
  │  4. ref guard + dist-tag (copies from origin/main)   │
  │  5. throwaway worktree of the commit:                │
  │     scripts/release-pack.sh (npm ci, lint, format,   │
  │     typecheck, tests, build, npm pack, 3 smokes)     │
  │  6. re-reads latest, npm publish <tarball> --tag …   │
  │  7. read-back: registry serves version and dist-tag? │
  │  8. tag push                                         │
  │  9. gh release create --verify-tag (+ tarball)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The three surfaces move together: the git tag, the npm version and the GitHub Release. The irreversible steps — publish, tag push, Release — come last, so a refusal never leaves half a release behind. A run that stopped half-way (the registry was slow, the network dropped) resumes by running the same command again.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
A release is two steps, with the PR review in between:

make release TAG=0.1.5       # 1. opens the release PR (no tag, no publish)
# ... review and merge the PR into main ...
make release-tag TAG=0.1.5   # 2. build + smokes + npm publish + tag + GitHub Release

docs.title: make release TAG=0.1.5
docs.text:
Opens the release PR: branch release/v0.1.5, bump, [Unreleased] closed into [0.1.5], RELEASES.md regenerated, make check, branch push and PR via gh. Creates and pushes no tag and publishes nothing. Needs a clean working tree and a tag that exists neither locally nor on the remote.

Blocks if CHANGELOG.md mentions neither [TAG] nor [Unreleased] (with a prompt to force continuing).

The provisional RELEASES.md tag

make releases-md builds the table from the git tags, and the new version's row must be in the commit that gets tagged (which test/docs-counts.test.ts checks). The script creates a provisional local tag only for that command and deletes it right after. The new row's Commit column points at the branch's chore: release; the next make releases-md rewrites it with the real tag's commit.

docs.title: make release TAG=0.1.5 DRY_RUN=1
docs.text:
Same, but stops before the push — inspect the local branch before continuing by hand:

git push -u origin release/v0.1.5
gh pr create --base main --head release/v0.1.5 --title "chore: release v0.1.5"
# after the merge:
make release-tag TAG=0.1.5

docs.title: make release-tag TAG=0.1.5
docs.text:
Runs after the merge of the release PR, from any clean checkout of the repository: the build happens in a throwaway git worktree of the published commit, so your checkout is not touched. It needs npm login (your npm credential publishes) and gh auth login (gh creates the Release). Without an npm login the script stops before building anything.

  1. Credentials and tree. npm whoami and gh auth status; clean working tree.
  2. The commit. The first one in the first-parent history of origin/main whose package.json is at 0.1.5: the merge (or squash) of the release PR. A PR merged after it, still at the same version, is left out — it is in [Unreleased] and cannot reach npm under a version that does not document it.
  3. Checks. The | v0.1.5 | row in that commit's RELEASES.md. A tag that already exists — locally or on origin — must point at that same commit: on the same commit it is a resume; on another one, a refusal.
  4. Ref guard (scripts/check-release-ref.sh) and dist-tag rule (scripts/release-dist-tag.sh), copied from origin/main (see Who decides who publishes), against the latest the registry serves now (npm view, read-only). The guard refuses a version that does not match the commit's package.json, a commit off main (#472) and a backport from a line nobody opened (#527) — before installing anything.
  5. Build and smokes (the commit's scripts/release-pack.sh, in the throwaway worktree): npm ci, lint, format, typecheck, the suite, build, npm pack and the four tarball smokes — bundler + bare Node with the node-css-loader (scripts/smoke-bundle.sh), a consumer Vitest suite (scripts/smoke-vitest.sh), the tempest bin (scripts/smoke-cli.sh) and the npm audit of an app freshly generated by create-tempest-app (scripts/smoke-scaffold-audit.sh). The suite runs again because the merge commit is another tree whenever main moved during the review.
  6. Publish. latest is read again and the dist-tag picked again seconds before the upload; then npm publish <tarball> --access public --tag <dist-tag> publishes the file the smokes exercised, not a fresh pack — a tarball publish runs no lifecycle script. A version the registry already serves is not published again (resume) — but only when its dist.integrity is the sha512 of the tested tarball; another artifact under the same version stops everything before any tag or Release. With 2FA on npm, npm publish asks for the code.
  7. Read-back. The registry serves tempest-react-sdk@0.1.5, its dist-tag points at it, and the served dist.integrity is the sha512 of the tarball the smokes exercised — when it is not, the command fails here, with no tag and no Release. The window is 30 minutes (RELEASE_READBACK_ATTEMPTS=120 × RELEASE_READBACK_SECONDS=15): npm processes the upload asynchronously, and v0.76.0 took 18 minutes to show up. When the window runs out the tag is not pushed; run the same command once the version shows.
  8. Tag push of v0.1.5 on the published commit.
  9. GitHub Release. Checks that the tag on GitHub resolves to the published commit and creates the Release with gh release create --verify-tag (an API call; GitHub Actions is not involved), notes from the CHANGELOG.md section and the tested tarball attached — steps 6 and 7 already made sure it is what npm serves. An existing Release becomes gh release edit + upload --clobber, leaving its Latest mark alone.

Variables:

  • DRY_RUN=1 runs steps 1 to 5 and an npm publish --dry-run; it creates no tag, publishes nothing, creates no Release, and needs no login.
  • REF=<sha> publishes a specific commit, for when main already moved to another version. It must be on main and carry the right version.
  • BASE_BRANCH=release-0.75 and BACKPORT_LINES=release-0.75 publish a backport (see Dist-tags).

No provenance

Provenance (npm's Verified provenance badge) needs the OIDC identity of a CI runner, which does not exist on a local machine. Versions up to v0.82.0 shipped with provenance; the ones make release-tag publishes ship without. Provenance is now checked through the GitHub Release: it points at the tag's commit and attaches the tarball whose sha512 is npm's dist.integrity.

docs.title: make release TAG=0.1.5 SKIP_VALIDATE=1
docs.text: Skips the local make check — the only place budgets, coverage and the gallery e2e run. make release-tag still runs lint, format, typecheck, tests, build and the smokes before publishing, but not size-limit nor the e2e. Emergencies only.

docs.title: make validate
docs.text: A fast subset of make check, with no release.

docs.title: make publish
docs.text: Refuses and exits 1 (#532). A bare npm publish skips the ref guard, the check against main, the tarball smokes, the read-back and the GitHub Release. Publishing goes through make release-tag only. make publish-dry stays: it runs npm publish --dry-run and publishes nothing.

docs.title: make docs-deploy
docs.text:
Publishes the MkDocs site to GitHub Pages from the local machine (scripts/docs-deploy.sh):

  1. fetches origin/main and opens a throwaway worktree of it — the site is always main's, never your checkout's;
  2. creates a throwaway venv with uv and installs docs/requirements.txt with --require-hashes (#532): every dependency's version and hash pinned;
  3. node scripts/gen-llms.mjs and mkdocs build --strict;
  4. checks both languages were built (index.html and en/index.html);
  5. pushes that directory to the gh-pages branch with the same venv's ghp-import. Not mkdocs gh-deploy, which would build a second time;
  6. before the push, scripts/pages-check.sh checks (read-only, gh api) that Pages will actually publish: public repository, source on gh-pages, and Actions on with GitHub-owned actions only. If anything is missing, the deploy stops without pushing and prints the command that fixes it; with DRY_RUN=1, it only prints.

✓ site on gh-pages without Actions was a lie

From 2026-11-13 to 2026-11-22 Actions was off (item 5 of the checklist below, in its old wording), every make docs-deploy ended with ✓, and the site stayed on the last docs.yml deploy, from 2026-11-02. pages-check.sh exists so that does not come back.

DRY_RUN=1 make docs-deploy stops after step 4. Measured on 2026-11-13: the dry-run build takes ~13 s with a warm uv cache and produces the pages of both languages (time DRY_RUN=1 make docs-deploy).

A docs-only change is still a docs: commit straight to main; the site changes when someone runs make docs-deploy, not on push.

docs.title: make releases
docs.text: Lists every v*.*.* tag sorted by version (newest first).

docs.title: make releases-md
docs.text: Regenerates RELEASES.md from the git tags. Called by scripts/release.sh, with a provisional local tag of the new version that is deleted right after.

docs.title: make releases-check
docs.text:
Sync report of the three surfaces — one line per git tag, saying whether the version is on npm and whether the tag has a GitHub Release:

TAG          NPM      RELEASE  STATUS
v0.24.0      ok       ok       sincronizado
v0.23.0      ok       FALTA    DESSINCRONIZADO

Read-only, always safe. Use it before and after a release.

docs.title: make releases-sync / make releases-sync-dry
docs.text:
Creates the missing GitHub Releases for tags that already exist (backfill), with notes from the matching CHANGELOG.md section. Tags that already have a Release are skipped — the script is idempotent and never rewrites an existing Release.

make releases-sync-dry   # lists what it would do, creates nothing
make releases-sync       # creates for real

Backfill notes never inherit [Unreleased]

scripts/changelog.mjs notes <version> falls back to the [Unreleased] block only with --allow-unreleased (which make release-tag passes, for a release cut before its section was dated). The backfill does not pass it — so an old tag never gets the next cycle's notes.

docs.title: Dist-tags
docs.text:
latest is monotonic: it only moves forward. The rule lives in one script, scripts/release-dist-tag.sh, called by the guard, right before npm publish and when marking the GitHub Release.

Version Dist-tag Example, with latest at 0.77.0 prerelease (X.Y.Z-something) next v0.78.0-rc.1 → next stable, above latest (or no latest) latest v0.78.0 → latest stable, equal to latest (resume) latest v0.77.0 → latest stable, below latest release-<major>.<minor> v0.75.1 → release-0.75

Whoever wants the old line installs it by its dist-tag: npm install tempest-react-sdk@release-0.75.

How latest is read:

  • Through npm view <package> dist-tags --json, with the key extracted in Node. Never npm view <package> dist-tags.<name>: npm takes the dot as a path, and dist-tags.release-0.75 always comes back empty.
  • Only an explicit E404 is a new package (no latest). An empty answer with exit 0, or a package that exists without latest, fails — reading that as a new package would send a backport to latest. Other npm view failures are retried 10 times, 15 s apart.

Why release-0.75 and not v0.75

npm refuses a dist-tag that is a valid semver range, and v0.75 is one (>=0.75.0 <0.76.0-0): npm publish --tag v0.75 exits with Tag name must not be a valid SemVer range: v0.75 (measured on npm 12.2.0).

Where a backport may come from

A commit off main publishes only if it is an ancestor of origin/release-<major>.<minor> — the maintenance branch of its own line —, if the picked dist-tag is that release-<major>.<minor> and if the line is opened for this run (#527): make release-tag TAG=0.75.1 BASE_BRANCH=release-0.75 BACKPORT_LINES=release-0.75. Creating the branch opens nothing. A maintenance branch never publishes to latest or next: those come from main only.

The GitHub Release follows the registry: --latest when npm's latest is this version, --latest=false otherwise (backport, or a prerelease, which also gets --prerelease).

test/release-workflow.test.ts exercises all of this in a fixture: a local bare origin, a fake npm and a fake gh first on the PATH, and a stub release-pack.sh in the commit — no network and no registry.

docs.title: Who decides who publishes
docs.text:
Up to v0.82.0, pushing a v* tag triggered the publish, and the question of issues #472 and #527 was "does whoever can push a tag publish?" — the answer hung on GitHub environments, the Trusted Publisher and rulesets. Since the publish left GitHub Actions, a tag publishes nothing. Publishing takes the npm credential of a package maintainer, on the machine of whoever runs make release-tag.

The ref guard still stops mistakes: a commit off main, a version that does not match, a backport from a line nobody opened. It runs from the copy on origin/main, not from the published commit (#527): in a fixture, a commit that rewrote its own check-release-ref.sh to approve everything is refused. But it is not an authorization boundary — whoever holds the npm credential can run npm publish by hand. The boundary is the npm account.

docs.title: Repository owner checklist
docs.text:
State read on 2026-11-13, read-only (gh api repos/mauriciobenjamin700/tempest-react-sdk/pages, …/environments, …/actions/secrets, …/actions/permissions). None of it is configured from the repository:

# Where What to do State on 2026-11-13 1 Settings → Pages → Source Deploy from a branch → gh-pages / (root), after the first make docs-deploy (the branch must exist first). Or: gh api -X PUT repos/mauriciobenjamin700/tempest-react-sdk/pages -f build_type=legacy -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/' build_type: workflow — the live site is frozen at the last docs.yml run 2 npmjs.com → account 2FA in Authorization and writes mode: npm publish asks for the code, and a leaked session token alone does not publish not observable from here 3 npmjs.com → tempest-react-sdk → Settings → Trusted Publisher remove the entry pointing at release-npm.yml: no workflow publishes any more, and it only serves to reopen a publish path through Actions configured since 0.7.0 4 Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions and Environments delete the NPM_TOKEN secret, the NPM_TOKEN, npm-release and github-pages environments, the RELEASE_BACKPORT_LINES variable if present, and revoke the token on npmjs.com the NPM_TOKEN secret and the three environments exist 5 Settings → Actions → General Allow select actions → GitHub's own only (no verified creators, no patterns): what Pages needs, and nothing more. Or: gh api -X PUT repos/mauriciobenjamin700/tempest-react-sdk/actions/permissions -F enabled=true -f allowed_actions=selected and gh api -X PUT …/actions/permissions/selected-actions -F github_owned_allowed=true -F verified_allowed=false. Disabling Actions (the 2026-11-13 instruction) stops the site silently; scripts/pages-check.sh checks this item enabled: true, allowed_actions: all; on 2026-11-22, selected with GitHub's own only 6 Settings → Rules → Rulesets, targeting main and release-* required PR, block force push and deletion — what makes "is on main" mean "was reviewed" main unprotected

The maintainer's machine is now the perimeter

With no runner, nothing separates the code that installs dependencies from the credential that publishes: the npm ci of make check and make release-tag runs on the same machine where npm login stored the token. Prefer a session login (npm login) over a long-lived automation token in ~/.npmrc, and let 2FA ask for the code on publish (item 2).

docs.title: Resumable upload (tus)
docs.text:
uploadWithProgress makes one request. That works until the file gets big: a 40-minute recording from useAudioRecorder, a video, a dump. Then a 4G connection that wobbles for three seconds throws away the 300 MB already sent, and reloading the page throws it away again.

createResumableUpload splits the file into chunks, remembers where it stopped, and carries on — after a network drop or a reload.

Protocol: tus 1.0.0, not something we invented

The client speaks tus (core plus the creation and termination extensions). That is deliberate: a resumable client with a private wire format means the backend is ours forever. With tus you can point it at tusd, tus-node-server or py-tus without writing a server at all — and the What your backend must implement section fits in one table.

Section recipe-resumable-upload of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: The minimal example
docs.text:
import { createResumableUpload, type ResumableUpload } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { useRef, useState } from "react";

export function SendRecording({ file }: { file: File }) {
  const upload = useRef<ResumableUpload | null>(null);
  const [percent, setPercent] = useState(0);
  const [state, setState] = useState("idle");

  async function start() {
    upload.current ??= createResumableUpload({
      endpoint: "/api/uploads",
      file,
      metadata: { filename: file.name },
      onProgress: ({ fraction }) => setPercent(Math.round(fraction * 100)),
      onStateChange: setState,
    });

    const done = await upload.current.start();
    if (done) await fetch(`/api/recordings?url=${encodeURIComponent(done.url)}`, { method: "POST" });
  }

  return (
    <>
      <progress value={percent} max={100} />
      <button type="button" onClick={() => void start()}>Send</button>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => upload.current?.pause()}>Pause</button>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => void upload.current?.resume()}>Resume</button>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => void upload.current?.abort({ discard: true })}>
        Cancel
      </button>
      <p>{state}</p>
    </>
  );
}

What happens: a POST creates the upload, a series of PATCHes pushes 5 MiB at a time, onProgress gets every byte tick, and at the end start() resolves with { url, size } — the tus URL, which you store next to the record.

start() resolves null when you paused or cancelled

Only a failure rejects. pause() and abort() are not failures, so the promise resolves null and you do not need a try/catch around a pause button.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
upload.state (and onStateChange) walks through:

State Meaning idle Nothing started creating The creation POST is in flight uploading Chunks are going out paused pause() — the resume point is kept done Finished; the persisted record was deleted error The retries ran out; start() rejected aborted abort() — with discard: true, the record was deleted

docs.title: Resuming after a reload
docs.text:
That is the reason it exists. The client stores { url, offset, size, idempotencyKey } (plus owner, with getPrincipal or getToken) under a resume key and, on the next start(), re-attaches to the upload:

const upload = createResumableUpload({ endpoint: "/api/uploads", file });
// Page reloaded, the user picked the same file, called start() again:
// → HEAD on the old upload, the offset comes back as 312 MB, the PATCHes carry on from there.

The default key is a fingerprint of endpoint + name + size + type + lastModified — the same criterion the reference tus clients use. Cheap (it does not hash 400 MB) and it changes whenever the file does, which is the property that matters: resuming into the wrong file would corrupt both.

A nameless Blob has a weak fingerprint

Blob has no name and no lastModified, so two blobs of the same size and type collide. Pass an explicit key when what you upload is not a File.

docs.title: Where the state lives
docs.text:
By default, localStorage, through createLocalUploadStorage(). Not IndexedDB, and that is a choice: the record is four fields and a URL, the requirement is only to survive a reload, and pulling Dexie in for that would put IndexedDB in the bundle of every app that uploads a file.

If your app already has a Dexie database open, plug yours in:

import {
  createOfflineStore,
  createResumableUpload,
  type ResumableUploadRecord,
} from "tempest-react-sdk";

const store = createOfflineStore<{ id: string; record: ResumableUploadRecord }, string>({
  databaseName: "Uploads",
  version: 1,
  tableName: "resume",
  indexes: "&id",
});

createResumableUpload({
  endpoint: "/api/uploads",
  file,
  storage: {
    get: async (key) => (await store.get(key))?.record ?? null,
    set: async (key, record) => {
      await store.put({ id: key, record });
    },
    delete: async (key) => {
      await store.delete(key);
    },
  },
});

An asynchronous storage can also implement deleteIf(key, matches): it deletes the record only when matches accepts what is stored now, reading and deleting in one transaction. The upload uses it to forget the record of a run whose account left, and without it falls back to get followed by delete — between the two, the next account may have written its own record under the same key, and that is the one that would be deleted (its upload would start over; #657). createLocalUploadStorage() already ships deleteIf, and being synchronous needs nothing else.

storage: null turns persistence off: resuming then survives a network drop, but not a reload.

docs.title: One record per user — getPrincipal and clear()
docs.text:
The record survives a reload — and, for that very reason, a logout. The default key carries no user at all: if A signs out leaving an upload half-done and B picks a file with the same fingerprint, B's client would send HEAD and PATCH to A's upload URL with B's token and, if the server refused, send the creation POST with A's Idempotency-Key (#479).

Two pieces close this:

import { createLocalUploadStorage, createResumableUpload } from "tempest-react-sdk";

declare const file: File;
declare const auth: { getToken: () => string | null };
declare const session: { userId: string | null };

const upload = createResumableUpload({
  endpoint: "/api/uploads",
  file,
  getToken: () => auth.getToken(),
  getPrincipal: () => session.userId,
});

await upload.start();

export function onSessionEnd(): void {
  createLocalUploadStorage().clear();
}
  • getPrincipal — the same getter the error reporter and provideBackgroundSyncCredentials take. The record gets a one-way fingerprint of the user (owner, never the raw id), and a record with another owner — another user, nobody, or no owner, written before 0.78.0 — is deleted instead of resumed: its URL gets no request, and its Idempotency-Key is never reused.
  • clear() — removes every record under createLocalUploadStorage()'s tempest-upload: prefix. Call it from onSessionEnd (see Auth → Ending the session). A custom storage implements the equivalent on its side.

And if the account switch happens while the upload runs? getPrincipal is read again before every chunk and every record write: once it names someone else, the run stops with ResumableUploadSupersededError (reason: "principal"), before the new account's token reaches the previous one's upload URL. A clear() mid-run does the same (reason: "cleared") instead of the record being written back. It is not a pause — the run cannot go on as the new account: the state moves to "error".

Since 0.88.0 the check also runs when each answer arrives (#642). An answer A's request got back after the switch — a confirmed chunk, a creation refused with A's error envelope, the offset HEAD — rejects with ResumableUploadSupersededError instead of landing in B's catch with A's data; and a HEAD answered after the switch no longer falls through to a creation sent with B's bearer and A's Idempotency-Key. With reason: "principal", the record the run wrote for A is deleted too: it holds A's upload URL — which many tus servers treat as the credential — and A's key, now in B's storage, and nobody can use it (the owner stamp keeps B from adopting it, and an auth.getToken session never comes back under the same key). A record B wrote under the same key in the meantime stays. Up to 0.87.0 A's record was left as it was.

import { ResumableUploadSupersededError, createResumableUpload } from "tempest-react-sdk";

declare const file: File;
declare const session: { userId: string | null };

export async function send(): Promise<string | null> {
  const upload = createResumableUpload({
    endpoint: "/api/uploads",
    file,
    getPrincipal: () => session.userId,
  });
  try {
    return (await upload.start())?.url ?? null;
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ResumableUploadSupersededError) return null;
    throw error;
  }
}

clear() only removes values shaped like an upload record: a prefix with no delimiter ("app") does not take the app's own keys ("appSettings") with it.

docs.title: Without getPrincipal: the record belongs to the token (0.82.0)
docs.text:
Up to 0.81.0, without getPrincipal any record under the same key was resumed, whoever wrote it (#528). Since 0.82.0, with getToken and no getPrincipal, the record is stamped with a one-way fingerprint of the token (owner: "t:…", never the token itself), and a record stamped by another token — or not stamped at all — is deleted instead of resumed. B never again sends a HEAD to A's URL or reuses A's Idempotency-Key.

The price is that tokens rotate. The stamp is rewritten on every record write, and the handle itself carries on with its upload after a refresh (pause() → resume()). But a reload after a refresh during which no chunk was written finds the old token's stamp and starts over. getPrincipal has no such cost — the user does not rotate — so it stays the recommendation:

Configuration Another user's record Resumes after refresh + reload Account switch while uploading getPrincipal deleted yes stops with ResumableUploadSupersededError getToken: auth.getToken from createTempestAuth (0.82.0) deleted yes stops with ResumableUploadSupersededError getToken only, any other getter (0.82.0 default) deleted only if a chunk was written after the refresh carries on, with the new token on the previous upload's URL neither (anonymous, cookie session) resumed yes carries on

With any other getter, the handle cannot tell a refresh from another account's sign-in — both are just a new token. So abort() also ends the own-record exception: a start()/resume() after it behaves like a new handle, which resumes the record only if the current owner stamped it and otherwise creates another upload with a fresh Idempotency-Key. Up to 0.82.0, a resume() after the abort() this page tells you to call from onSessionEnd carried on "its own" upload with whoever's token was current — B's, on A's URL, with A's Idempotency-Key (#561). Without abort(), the row above still applies: switch the getter to auth.getToken or pass getPrincipal.

docs.title: getToken: auth.getToken — the record belongs to the session
docs.text:
When getToken is the very getter createTempestAuth returned, the upload reads the preset's session from it (auth.sessionKey()) and uses it as getPrincipal. The session does not rotate on refresh, so a reload after a rotation resumes; and it changes on another account's login(), so the run stops before the new token reaches the previous upload's URL:

import { createResumableUpload, createTempestAuth } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export const auth = createTempestAuth({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com" });

export function sendRecording(recording: File) {
  return createResumableUpload({
    endpoint: "/api/uploads",
    file: recording,
    getToken: auth.getToken,
  }).start();
}
