This also holds for a session restored by auth.refresh() — the boot restore from the cookie, an OAuth callback: since 0.83.0 it gets a session of its own, and the next account restored the same way does not resume the previous one's upload (up to 0.82.0 both answered the same key, see auth.sessionKey()).

Measured in src/http/resumable-upload.session.test.ts (npx vitest run src/http/resumable-upload.session.test.ts): on main before this change, B's login() between the first and second PATCH let the upload finish, with the following PATCHes carrying Bearer B-tok-1 to A's upload URL; and a reload after a refresh started over with a new POST. Now the run rejects with ResumableUploadSupersededError and the reload resumes with a HEAD.

The getter, not a wrapper

getToken: () => auth.getToken() is another function and carries no session: it stays bound to the token, like the "any other getter" row. A login() into the same account is a new session — the upload starts over; to resume across logins, pass getPrincipal with the user's id. In a development build, a getToken without getPrincipal that is not the preset's getter logs a console.warn (once per getter, #657) — production stays silent.

A cookie session: clear() at session end, or getPrincipal

Without getToken — a cookie-only session, outside createTempestAuth, which always has a token — the SDK cannot see who is signed in: the cookie is HttpOnly, and nothing in the browser announces an account switch. The record has no owner and is resumed by whoever comes next. The teardown that reaches this case is createLocalUploadStorage().clear() at session end, and it is enough: it removes the records, stops the run in flight (reason: "cleared") and, since 0.84.0, makes a handle paused before it start over with a fresh Idempotency-Key instead of carrying the previous session's into the next account's upload creation (#528 — until 0.83.0 B's resume() reused A's key). abort() is no longer needed here. To resume across reloads without relying on the teardown, pass getPrincipal.

Whether this crosses accounts still depends on the tus server. tempest-fastapi-sdk has no tus server (in 0.345.0 no handler answers Upload-Offset), so what authorizes HEAD/PATCH on an upload URL is the server you deployed — many treat the URL itself as the credential. Its IdempotencyMiddleware, on the other hand, scopes the key by a digest of Authorization, Cookie, X-Token and X-API-Key: A's key repeated by B does not hand back A's upload.

docs.title: The failure that actually happens
docs.text:
It is not the chunk that gets lost. It is the chunk the server stored and whose response never came back. The client cannot tell that from a lost chunk, and re-sending it blindly would duplicate bytes.

Two things prevent that:

1. Writes are addressed, not appended. Every PATCH states the offset it writes at (Upload-Offset). If the response was lost and the client repeats it, it is asking to write bytes the server already has — and gets 409. On any retry the client re-reads the truth with HEAD before writing and continues from where the server really is.

2. Creation carries an Idempotency-Key. tus has no idempotent creation; without this, a lost 201 would leave an orphan upload on the server and the client would create a second one. The key (from generateIdempotencyKey) is stored before the first attempt and reused on retry. A backend that honours the header returns the same Location; one that ignores it works just the same, it only keeps the orphan.

The backoff is the SDK's retry

There is no second backoff here: every chunk runs inside retry — exponential, honouring Retry-After. Tune it with retry: { retries, initialDelay, shouldRetry }.

What the chunk loop retries, and what it does not

Two of these decisions are specific to the resume protocol and do not follow the SDK's general policy:

Answer Retried? Why network failure, 408, 425, 429, 5xx yes the standard policy: it can change on its own 409, 412 yes the offset-divergence signal — the replay is the fix, and the resync HEAD performs it 200/204 with an Upload-Offset not past the one sent yes, within retries tus says the new offset is the previous one plus the bytes received; confirming without moving is a protocol error (code: "UPLOAD_OFFSET_STALLED", 0.83.0). The resync HEAD checks whether the server stored the bytes anyway 404, 410 no the upload is gone from the server. Recreating one only happens at attach, never inside the loop 400, 403, 413, 415, 422 no a deliberate refusal; the 5th attempt gets the same answer

409 is the interesting case: the SDK's general policy refuses 4xx, and it is right to — but here it means "your offset is wrong", which is exactly what the retry fixes.

404 is the inverse. A resource that vanished looks transient, but the resync HEAD hits the same 404, so retrying meant probing a dead resource five times before reporting "the upload expired" — with the backoff stacked on top. Start a fresh upload for that one.

Your own shouldRetry replaces this policy entirely, in both directions.

docs.title: What your backend must implement
docs.text:
Every request carries Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0.

Step Request Expected response Create POST {endpoint} + Upload-Length, Upload-Metadata, Idempotency-Key 201 + Location (the upload URL, absolute or relative) Probe HEAD {uploadUrl} 200/204 + Upload-Offset Write PATCH {uploadUrl} + Upload-Offset, Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream, body = chunk 204 + the new Upload-Offset, greater than the one sent; 409 when the offset does not match Discard DELETE {uploadUrl} 204

Details that tend to bite:

  • Location may be relative. The client resolves it against the endpoint the POST went to (RFC 9110), so /files/abc from https://tus.example.com/files/ becomes https://tus.example.com/files/abc. Up to 0.81.0 it resolved against the page and sent the chunks to the app's origin.
  • Upload-Metadata is comma-separated key base64(value), with the value encoded as UTF-8 before base64 — that is how note-ação.webm survives an HTTP header.
  • HEAD answering 404/410 is read as "the server forgot this upload": the client recreates it from scratch instead of getting stuck.
  • A missing Upload-Offset on a successful PATCH is tolerated — the client assumes the end of the chunk — but sending it is better.
  • An Upload-Offset that does not advance on a successful PATCH — the offset sent, or a smaller one — becomes a TempestApiError with code: "UPLOAD_OFFSET_STALLED" and the response's status, counted as a chunk failure: the next attempt re-reads the offset with HEAD, and the upload rejects once retries runs out (retries: 0 sends one PATCH; the default, five). Up to 0.82.0 the loop took the answer as success and re-sent the same chunk forever — measured in #569, more than 1500 requests in 4 s even with retries: 0; the real case was a 303 redirect turned into a GET answered 200 with the same offset. Refusing without a retry was rejected: the server may have stored the bytes and only answered badly, and the HEAD settles that for free. It is the same rule as the reference client (tus-js-client), where only an offset that moved refills the retry counter.
  • Keep a table of Idempotency-Keys if you want to avoid orphans.

Off-the-shelf servers

tusd (Go), tus-node-server (Node) and tuspy/py-tus (Python) already implement the table. In a FastAPI app of your own it is four routes.

docs.title: Progress and pausing, precisely
docs.text:
const upload = createResumableUpload({
  endpoint: "/api/uploads",
  file,
  chunkSize: 1024 * 1024, // 1 MiB: finer ticks, more round-trips
  // the default is DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE (5 MiB), exported so a settings UI can show it
  getToken: () => auth.getToken(),
  withCredentials: true,
  retry: { retries: 8, initialDelay: 500 },
  onProgress: ({ loaded, total, fraction, resumedFrom }) => {
    console.log(`${loaded}/${total} (${Math.round(fraction * 100)}%), resumed at ${resumedFrom}`);
  },
});
  • onProgress reports bytes of the whole file, not of the chunk. resumedFrom says how many were already on the server when this run started — useful so you do not announce "0%" for an upload that resumed at 80%.
  • pause() drops the in-flight chunk; the persisted offset stays at the last confirmed chunk. resume() does a HEAD first, so partial bytes the server accepted are not lost.
  • abort({ discard: true }) sends DELETE and clears the record; without discard, the resume point stays. On a handle from before an account switch (the getPrincipal/session changed, or the storage was cleared), the discard does not reach the server — the DELETE would carry the new account's credential — and deletes the record only while it is still this upload's: a record the other account wrote under the same key (the file fingerprint) stays. An abort() without discard on such a handle also deletes this upload's record (chunk in flight or paused): nobody can resume it any more, and it kept the previous account's URL and Idempotency-Key in the next account's storage until a clear() (#657). The same holds for a handle with no binding (a cookie session or an anonymous upload, with neither getToken nor getPrincipal): kept from before a clear(), its discard sends no DELETE and leaves the next session's record alone — up to 0.90.0 it went out with the new account's cookies and deleted that account's record (security audit run-17). A getPrincipal that throws during abort() counts as a moved owner: nothing reaches the server, and abort() does not reject. And a handle that has run only deletes the record carrying its own Idempotency-Key, even when it cannot see the switch: a handle bound only to a getToken of your own (no getPrincipal, no createTempestAuth getter, no clear() at session end) deleted the record the next account wrote for the same file — up to 0.91.0 (#684). That handle's DELETE still goes to the previous account's upload URL with the current credential: only the server can refuse it, so pass getPrincipal or createTempestAuth's getToken. A handle that never ran still forgets the file's record.

The token does not follow Location off your origin

tus answers creation with a Location the server chooses, and the spec allows an absolute URL on another host — handing the upload to object storage is ordinary operation, not an attack. Up to 0.65.0 the bearer token followed that header wherever it pointed, along with the file bytes.

Since 0.66.0 the credential is bound to the endpoint's origin. When Location points elsewhere, the creation POST still carries the token — that one went to your backend — and the following HEAD/PATCH/DELETE go without it. The upload completes normally, which is what a presigned storage URL expects anyway.

When the storage host genuinely needs your API's token, declare it:

createResumableUpload({
  endpoint: "/api/uploads",
  file,
  getToken: () => auth.getToken(),
  trustedOrigins: ["https://storage.example.com"],
});

The same applies to the persisted record: a url in localStorage pointing off-origin does not get the token back on resume.

Since 0.82.0 the static headers follow the same scope: an X-Api-Key goes on the creation POST and not to a Location on another origin, which gets only the tus headers.

The csrf option follows the same rule: the CSRF token goes on the creation POST, every PATCH and the discarding DELETE — never on the offset HEAD — and only to the endpoint's origin and the trustedOrigins. See CSRF.

XMLHttpRequest, not fetch — except with static headers

As in uploadWithProgress: fetch still cannot report upload progress in any browser. There is a second reason here — tus returns the new offset in a response header, and uploadWithProgress only hands back a parsed body, so it could not be reused.

The exception is a request carrying the static headers (since 0.83.0, #564). XMLHttpRequest follows every redirect and has no way to refuse one. Measured in Chrome 150 with the packaged createResumableUpload (the npm pack tarball bundled with esbuild), a server on 127.0.0.1:5340 answering 301/302/303/307/308 towards localhost:5341, which echoes the headers with CORS: X-Api-Key reached the other origin on all 5 codes, on the creation POST and on the chunk PATCH, along with the bytes; so did X-CSRF-Token; only Authorization was stripped by the browser. The XHR's responseURL shows where the request ended up (http://localhost:5341/files/1, measured), but by the time it is readable the header is gone.

So such a request goes out over fetch with redirect: "manual", and a redirect answering it becomes a TempestApiError with code: "REDIRECT_REFUSED", not retried — the same rule as createApiClient (HTTP). Measured again after the change: no request reached the other origin in the 10 cases (5 codes × redirect on the PATCH and on creation), and an endpoint on another origin without a redirect still works.

The cost is the progress inside a chunk: with static headers, onProgress advances once per confirmed chunk. For a finer bar, lower chunkSize; or send the credential through getToken, which keeps the XMLHttpRequest — the browser strips Authorization on a cross-origin redirect by itself. X-CSRF-Token alone does not switch the transport, for the reason HTTP documents for createApiClient.

Migration: a server that answers creation or a chunk with a redirect — same-origin included, like FastAPI's trailing-slash 307 — now fails with REDIRECT_REFUSED when there are static headers. Point endpoint at the final URL (/api/uploads/).

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• createResumableUpload({ endpoint, file }) — 5 MiB chunks, resume across network drops and reloads, tus 1.0.0 on the wire.
  • start() / pause() / resume() / abort({ discard }); start() resolves null when you stopped on purpose.
  • The resume point lives in localStorage by default; swap it with storage, disable it with null.
  • getPrincipal binds the record to the user; without it, since 0.82.0, the record belongs to the getToken token — or to the session, when the getter is createTempestAuth's auth.getToken. createLocalUploadStorage().clear() in onSessionEnd removes what is left.
  • A lost response is handled by addressed offsets + a HEAD before every retry, and creation by an Idempotency-Key.
  • The backoff is the SDK's retry — there is no second one.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• HTTP — uploadWithProgress (single request), retry, generateIdempotencyKey
  • Audio — useAudioRecorder, which produces the long files that motivated this
  • Offline — createOfflineStore, if you would rather keep resume state in IndexedDB

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
The routing module in tempest-react-sdk wraps React Router in declarative mode (^7 || ^8) and gives you a single import surface: you declare your route tree with defineRoutes, wire everything up with one <AppRouter>, and import every primitive (Link, Outlet, useNavigate, …) straight from the SDK. On top of that, the SDK adds what every Tempest app rewrites by hand: code-splitting with automatic retry on a stale chunk, declarative route guards, and a ready-made <Suspense> boundary. This page takes you from zero to a tree with nested layouts, lazy loading, and protected routes.

react-router is a peer dependency — install it in your app

npm install react-router

The SDK does not bundle react-router, because it holds React context: a copy nested under tempest-react-sdk/node_modules would be a different <Router> than yours, and every SDK hook would throw useNavigate() may be used only in the context of a <Router>. The accepted range is ^7 || ^8 — the surface re-exported here is identical across both majors, and neither uses react-router-dom (the DOM bindings ship inside react-router itself).

docs.title: Why the SDK owns routing now
docs.text:
Before, each app built its own <Suspense>, wrote its own guard helper, and reinvented chunk retry. That bred divergence across Tempest apps and import paths scattered everywhere.

With the routing module you get:

  • One import surface. Everything comes from "tempest-react-sdk" — components, hooks, and the re-exported React Router primitives. Your app installs react-router (the peer) but imports from a single place.
  • Declarative. You describe what the routes are (a tree of objects), not how to assemble them imperatively.
  • Batteries included. <AppRouter> already builds the router, the <Suspense>, and the <Routes>. defineRoutes gives you typing. Guards and lazy loading are fields on the route itself.

Re-exported primitives

The SDK re-exports React Router's whole client-side surface so you import everything from one place — components (BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Outlet, Link, NavLink, Navigate, …), hooks (useNavigate, useParams, useSearchParams, useLocation, useMatch, useRouteError, …) and utilities (matchPath, generatePath, redirect, …). The full list is in Everything that comes from React Router.

Importing straight from react-router also works and resolves to the same copy — the re-export is a convenience, not an isolation boundary. That is what makes incremental adoption possible: an app already importing react-router directly can start using the SDK without rewriting a single import.

docs.title: Building the tree with defineRoutes
docs.text:
defineRoutes is an identity helper: it takes an array of TempestRouteObject and returns the same array, but fully typed. You get autocomplete and type-checking on the tree without annotating anything by hand.

// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { Home } from "@/pages/Home";
import { Login } from "@/pages/Login";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <Home />,
  },
  {
    path: "login",
    element: <Login />,
  },
]);

Each TempestRouteObject accepts:

Field Type Description path string The route's URL segment. index boolean The parent's index route. Mutually exclusive with path. element ReactNode What to render when the route matches. lazy () => Promise<{ default: ComponentType }> Loads the component on demand (code-split). Automatic retry on a stale chunk. children TempestRouteObject[] Nested routes. guard boolean \| (() => RouteGuardResult) false redirects, true renders, "pending" holds the decision. guardFallback ReactNode Rendered while the guard answers "pending". Defaults to the <AppRouter> fallback. redirectTo string The guard's redirect target. Default "/". preserveFrom boolean Carries the blocked path in the redirect, so login can return to it. Default false. caseSensitive boolean Makes the path match case-sensitive.

A lazy page may declare props

ComponentType there is literal: any component works, whether its props are required, optional or absent. A page typed ({ id }: Props) => … goes into the tree without a cast. Props the route needs to supply still come from the element or a context — lazy mounts the component with no arguments.

Then just hand the tree to <AppRouter>:

// App.tsx
import { AppRouter } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { routes } from "@/routes";

export function App() {
  return <AppRouter routes={routes} />;
}

<AppRouter> builds the router, the <Suspense>, and the <Routes> from the tree all on its own. Available props:

Prop Type Default Description routes TempestRouteObject[] — The route tree (required). router "browser" \| "hash" \| "memory" "browser" Which router kind to use. basename string — A path prefix shared by every route. initialEntries string[] — Initial history — only for the "memory" router. fallback ReactNode — The <Suspense> fallback shown while a lazy chunk loads.

docs.title: index vs path
docs.text:
Every route with children has to decide what to show when the URL matches the parent exactly. That is the index route: it has no path of its own, it just sets index: true.

// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { RootLayout } from "@/layouts/RootLayout";
import { Home } from "@/pages/Home";
import { About } from "@/pages/About";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <RootLayout />,
    children: [
      { index: true, element: <Home /> },
      { path: "about", element: <About /> },
    ],
  },
]);

Here, opening / renders <RootLayout> with <Home> inside it; opening /about renders <RootLayout> with <About> inside it.

index and path are mutually exclusive

A route is either an index (index: true) or it has a path, never both. Setting both is a configuration error.

docs.title: Nested layouts with Outlet
docs.text:
The parent route renders the layout; the children render inside it through <Outlet>. The <Outlet> is the spot where React Router injects the matched child route.

// RootLayout.tsx
import { Link, Outlet } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function RootLayout() {
  return (
    <div>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">Home</Link>
        <Link to="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
      </nav>
      <Outlet />
    </div>
  );
}

The <nav> stays visible across every child route; the <Outlet> swaps content as the URL changes. Use <Link> (also re-exported by the SDK) to navigate without reloading the page.

Programmatic navigation

To navigate from code (after a submit, for example), use useNavigate: const navigate = useNavigate(); navigate("/dashboard");.

docs.title: Lazy loading + the Suspense fallback
docs.text:
Heavy pages don't need to land in the initial bundle. Use the lazy field to load the component on demand. It takes a function that does a dynamic import() and returns the module with a default.

// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { RootLayout } from "@/layouts/RootLayout";
import { Home } from "@/pages/Home";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <RootLayout />,
    children: [
      { index: true, element: <Home /> },
      {
        path: "dashboard",
        lazy: () => import("@/pages/Dashboard"),
      },
    ],
  },
]);

Since the chunk takes a moment to download, <AppRouter> wraps everything in a <Suspense>. Pass a fallback to show something while it loads:

// App.tsx
import { AppRouter } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { routes } from "@/routes";

export function App() {
  return <AppRouter routes={routes} fallback={<p>Loading…</p>} />;
}

Automatic retry on a stale chunk

When you ship a new deploy, chunk names change. A user who left a tab open for hours may request a chunk that no longer exists and hit an import error. The SDK's lazy detects that case and reloads automatically — you don't have to write that retry by hand.

docs.title: Guards: protecting routes
docs.text: Almost every app has routes only authenticated users should see. The guard field handles this right on the tree: when the value is falsy, <AppRouter> renders a redirect instead of the element.

docs.title: Boolean form
docs.text:
If the condition is already available as a value, pass a boolean:

// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { Dashboard } from "@/pages/Dashboard";

const isAuthenticated = false;

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  {
    path: "dashboard",
    element: <Dashboard />,
    guard: isAuthenticated,
    redirectTo: "/login",
  },
]);

docs.title: Function form (auth store)
docs.text:
In practice, the auth state lives in a store. Pass a function that reads the store at render time — that way the guard always sees the current value:

// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { useAuth } from "@/stores/auth"; // a createAuthStore-based store
import { RootLayout } from "@/layouts/RootLayout";
import { Home } from "@/pages/Home";
import { Login } from "@/pages/Login";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <RootLayout />,
    children: [
      { index: true, element: <Home /> },
      { path: "login", element: <Login /> },
      {
        path: "dashboard",
        lazy: () => import("@/pages/Dashboard"),
        guard: () => useAuth.getState().isAuthenticated,
        redirectTo: "/login",
      },
    ],
  },
]);

The guard runs on render — read your store via getState() or a hook

The guard function is evaluated during the route's render. So it must read the state at that moment: use useAuth.getState().isAuthenticated (an imperative read, outside React) or call a hook straight in the guard function, which runs inside the render cycle — see the next section. Don't capture the value once outside the function: you'd freeze the auth state at initial load.

When guard is falsy, the user is redirected to redirectTo (default "/"). In the example above, anyone not authenticated who tries to open /dashboard lands on /login.

docs.title: The async function form: the third state "pending"
docs.text:
A two-answer guard cannot talk about a permission that has not resolved yet — and the SDK ships exactly one of those: useCan, which returns { allowed, isLoading }. With only true/false, the guard has to answer something while the check is in flight, and both possible answers are wrong:

  • answering false redirects the person who does have the permission, in a flash, every time the route is opened cold (F5 straight on the URL, an external link);
  • answering true renders the screen for someone who does not, until the answer lands.

So the guard takes a third answer:

type RouteGuardResult = boolean | "pending";

"pending" holds the decision and renders guardFallback instead — no redirect, no leaked screen:

// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes, useCan } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { Spinner } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { RootLayout } from "@/layouts/RootLayout";
import { Home } from "@/pages/Home";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <RootLayout />,
    children: [
      { index: true, element: <Home /> },
      {
        path: "finance",
        lazy: () => import("@/pages/Finance"),
        redirectTo: "/",
        guardFallback: <Spinner size="lg" />,
        guard: function useFinanceGuard() {
          const { allowed, isLoading } = useCan({ action: "read", resource: "finance" });
          return isLoading ? "pending" : allowed;
        },
      },
    ],
  },
]);

Name the function use… — ESLint rejects it otherwise

The guard runs inside the render, so it may call hooks. But react-hooks/rules-of-hooks only accepts a hook inside a function whose name starts with use (or a PascalCase component). Written as an anonymous arrow, the example above fails linting with:

React Hook "useCan" is called in function "guard" that is neither a React
function component nor a custom React Hook function.

The form that passes is the named function expression, exactly as in the example:

guard: function useFinanceGuard() { … }   // ✅ passes
guard: () => { … useCan() … }             // ❌ lint error

A guard with no hook (() => useAuth.getState().isAuthenticated) can stay an anonymous arrow — getState() is not a hook.

One spinner covers lazy and pending

When the route defines no guardFallback, the SDK uses the fallback you already handed <AppRouter> — the same one covering the lazy chunk load. Both are "not ready yet", and in most apps they deserve the same spinner.

Each guarded route remounts, and that is deliberate

React Router renders the matched route's element at the same position in the tree. Without a distinct key per route, React would reconcile two different routes onto the same guard instance, and the previous route's hook state would survive into the next — a guard reading useState("from-a") would still read "from-a" after navigating to a route whose guard initialises it to "from-b". <AppRouter> keys by route object for exactly that reason, and a named test fails if the key ever goes away.

docs.title: The standalone RouteGuard
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to protect a piece of UI that isn't a route — or you just prefer the guard explicit in JSX. That's what <RouteGuard> is for: it renders the children when when is truthy, otherwise it emits a <Navigate>.

// ProtectedDashboard.tsx
import { RouteGuard } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { useAuth } from "@/stores/auth";
import { Dashboard } from "@/pages/Dashboard";

export function ProtectedDashboard() {
  const isAuthenticated = useAuth((state) => state.isAuthenticated);

  return (
    <RouteGuard when={isAuthenticated} redirectTo="/login" replace>
      <Dashboard />
    </RouteGuard>
  );
}

<RouteGuard> props:

Prop Type Default Description when RouteGuardResult — true renders the children, false redirects, "pending" holds. fallback ReactNode null Rendered while when is "pending". redirectTo string "/" Target when when is false. replace boolean true Replaces the history entry instead of pushing. preserveFrom boolean false Carries state: { from } in the redirect — see the next section. children ReactNode — What to protect.

Same state-reading rule

Here you're inside a React component, so read the store with the hook (useAuth((state) => state.isAuthenticated)) to re-render when auth changes. The tree's guard runs inside the render too, so it has both options: getState() for a simple imperative read, or hooks — as long as the function is named use…, as in the "pending" section above.

docs.title: Going back to where you were after signing in
docs.text:
The classic flow: someone opens /reports/42?year=2026, is not signed in, lands on /login — and after signing in should go back to /reports/42?year=2026, not to the home page. For that, the redirect has to carry where it came from, and the login screen has to read it back.

There are two pieces:

  • preserveFrom on the guard (on <RouteGuard> or on the route object) makes the redirect carry state: { from: pathname + search + hash }.
  • useReturnTo(fallback) on the login screen returns that from — or fallback when there is nothing valid to go back to.
// routes.tsx
import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { useAuth } from "@/stores/auth";
import { Dashboard } from "@/pages/Dashboard";
import { Login } from "@/pages/Login";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  { path: "login", element: <Login /> },
  {
    path: "dashboard",
    element: <Dashboard />,
    guard: () => useAuth.getState().isAuthenticated,
    redirectTo: "/login",
    preserveFrom: true,
  },
]);

// pages/Login.tsx
import { Button, useNavigate, useReturnTo } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { signIn } from "@/lib/auth";

export function Login() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const returnTo = useReturnTo("/dashboard");

  async function handleSignIn() {
    await signIn({ email: "ana@example.com", password: "secret" });
    navigate(returnTo, { replace: true });
  }

  return <Button onClick={handleSignIn}>Sign in</Button>;
}

On <RouteGuard> it is the same prop: <RouteGuard when={isAuthenticated} redirectTo="/login" preserveFrom>.

useReturnTo falls back to fallback (default "/") when the login page is opened directly, when it is reloaded without state, or when from is not a path inside this app.

Why not read location.state?.from by hand

from travels in history.state, which any same-origin code can write. Followed without a check, it is an open redirect: https://fake-site.example/login in place of the path sends the freshly signed-in person out of the app. useReturnTo accepts only a same-origin relative path — starts with /, no //, no backslash, no control character (the URL parser turns /\host and /<TAB>/host into //host). Anything else becomes the fallback.

Measured on react-router 8.3.1: navigate("https://fake-site.example") does not redirect, but throws External navigation is not allowed — the login screen breaks instead of following it. With window.location.assign(from) the redirect does happen. With useReturnTo, neither ever does.

Use the value with navigate, not window.location

The path is relative to the router's basename, exactly like useLocation(). navigate() puts the basename back; window.location does not.

docs.title: Choosing the router kind
docs.text:
<AppRouter> accepts three kinds via the router prop:

  • "browser" (default) — uses the History API; clean URLs (/dashboard). This is what you want in production.
  • "hash" — URLs with a # (/#/dashboard). Useful when the server can't fall back every route to index.html.
  • "memory" — in-memory history, never touching the browser URL. Ideal for tests and non-DOM environments.

In tests, combine "memory" with initialEntries to start on a specific route:

// App.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import { AppRouter } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { routes } from "@/routes";

test("renders the dashboard route", () => {
  render(
    <AppRouter
      routes={routes}
      router="memory"
      initialEntries={["/dashboard"]}
      fallback={<p>Loading…</p>}
    />,
  );

  expect(screen.getByRole("heading", { name: /dashboard/i })).toBeInTheDocument();
});

initialEntries is memory-only

initialEntries sets the initial history and only makes sense with router="memory". On the browser/hash routers the initial route comes from the browser URL itself.

docs.title: Everything that comes from React Router
docs.text:
Need matchPath to tell whether the current URL matches a pattern, or generatePath to build a link from params? Import it from the SDK, like everything else:

// ActiveTourBanner.tsx
import { generatePath, Link, matchPath, useLocation } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function ActiveTourBanner() {
  const { pathname } = useLocation();
  const match = matchPath("/tours/:tourId/*", pathname);

  if (match === null) return null;

  const editUrl = generatePath("/tours/:tourId/edit", { tourId: match.params.tourId ?? "" });
  return <Link to={editUrl}>Edit tour {match.params.tourId}</Link>;
}

The SDK re-exports all of react-router's client-side surface that is identical across v7 and v8:

Group Names Routers BrowserRouter, HashRouter, MemoryRouter, Router, RouterProvider, createBrowserRouter, createHashRouter, createMemoryRouter Components Routes, Route, Outlet, Navigate, Link, NavLink, Await, ScrollRestoration, RouterForm (React Router's Form) Navigation and URL useNavigate, useLocation, useParams, useSearchParams, useMatch, useMatches, useHref, useResolvedPath, useLinkClickHandler, useInRouterContext, useNavigationType, useOutlet, useOutletContext, useRoutes, useViewTransitionState Data router useLoaderData, useActionData, useRouteLoaderData, useRouteError, useNavigation, useRevalidator, useFetcher, useFetchers, useSubmit, useFormAction, useAsyncValue, useAsyncError, useBlocker, useBeforeUnload Utilities matchPath, matchRoutes, generatePath, resolvePath, createPath, parsePath, createSearchParams, createRoutesFromElements, createRoutesFromChildren, renderMatches, redirect, redirectDocument, replace, data, isRouteErrorResponse Constants NavigationType, IDLE_NAVIGATION, IDLE_FETCHER, IDLE_BLOCKER

The most used types come along too: Location, NavigateFunction, NavigateOptions, To, Params, PathMatch, PathPattern, RouteObject, LoaderFunctionArgs, ActionFunctionArgs, SetURLSearchParams, LinkProps, NavLinkProps, RouterFormProps, among others.

Why Form becomes RouterForm

The SDK root already exports its own Form (the react-hook-form one). So both can live together, React Router's Form ships as RouterForm — same component, different name. For the same reason React Router's Path type is not re-exported: the root's Path is the field path from the forms module.

What is left out, on purpose

The SDK is client-side, so it does not re-export what only exists in framework mode or on the server: Links, Meta, Scripts, PrefetchPageLinks, href, ServerRouter, StaticRouter, createStaticHandler, createRequestHandler, cookies and sessions. Route middleware (createContext, RouterContextProvider), createRoutesStub and every UNSAFE_/unstable_ name stay out too. If you need one of them, import it from react-router — it is the same copy.

A guard (test/router-reexports.test.ts) fails the build when a new react-router release brings an export that is neither re-exported nor excluded with a reason. The list does not go stale silently.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The routing module wraps declarative React Router v8 and gives you a single import surface — everything comes from "tempest-react-sdk".
  • defineRoutes types your tree; <AppRouter routes={...} /> builds router + <Suspense> + <Routes> on its own.
  • Use index: true for a layout's default route and path for the rest — never both together.
  • Nested layouts render children in the <Outlet>; navigate with <Link>.
  • lazy does code-splitting with automatic retry on a stale chunk; show the Suspense fallback while it loads.
  • Protect routes with guard (boolean or function) + redirectTo, or with <RouteGuard when={...}> in JSX. The guard runs on render, so it may call hooks — name the function use… for ESLint to accept it.
  • preserveFrom carries the blocked path in the redirect; useReturnTo(fallback) reads it back on the login screen, accepting only a same-origin path.
  • A permission that resolves asynchronously answers "pending": the decision is held and guardFallback (or the <AppRouter> fallback) shows, instead of redirecting someone who has access or leaking the screen to someone who does not.
  • Pick the router with the router prop: "browser" in production, "memory" + initialEntries in tests.
  • Need matchPath, generatePath, useOutletContext or any other client-side React Router name? It also comes from "tempest-react-sdk"; its Form ships as RouterForm.

docs.title: Scaffold — create-tempest-app
docs.text:
create-tempest-app is the official Tempest scaffolding CLI. With one command you create a React 19 + Vite + TypeScript app already wired up with tempest-react-sdk: providers, routing, an auth store, and an HTTP client come ready to run. The CLI is not a separate package — it ships inside tempest-react-sdk itself as the package's bin (create-tempest-app), alongside a bundled template/ in the tarball.

"bin": { "create-tempest-app": "./bin/create-tempest-app.mjs" }

This page is a tutorial: we go from an empty command to the app running in your browser, then walk through every generated file to understand which SDK feature it shows off. 🚀

Versioned with the SDK

Because the CLI lives inside tempest-react-sdk, it's versioned together with the SDK. Pinning a version means pinning the SDK version: npx -p tempest-react-sdk@0.5.1 create-tempest-app …. And the generated app's tempest-react-sdk dependency is stamped to the very SDK version that produced it — no hardcoded number that drifts out of date.

docs.title: Create your first app
docs.text:
The recommended path is to create the folder yourself and scaffold into it with .:

mkdir my-app
cd my-app
npx -p tempest-react-sdk create-tempest-app .
npm install
cp .env.example .env
npm run dev            # http://127.0.0.1:5173

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173 — the app is already live with providers, routes, and the store working.

docs.title: What each piece of the command does
docs.text:
Piece What it does npx Downloads and runs a binary without installing anything globally — then throws the download away. -p tempest-react-sdk Says which package the binary comes from. Needed because the CLI lives inside the SDK, under a different name. create-tempest-app The bin name inside that package — the thing that actually runs. . The destination: the current directory (recommended). A name instead of . creates the folder and requires it empty.

Prefer . over create-tempest-app my-app

Both work, but . is nicer day to day:

  • You own the folder and its name — the package.json name comes from the current directory, with no risk of ending up with my-app/my-app because you were already inside the folder.
  • It coexists with what's there — git init, README.md, LICENSE and friends are preserved (the CLI lists what it skipped). The named mode aborts when the folder isn't empty.
  • One command for both a fresh folder and an existing project.

No argument = .

npx -p tempest-react-sdk create-tempest-app (nothing after it) does exactly what . does: scaffold into the current directory. The CLI does not prompt for a project name.

npm create tempest-app does not work

There is no create-tempest-app package on npm — the CLI is the bin of tempest-react-sdk, so npm create tempest-app fails with a 404. Use npx -p tempest-react-sdk create-tempest-app .; inside a project that already has the SDK installed, -p is unnecessary.

In named mode the folder must be empty

With create-tempest-app my-app, the target directory must not exist or must be empty — this keeps you from overwriting one of your projects by accident. If the folder already has files, the CLI suggests using . to merge into the current directory instead of aborting (see the next section). A my-app that is a symbolic link is refused as well, even when it points to an empty folder: the project would be created where the link points, not where you named it.

docs.title: The two modes, side by side
docs.text: You type Destination If the folder has files Project name create-tempest-app . current directory preserves yours and reports what it skipped current folder name create-tempest-app (bare) current directory same current folder name create-tempest-app my-app ./my-app aborts if it exists and isn't empty my-app

docs.title: Scaffold into an existing project
docs.text:
If you already have a project that depends on the SDK, you can generate src/ + configs into the current directory, without creating a new folder:

npm install tempest-react-sdk
npx create-tempest-app .

Here npx create-tempest-app resolves the bin from the tempest-react-sdk you just installed — no -p needed. Running with no argument behaves the same as ..

In this "current directory" mode:

  • Existing files are left untouched — the CLI skips each one that already exists and reports what it skipped, never overwriting anything of yours.
  • A symlink in the destination is never followed — a src -> ../elsewhere (common in a monorepo or a cloned repository) is skipped and reported whole, and so is a package.json that is a link: the CLI never writes outside the project folder.
  • An existing package.json has the Tempest scripts and deps merged in: your name/version and the scripts/deps already there are preserved, and tempest-react-sdk is pinned to the SDK's own version running the scaffold. The template's overrides come along too (an override you already declare for the same package wins): they are what keeps npm audit clean while a tooling dependency has not shipped its fix yet.

The .env

.env.example declares VITE_API_URL, the base used by the HTTP client in src/lib/api.ts. Copy it to .env and point it at your backend.

docs.title: Available scripts
docs.text:
The generated package.json ships these scripts:

Script What it does npm run dev vite — dev server at 127.0.0.1:5173 npm run build tsc --noEmit && vite build — type-check and bundle npm run preview vite preview — serve the production build npm run typecheck tsc --noEmit — type-check only npm run lint eslint . — ESLint 9 flat config (react-hooks + refresh) npm run lint:fix eslint . --fix — auto-fix what it can

docs.title: Tour of what gets generated
docs.text:
The generated project is lean on purpose: each file exists to demonstrate an SDK feature you'll reuse. Here's the full structure:

my-app/
├── index.html
├── package.json          # deps: react, react-dom, tempest-react-sdk; devDeps: vite, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, @types/*
├── tsconfig.json         # @ -> ./src alias in "paths"
├── vite.config.ts        # createViteConfig({ plugins: [tempestCsp()] })
├── .env.example          # VITE_API_URL
├── .gitignore
└── src/
    ├── main.tsx          # createRoot + "tempest-react-sdk/styles.css" + <App/>
    ├── App.tsx           # <AppProviders> wrapping <AppRouter routes fallback/>
    ├── routes.tsx        # defineRoutes([...]) with index, login, and a lazy + guarded dashboard
    ├── layouts/RootLayout.tsx   # nav (Link) + <Outlet/>, reads useAuth.use.isAuthenticated()
    ├── pages/Home.tsx
    ├── pages/Login.tsx          # fakes a session via useAuth.use.setSession() then navigate("/dashboard")
    ├── pages/Dashboard.tsx      # default export (lazy), protected route
    ├── stores/auth.ts           # createSelectors(createAuthStore<User>({ name: "app-auth" }))
    └── lib/api.ts               # createApiClient({ baseURL, getToken, onUnauthorized }) + createQueryKeys

docs.title: Each file → the SDK feature it shows
docs.text:
File SDK feature demonstrated vite.config.ts createViteConfig — Vite config ready for the SDK src/App.tsx AppProviders + AppRouter — providers and routing src/routes.tsx defineRoutes with a lazy route + auth guard src/stores/auth.ts createAuthStore + createSelectors — typed auth store src/lib/api.ts createApiClient + createQueryKeys — HTTP client + cache

Let's look at the three most important ones.

docs.title: vite.config.ts → createViteConfig
docs.text:
import { createViteConfig, tempestCsp } from "tempest-react-sdk/vite";

export default createViteConfig({
    plugins: [tempestCsp()],
});

One call. createViteConfig already wires up the React plugin, the @ -> ./src alias, and the defaults the SDK expects. See the Vite Config page to customize. tempestCsp() writes the Content-Security-Policy into index.html, in dev and build alike, with connect-src taken from the VITE_* URLs in .env — which is why the first step's cp .env.example .env matters. See Content-Security-Policy.

docs.title: src/App.tsx → AppProviders + AppRouter
docs.text:
import { AppProviders, AppRouter } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { routes } from "@/routes";

export function App() {
  return (
    <AppProviders errorBoundary={{ fallback: <p>Something went wrong.</p> }}>
      <AppRouter routes={routes} fallback={<p>Loading…</p>} />
    </AppProviders>
  );
}

AppProviders mounts React Query, the error boundary, the theme, and the router in one shot. AppRouter consumes the routes array and renders the fallback while lazy routes load. Details in App Providers.

docs.title: src/stores/auth.ts → createAuthStore + createSelectors
docs.text:
import { createAuthStore, createSelectors } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

export const useAuth = createSelectors(createAuthStore<User>({ name: "app-auth" }));

createAuthStore<User> creates a persisted Zustand auth store (name: "app-auth" is the storage key). createSelectors gives you atomic access via useAuth.use.<field>() — that's how RootLayout.tsx reads useAuth.use.isAuthenticated() and Login.tsx calls useAuth.use.setSession(). More patterns in State.

The rest is self-explanatory

routes.tsx uses defineRoutes([...]) with an index route, a login route, and a dashboard that is both lazy and guarded. lib/api.ts instantiates createApiClient with baseURL/getToken/onUnauthorized and exports createQueryKeys so you can organize your cache keys.

docs.title: PWA mode (--pwa)
docs.text:
Want the app to be installable (home-screen icon), able to emit web push notifications, and to work offline (app shell + cache) out of the box? Pass the --pwa flag:

npx -p tempest-react-sdk create-tempest-app . --pwa

The flag works in both modes (new folder and ./merge). It overlays the PWA template on top of the base: everything from the normal app stays the same, plus a few new files and a few overwritten ones.

No vite-plugin-pwa, no Workbox

Install, push and offline caching are assembled from the SDK's own helpers (tempest-react-sdk/sw + tempest-react-sdk/vite) and bundled by a dedicated build. No extra PWA dependency — the PWA app uses the exact same deps as the base app. (Full comparison vs vite-plugin-pwa below.)

docs.title: What the flag adds
docs.text:
my-app/
├── index.html                  # (overwritten) manifest link + theme-color + apple metas
├── vite.config.ts              # (overwritten) createViteConfig + tempestPwaIcons + Manifest + DevSw + Csp
├── vite.sw.config.ts           # dedicated build that bundles src/sw.ts -> dist/sw.js
├── public/
│   ├── manifest.webmanifest    # install metadata (points at the generated PNGs)
│   └── icon.svg                # source icon (swap for yours — the PNGs come from it)
└── src/
    ├── sw.ts                   # service worker: push + notificationclick + skip-waiting + cache
    ├── main.tsx                # (overwritten) registers /sw.js in dev and prod
    ├── vite-env.d.ts           # (overwritten) types VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY
    └── pages/Dashboard.tsx     # (overwritten) Install button + notifications toggle

package.json is patched too: the build script now bundles the SW (tsc --noEmit && vite build && npm run build:sw) and gains a build:sw; sharp is added as a devDependency (generates the icons). The build emits a dist/precache-manifest.json (the asset list for offline caching) via tempestPwaManifest() and the PNG icon set (dist/icons/*.png + apple-touch-icon.png) via tempestPwaIcons().

In merge mode, your files are preserved

In . mode (merging into an existing project), the CLI never overwrites a file of yours — only the ones it just generated. If you already had an index.html, it is skipped and reported, and its PWA bits are up to you.

docs.title: 1. Install → useBeforeInstallPrompt
docs.text:
index.html links the manifest.webmanifest, and Dashboard.tsx shows an Install button only when the browser offers the prompt:

const install = useBeforeInstallPrompt();
// ...
{
  install.installable && <Button onClick={() => void install.prompt()}>Install app</Button>;
}

docs.title: 2. Service worker → tempest-react-sdk/sw
docs.text:
src/sw.ts is just glue over the SDK helpers:

/// <reference lib="webworker" />
import {
  installNotificationClickHandler,
  installPushHandler,
  installSkipWaitingListener,
} from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installPushHandler({ defaultTitle: "Notificação", defaultIcon: "/icon.svg" });
installNotificationClickHandler();
installSkipWaitingListener();

vite.sw.config.ts bundles that file (and the helpers it imports) into a classic service worker at dist/sw.js, and main.tsx registers it via registerServiceWorker. In dev, the tempestPwaDevSw() plugin compiles sw.ts on the fly and serves it at /sw.js — so push and caching work under npm run dev too (without it, the SW would only exist in the build). Compilation goes through one incremental esbuild context, created on the first request: the browser re-fetches the worker script on every navigation and on its own update checks, so a cold bundle per request would mean cold bundles all day. See the helper details in Web Push.

docs.title: 3. Web push → usePushSubscription
docs.text:
Dashboard.tsx wires the notifications toggle to the hook, reading the VAPID key from .env:

const push = usePushSubscription({
  vapidPublicKey: import.meta.env.VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY ?? "",
  onSubscribe: async (subscription) => {
    // send the subscription to your backend to deliver pushes
    await api.post("/webpush/subscribe", { body: subscription });
  },
  onUnsubscribe: async () => {
    await api.delete("/webpush/my");
  },
});

docs.title: 4. Offline → installPrecache + installRuntimeCache
docs.text:
vite.config.ts adds the tempestPwaManifest() plugin, which emits a dist/precache-manifest.json listing every built asset (the dependency-free counterpart to Workbox's __WB_MANIFEST). In sw.ts, two helpers consume it:

import { installPrecache, installRuntimeCache } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

// Specific routes FIRST (they win over the precache catch-all):
installRuntimeCache([
  {
    match: (url) => url.pathname.startsWith("/api/"),
    strategy: "network-first", // or "cache-first" / "stale-while-revalidate"
    cacheName: "tempest-api",
    networkTimeoutSeconds: 5,
    maxEntries: 50,
    maxAgeSeconds: 60 * 5,
  },
]);

// App shell last — launches offline:
installPrecache({ navigateFallback: "/index.html", navigateFallbackDenylist: [/^\/api\//] });
  • installPrecache caches the app shell on install, serves assets cache-first, and returns the navigateFallback (SPA) when a navigation happens offline. It versions the cache by the manifest's version and cleans up old versions on activate.
  • installRuntimeCache applies per-route strategies (cache-first / network-first / stale-while-revalidate) with maxEntries and maxAgeSeconds.

docs.title: 5. Icons → tempestPwaIcons
docs.text:
vite.config.ts adds tempestPwaIcons({ source: "public/icon.svg" }), which at build time rasterizes a single source SVG into the full icon set — the dependency-free counterpart to @vite-pwa/assets-generator:

import { tempestPwaIcons } from "tempest-react-sdk/vite";

tempestPwaIcons({ source: "public/icon.svg" });
// emits: dist/icons/icon-192.png, icon-512.png, maskable-512.png, dist/apple-touch-icon.png

Rasterization uses sharp (already a template devDependency). The manifest.webmanifest points at the generated PNGs, and tempestPwaManifest() includes them in the precache automatically. Changing the app icon = swapping public/icon.svg.

sharp is optional

The plugin imports sharp lazily: if it isn't installed the build doesn't fail — it just logs a warning and skips generation. The template ships sharp as a devDep, so it works out of the box.

Push and offline only work in a production build

Icon generation happens at build time, and the app shell is only precached after npm run build. In npm run dev the tempestPwaDevSw() plugin serves the SW (push + runtime caching work), but offline precache and the PNGs only exist in the build. To test full install + offline, run npm run build && npm run preview (then tick Offline under DevTools › Network to watch the app shell serve).

docs.title: --pwa vs vite-plugin-pwa
docs.text:
--pwa now covers the same ground as vite-plugin-pwa for the common case, with no new runtime dependency:

Feature vite-plugin-pwa (Workbox) --pwa (SDK) Manifest + installable ✅ ✅ Install prompt manual ✅ useBeforeInstallPrompt Web push + notificationclick you write it ✅ SDK helpers Update flow (skip-waiting) ✅ ✅ registerServiceWorker App-shell precache ✅ (__WB_MANIFEST) ✅ tempestPwaManifest + installPrecache Runtime caching (cache/network/SWR) ✅ ✅ installRuntimeCache navigateFallback (SPA offline) ✅ ✅ Old-cache cleanup ✅ ✅ (version on activate) Automatic icon generation ✅ (sharp) ✅ tempestPwaIcons (sharp, optional) SW in dev ✅ (devOptions) ✅ tempestPwaDevSw (esbuild) Background Sync ✅ (BackgroundSyncPlugin) ✅ installBackgroundSync Range requests (media) ✅ (RangeRequestsPlugin) ✅ installRuntimeCache({ rangeRequests }) Splash screens (Apple) ✅ (assets generator) ✅ tempestPwaIcons({ appleSplash })

Full coverage of the common case. For very specific edges (partial-content precache, exotic Workbox strategies), vite-plugin-pwa still exists and can be passed via plugins: [...] in createViteConfig.

docs.title: Background Sync — offline mutations that resend themselves
docs.text:
installBackgroundSync queues POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE that fail offline (in IndexedDB) and replays them when connectivity returns — via the Background Sync API where available, opportunistically (on the next request) where not:

import { installBackgroundSync } from "tempest-react-sdk/sw";

installBackgroundSync({
  match: (url) => url.origin === self.location.origin && url.pathname.startsWith("/api/"),
});

The original fetch still rejects for now (your app shows an offline state), but the request is replayed later. maxRetentionMinutes drops stale entries; 4xx responses are discarded (a client error won't fix itself).

docs.title: Range requests — offline audio/video seeking
docs.text:
Mark a route with rangeRequests: true to serve 206 Partial Content by slicing the cached resource — without it, media can't seek offline:

installRuntimeCache([
  {
    match: (url) => /\.(mp3|mp4|webm)$/.test(url.pathname),
    strategy: "cache-first",
    cacheName: "tempest-media",
    rangeRequests: true,
  },
]);

The createPartialResponse(request, response) helper is also exported for manual use.

docs.title: Apple splash screens — iOS launch images
docs.text:
tempestPwaIcons({ appleSplash: true }) generates the per-device launch images (iPhone/iPad, portrait) and injects the <link rel="apple-touch-startup-image" media=...> tags into index.html. Pass an array to customize the sizes:

tempestPwaIcons({
  source: "public/icon.svg",
  appleSplash: [{ width: 390, height: 844, ratio: 3 }],
});

docs.title: PWA mode recap
docs.text: --pwa hands you manifest + service worker + push + offline cache + generated icons + SW in dev + background sync + range requests + splash screens, already wired on top of the same base app, using tempest-react-sdk/sw (installPushHandler, installPrecache, installRuntimeCache, installBackgroundSync, createPartialResponse), tempest-react-sdk/vite (tempestPwaManifest, tempestPwaIcons, tempestPwaDevSw), usePushSubscription and useBeforeInstallPrompt — without vite-plugin-pwa. Generate the VAPID key on your backend, fill in VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY in .env, swap public/icon.svg, and test with npm run build && npm run preview. 🚀

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: With the app running, here's how to grow from it:

docs.title: 1. Add a page
docs.text:
Create src/pages/About.tsx and register the route in src/routes.tsx:

import { defineRoutes } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export const routes = defineRoutes([
  // ...existing routes
  { path: "/about", element: <About /> },
]);

docs.title: 2. Add a store
docs.text:
For non-auth state, use the SDK's createStore:

import { createStore } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export const useCounter = createStore<{ count: number; inc: () => void }>((set) => ({
  count: 0,
  inc: () => set((state) => ({ count: state.count + 1 })),
}));

docs.title: 3. Fetch data with React Query + queryKeys + api
docs.text:
Combine the HTTP client, the query keys, and useQuery (already available through AppProviders):

import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { api, queryKeys } from "@/lib/api";

export function UserList() {
  const { data, isLoading } = useQuery({
    queryKey: queryKeys.users.all,
    queryFn: () => api.get("/users"),
  });

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  return <pre>{JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}</pre>;
}

Go deeper in Query and HTTP.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The CLI is tempest-react-sdk's own bin (create-tempest-app), with a bundled template/ in the tarball — versioned together with the SDK, not a separate package. ✅
  • Recommended path: mkdir my-app && cd my-app && npx -p tempest-react-sdk create-tempest-app . — . (same as running with no argument) generates into the current directory, preserves existing files and takes the project name from the folder. Use @X on -p to pin the SDK version.
  • Named mode: npx -p tempest-react-sdk create-tempest-app my-app creates the folder but aborts if it already exists and isn't empty. The CLI never prompts for a project name.
  • Existing project: npm install tempest-react-sdk then npx create-tempest-app . (no -p — the bin comes from node_modules) — package.json has scripts/deps merged (tempest-react-sdk pinned to the SDK version).
  • npm install && cp .env.example .env && npm run dev takes you to http://127.0.0.1:5173 with providers, routes, and auth working.
  • Every generated file demonstrates a feature: createViteConfig, AppProviders + AppRouter, defineRoutes (lazy + guard), createAuthStore + createSelectors, createApiClient + createQueryKeys.
  • To grow: add pages in pages/ + entries in routes.tsx, create stores with createStore, and fetch data with useQuery + queryKeys + api.

docs.title: Web Share
docs.text:
share() is a wrapper over the Web Share API (navigator.share) that returns a uniform result instead of throwing. You decide what to do in each case — including a custom fallback (copy link, social buttons) when the browser does not support it.

Why wrap navigator.share?

The native API rejects the promise both when the user cancels the dialog and on real errors, and not every browser exposes it. Handling that by hand turns into a try/catch full of checks at every call site. share() collapses it all into a ShareResult object with clear booleans (shared / unsupported / cancelled), so your code becomes a simple if.

Section meta of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import { share } from "tempest-react-sdk";

async function shareEvent() {
  const result = await share({
    title: "Tempest",
    text: "Check out this event",
    url: window.location.href,
  });

  if (result.unsupported) {
    copyLinkInstead(); // fallback: copy the link
  } else if (result.cancelled) {
    // user closed the sheet — silent, do nothing
  } else if (result.shared) {
    toast.success("Shared");
  } else if (result.error) {
    reportError(result.error); // a real error — send to telemetry
  }
}

declare function copyLinkInstead(): void;
declare function reportError(error: unknown): void;
declare const toast: { success: (message: string) => void };

docs.title: The payload (SharePayload)
docs.text:
All fields are optional — pass the ones that make sense:

Field Type Description title string Content title text string Text/description url string URL to share files File[] Files (supported only on a subset of browsers)

docs.title: The result (ShareResult)
docs.text:
Field Type Meaning shared boolean navigator.share resolved OK unsupported boolean API missing, or the payload (files) is unsupported cancelled boolean User closed the sheet (AbortError) error unknown Another error — capture for telemetry

cancelled is not an error

When the user closes the share sheet, it comes back as cancelled: true, not in error. Treat it as a silent no-op — showing an error toast here annoys the user.

docs.title: Detecting support upfront
docs.text:
Use isShareSupported() to decide whether to show the "Share" button or go straight to the fallback, without waiting for the click:

import { isShareSupported, share } from "tempest-react-sdk";

export function ShareButton({ url }: { url: string }) {
  if (!isShareSupported()) {
    return <CopyLinkButton url={url} />;
  }

  return <button onClick={() => share({ title: "Tempest", url })}>Share</button>;
}

declare function CopyLinkButton(props: { url: string }): JSX.Element;

docs.title: Sharing files
docs.text:
Pass files to share images, PDFs, etc. share() calls navigator.canShare({ files }) before trying — if the browser does not allow files (old iOS, Firefox desktop), you get unsupported: true instead of an exception:

import { share } from "tempest-react-sdk";

async function shareImage(imageFile: File) {
  const result = await share({ title: "Image", files: [imageFile] });
  if (result.unsupported) {
    // this browser does not share files — offer a download
    downloadFile(imageFile);
  }
}

declare function downloadFile(file: File): void;

Web Share API requires HTTPS and a user gesture

navigator.share only works in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost) and must be called inside a user-gesture handler (e.g. onClick). Calling it outside a click makes the browser reject — which lands in error, not unsupported.

docs.title: Export a file — shareOrDownloadBlob
docs.text:
The most common use of files is "I generated an artifact, now hand it to the user": on mobile it opens the native share sheet, and on desktop (or wherever file sharing is unsupported) it falls back to a plain download. shareOrDownloadBlob(blob, fileName, options?) wraps exactly that flow — a companion to share() built on top of it:

import { shareOrDownloadBlob } from "tempest-react-sdk";

async function exportReport(bytes: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>) {
  const zip = new Blob([bytes], { type: "application/zip" });
  await shareOrDownloadBlob(zip, "report.zip");
}

Under the hood it calls share({ title, files: [file] }). If the user shared or cancelled the sheet, the function returns and nothing else happens. Otherwise (browser without file-share support) it creates an <a download>, clicks it, and revokes the object URL — the classic download.

Parameter Type Description blob Blob The binary payload to share/download fileName string The file name presented to the user options.title string Title for the share sheet (defaults to the file name) options.text string Text sent in the same sheet as the file options.textOnlyFallback boolean Share the text alone when the file is not shareable (defaults to true when text is set)

docs.title: Text alongside the file
docs.text:
Pass text to send a caption with the file — an analysis result next to the photo, for example:

import { shareOrDownloadBlob } from "tempest-react-sdk";

async function shareResult(photo: Blob, score: number) {
  await shareOrDownloadBlob(photo, "result.webp", {
    title: "Analysis result",
    text: `FAMACHA grade ${score}`,
  });
}

The order is file + text → text only → download:

  1. The browser shares files: it opens one sheet with the file and the text. Shared or cancelled, done.
  2. The browser has Web Share but canShare({ files }) refuses the file: it opens a sheet with the text only and then downloads the file — whatever the outcome of that sheet.
  3. The browser has no Web Share: it downloads the file, as before.

Why does the download still happen after the text?

Whoever calls shareOrDownloadBlob asked for a file to reach the user. In that browser the file was always downloaded; the text sheet is an addition on top of that behavior, not a replacement. If it replaced the download, a user picking "Mail" would get the caption and lose the photo, with no warning. That is why the textOnlyFallback: true default is safe: the only change is that the text arrives too. Want the download alone, as before? Pass textOnlyFallback: false.

A real error skips the text sheet

If sharing the file fails with an error that is neither a cancellation nor missing support (a NotAllowedError, for example), the function goes straight to the download: the failed call usually consumed the user gesture, so a second sheet would be rejected too. text: "" counts as no text.

Pairs with writeXlsx / ZIP generation

Generate the spreadsheet with writeXlsx, wrap it in a Blob, and hand it to shareOrDownloadBlob — a full data export, from bytes to native sheet, with no extra dependency. With photos alongside, createZip returns the .zip Blob directly, with progress.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• share(payload) wraps navigator.share and returns ShareResult instead of throwing.
  • shareOrDownloadBlob(blob, fileName) shares the file when it can, otherwise downloads it via <a download>.
  • With text, the order is file + text → text only → download, and the download is never traded for the text.
  • Check in order: unsupported → fallback, cancelled → silence, shared → success, error → telemetry.
  • SharePayload accepts title, text, url, files (all optional).
  • isShareSupported() decides upfront between the native button and the fallback.
  • files is validated via canShare before trying; unsupported browsers return unsupported: true.
  • Requires HTTPS and a user gesture (call it from an onClick).

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Hooks — useClipboard for the "copy link" fallback

docs.title: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
A wrapper over EventSource with exponential reconnect, opt-in heartbeat, and JSON parsing. Original use case: the notifications stream (NEW-ALO, PAYMENT-SUCCESS, etc.) from alofans-frontend.

SSE vs WebSocket — which one?

SSE is one-way (server → client), runs over plain HTTP, reconnects on its own, and authenticates via cookies with no ceremony. If the client does not need to send messages, SSE is simpler and cheaper. For bidirectional traffic (chat, collaboration), use WebSocket.

Section recipe-realtime of the gallery — run it locally to interact.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• One-way server → client push, with no need for the client to send.
  • Cheap automatic reconnection.
  • Cookie-based authentication (withCredentials: true) against a backend that reads the cookie on the stream itself.

tempest-fastapi-sdk >= 0.331.0 backend: the stream does not read cookies

The backend's ready-made SSE router opens the stream only with ?ticket= (or Authorization: Bearer, which EventSource cannot send). The session cookie counts on the ticket request, not on the stream. For that backend, use useTicketEventStream — with a header or a cookie session.

docs.title: Imperative API — createEventStream
docs.text:
Use it outside React (services, bootstrap) when you manage the lifecycle yourself:

import { createEventStream } from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface StreamEvent {
  type: "NOTIFY" | "PAYMENT-SUCCESS";
  message: string;
}

const stream = createEventStream<StreamEvent>(
  `${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL}/notifications/stream`,
  {
    withCredentials: true,
    namedEvents: ["notification", "payment"],
    heartbeatEvents: ["ping"],
    maxRetries: 10,
    onOpen: () => console.log("SSE open"),
    onMessage: ({ event, data, id }) => {
      if (event === "payment") handlePayment(data);
      else addNotification(data);
    },
    onStatusChange: (status) => console.log("SSE", status),
    onError: (err) => console.error(err),
  },
);

// Later, on unmount / logout:
stream.close();

// Force an immediate reconnect (resets the retry counter):
stream.reconnect();

// Read the current status:
console.log(stream.status);

Each onMessage receives { event, data, id, raw }: event is the SSE event name (default "message"), data is already JSON-parsed (with raw-string fallback), id is the server's lastEventId, and raw is the original MessageEvent.

docs.title: Reconnection and heartbeat
docs.text:
Backoff: 1s → 2s → 4s → 8s → ... (capped at 30s), up to maxRetries (default 10)
  • On every error the stream closes, schedules a reconnect with exponential backoff, and emits status "closed". On a successful reopen the counter resets.
  • Once maxRetries is exhausted, the status becomes "error" and the stream stops trying.
  • Events listed in heartbeatEvents (default ["ping"]) do not fire onMessage — they only keep the socket alive.

Match heartbeatEvents to your backend

If the server sends keep-alives under a different event name (e.g. "keepalive"), list it in heartbeatEvents so it doesn't pollute onMessage with pings.

docs.title: Hook — useEventStream
docs.text:
Inside components, the hook ties the stream's lifecycle to the component — opens on mount, closes on unmount:

import { useEventStream } from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface Notification {
  id: string;
  message: string;
}

export function NotificationListener({ user }: { user: { id: string } | null }) {
  const { status, lastMessage, reconnect } = useEventStream<Notification>(
    `${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL}/notifications/stream`,
    {
      enabled: !!user, // only connects once the user exists
      withCredentials: true,
      onMessage: ({ data }) => addToInbox(data),
    },
  );

  return (
    <div>
      <span>Stream: {status}</span>
      {status === "error" && <button onClick={reconnect}>Reconnect</button>}
      {lastMessage && <p>Latest: {lastMessage.data.message}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}
  • enabled: false disconnects the stream (use it while waiting for user to load).
  • sessionKey (the user's id) binds the stream to the session: switching accounts closes the stream and clears lastMessage — see switching accounts. With client: auth.api from createTempestAuth, useTicketEventStream does it on its own.
  • Changing the URL re-opens the connection; changing onMessage does not (callback held in an internal ref — no pointless reconnects).
  • lastMessage holds the last received message (heartbeats don't count).
  • Automatic cleanup on unmount.

error means it exhausted its attempts

When the status reaches "error", the stream gave up on its own. Offer a button calling reconnect() (which resets the counter) instead of waiting for an automatic reconnect that won't come.

docs.title: Ticket authentication — useTicketEventStream
docs.text:
EventSource cannot send headers. For a long time the way to authenticate the stream was to put the access token in the URL (?access_token=…), which ends up in the log of every proxy along the way. tempest-fastapi-sdk 0.331.0 replaced that with a ticket: a normal authenticated call asks for a short-lived JWT, and only that goes in the stream URL.

Backend route What it does POST /sse/ticket authenticated (header or cookie). Responds { "ticket": "<jwt>", "expires_in": 60 } GET /sse/stream?ticket=<jwt> opens the stream; the channel comes from inside the ticket. Accepts ?ticket= or Authorization: Bearer — does not read cookies

The helper makes both calls for you — and repeats them on every reconnect:

import { createApiClient, useTicketEventStream } from "tempest-react-sdk";
import { z } from "zod";

const api = createApiClient({
    baseURL: "https://api.example.com",
    prefix: "/api",
    getToken: () => localStorage.getItem("token"),
});

const notificationSchema = z.object({ id: z.string(), message: z.string() });

type Notification = z.infer<typeof notificationSchema>;

export function Notifications({ signedIn }: { signedIn: boolean }) {
    const { status, lastMessage, reconnect } = useTicketEventStream<Notification>({
        client: api,
        enabled: signedIn,
        schema: notificationSchema,
        onUrlError: (error) => console.warn("ticket refused:", error),
    });

    return (
        <div>
            <span>Stream: {status}</span>
            {status === "error" && <button onClick={reconnect}>Reconnect</button>}
            {lastMessage && <p>{lastMessage.data.message}</p>}
        </div>
    );
}
  1. The ticket is requested through api: it carries Authorization (or the session cookie and X-CSRF-Token), and a 401 goes through the client's refresh before it reaches this code.
  2. The stream URL is built with api.url("/sse/stream", { ticket }) — same baseURL, same prefix. The access token never enters it.
  3. Every reconnect requests a new ticket. A ticket only opens streams for expires_in seconds; reconnecting with the old one after that is a 401.

What goes over the network, from the first stream to a drop after the ticket expired:

POST https://api.example.com/api/sse/ticket                   200  {"ticket":"eyJ…A","expires_in":60}
GET  https://api.example.com/api/sse/stream?ticket=eyJ…A      200  text/event-stream
     … 3 min later the network drops; 1 s backoff …
POST https://api.example.com/api/sse/ticket                   200  {"ticket":"eyJ…B","expires_in":60}
GET  https://api.example.com/api/sse/stream?ticket=eyJ…B      200  text/event-stream

An open stream does not drop when the ticket expires — the ticket only counts for opening. The reconnect is what needs a new one, and it asks for it.

Why useEventStream with a fixed URL does not work here

With useEventStream(`${API}/sse/stream?ticket=${ticket}`) the first stream opens, but the reconnect reuses the same string. If the network drops after 60 s, the backend answers 401 to every attempt, the stream spends its maxRetries on that and ends in "error" — with the user still signed in.

docs.title: Cookie session
docs.text:
If sign-in keeps the session in a cookie (AUTH_TOKEN_DELIVERY="cookie" on the backend), the ticket comes out the same way — only the client changes. POST /ticket is a write, so the cookie needs its CSRF pair:

import { createApiClient, useTicketEventStream } from "tempest-react-sdk";

const api = createApiClient({
    baseURL: "https://api.example.com",
    prefix: "/api",
    withCredentials: true,
    csrf: true,
});

export function Orders({ signedIn }: { signedIn: boolean }) {
    const { status } = useTicketEventStream<{ id: string; status: string }>({
        client: api,
        enabled: signedIn,
        onMessage: ({ data }) => console.log("order", data.id, data.status),
    });

    return <span>Stream: {status}</span>;
}

The cookie goes on POST /ticket (with X-CSRF-Token, echoed from the csrf_token cookie); GET /stream carries only the ticket. csrf details in HTTP → CSRF.

With an order changing status on the backend, the console shows:

order 8f2c paid
order 8f2c shipped

docs.title: When the ticket is refused
docs.text:
A ticket denied with a status no amount of waiting fixes is not retried: the stream goes straight to status: "error" and onUrlError receives the TempestApiError.

Ticket request failure What happens network, timeout, 429, 5xx retried with the usual backoff 401 (after the client's refresh) stops at "error" — the session is over 403 ACCOUNT_INACTIVE stops at "error" — account disabled response without ticket stops at "error" — contract differs from expected

The policy is isRetriableTicketError; pass shouldRetryUrl to replace it.

A disabled account, for instance, ends like this — a single request, no stream and no retry:

POST https://api.example.com/api/sse/ticket   403  {"detail":"…","code":"ACCOUNT_INACTIVE"}
status: "connecting" → "error"
onUrlError(error)  →  error.status === 403, error.code === "ACCOUNT_INACTIVE"

Prefix and parameter name

The defaults match the backend's make_sse_router: prefix: "/sse" and ticketParam: "ticket". If the router is mounted elsewhere, pass both. Outside React, createTicketEventStream({ client: api, ... }) does the same and returns the controller with close/reconnect/status.

docs.title: Switching accounts in the same tab — sessionKey
docs.text: The ticket opens the channel of the user who asked for it, and the backend checks the ticket only when the stream opens: neither logout nor refresh-token revocation ends a stream already open — it lives until the client leaves (checked in tempest-fastapi-sdk's make_sse_router and UserAuthService.sse_router). If the tab switches from user A to user B without enabled passing through false, A's stream keeps delivering A's events under B.

docs.title: With createTempestAuth's api: automatic
docs.text:
Since 0.82.0, when the client is the api that createTempestAuth built, the stream binds itself to that preset's session — you pass neither sessionKey nor enabled:

import { createTempestAuth, useTicketEventStream } from "tempest-react-sdk";

interface User {
    id: string;
}

const auth = createTempestAuth<User>({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com" });

export function Notices() {
    const { status, lastMessage } = useTicketEventStream<{ text: string }>({
        client: auth.api,
        onMessage: ({ data }) => console.log("notice", data.text),
    });

    return (
        <div>
            <span>Stream: {status}</span>
            {lastMessage && <p>{lastMessage.data.text}</p>}
        </div>
    );
}

The key is auth.sessionKey(): the lineage login() mints, kept across every token rotation and cleared when the session ends. What each event does to the stream:

Event Stream login() into another account (or the same one) in the tab closes the previous one, clears lastMessage, asks a ticket for the new session login or logout in another tab the same, as soon as the tab follows the storage token rotation (refresh(), 401 → refresh) nothing — same stream, same connection logout() or expired session closes and stays idle, without asking for a ticket nobody signed in on mount stays idle until the next login()

Measured with the mocked EventSource and backend in src/sse/session-auth.test.tsx (npx vitest run src/sse/session-auth.test.tsx): on main before this change, after login(B) A's stream was still the only EventSource, open.

Who keeps the old behaviour

A client createTempestAuth did not build — your own createApiClient, a wrapper, a spread copy — carries no session, and the stream follows only url, enabled and the sessionKey you pass. An explicit sessionKey always wins over the client's.

docs.title: With any other client: sessionKey
docs.text:
Pass the session identity as sessionKey and the hook takes care of it:
